-- THE JACKDAW AND THE RAVEN. (A FABLE.) A tame, precocious Jackdaw, fond of theft, Pounced on an oyster from the supper left, And thinking what a treat he had in store, Conned selfishly the bivalve o'er and o'er; But found when he to open !sully tried, The difficulty was to get inside. From such a dainty thus to be debarred, Seemed to the Jackdaw cruel and monstrous hard; But feeling much the need of something nice, Called in his friend the Raven for advice, In hopes that he by some effective way, Could to his hungry eyes the thing display. "My loving brother," said his sable friend, "My willing aid to you I'll quickly lend; No longer shall these shells your efforts mock, Just fly on high, and drop it on this rock." At once the Jackdaw, holding fast his prize, Rose in the air with loud triumphant cries; Then from his beak he let the oyster go, Crash on the rock some forty yards below; But sad to say, before he could descend, The dainty bit was swallowed by his friend!

(MORAL.) Don't hasty be in asking for advice, Before you know that friendship is the price; In ease by trusting to a pseudo-friend, You find yourself well bitten in the end. Leeds Weekly _Vercury. G. DE-NYS FAYERS.

The Firm for Dog Days—Doolittle and Swett. Learning by study must be won; 'Twas ne'er entailed from sire to son.—Gay Trials of every kind may await you, sterner and darker than any yet experienced. Do not anticipate them, but do not forget their possibility. When Jemima went to school she was asked why the noun "bachelor" was singular. "Because," she replied, "its so -very singular that they don't get mania," Discussion between a child and its tutor : "That star you see up there is bigger than this world." "No, it isn't." "Yes, it is." "Then why doesn't it keep the rain off ?" A quack doctor heads his advertisement: "Ho, all ye dyspeptics!" That's what dyspeptics won't do. If they would all hoe vigorously they might not need any medi- cine. "If ;it were customary in this country to confer titles upon individuals of rank in literature," asked a shallow but conceited journalist of an old one," what would I be ?" "Barren of ideas, my son," was the response. Faithful prayer always implies correlative exertion; and no man can ask honestly and hopefully to be delivered from temptation unless he has honestly and firmly determined to do the best he can to keep out of it.—John Ruskin. Charles 11. playing at tennis with a dignified Prebend who had struck the ball well, the former exclaimed, "That's a good stroke for a Dean." "I'll give it the stroke of a Bis- hop if your Majesty pleases," was the suggestive rejoinder. You must either soar or stoop, Fall or triumph, stand or droop; You must either serve or govern, Must be slave or must be sovereign; Must, in fine, be block or wedge, Must be anvil or be sledge.—Goethe.

A Judge and counsellor being upon indifferent terms, a client of the counsel's making his appearance at the bar with his jaw terribly swelled, the Judge remarked, "Mr. —, this client of yours would make an excellent coun- sellor, he's all jaw," which set the Court in a roar of laughter against the counsellor. On silence being restored, the counsel then remarked, "My Lord, I think he would make a better Judge, for his jaw is all on one side." The retort turned the laugh against the Judge, and from that day they were on the best terms of friendship. A man was accused of having stolen a pair of trousers. There were several witnesses, but the evidence was rather meagre, and so the accused was acquitted. He was told that he could go, but he remained. His lawyer, to whose success- ful defence he mainly owed his liberty, hinted to him again that he was free to depart, but still he stayed. There being no more cases to be heard, the Court was getting empty, when the lawyer, growing impatient, asked with some asperity why he didn't go. The innocent, injured man whispered in his ear, "The fact is, sir, I did not like to move till the witnesses had left the court." "Why so?' "Be- cause, sir, I have got on the trousers that I stole." A PLEA FOR OLD BACHELORS.—Ever since the days of Adam old bachelors have been the butt of everybody's ridicule; but there is a vast difference between Adam and the bachelors of our day. Adam could afford to marry— many bachelors nowadays cannot. What with crinoline, shawls, dresses, trinkets, and pin-money, it is no small undertaking at this age of the world. Again, Eve had no choice—it was Adam or nobody. She had no chance to get up a flirtation, for there was no one to flirt with. Seeing no other means of teasing her husband—a feminine peculiarity from that day to this—she ate the forbidden fruit. Give "old bachelors" the same chance Adam had, and my word for it, a majority of them would put on matri- mony in no time. Lepoon Ant.—The air we breathe indoors cannot be too often renewed nor too carefully regulated while sickness prevails; but more especially should the ventilation be at- tended to when that sickness is in the house in which we live. It gives a patient a far greater chance of life if, when ill, he is put in a room with a southern or south-western exposure—a room from which the carpet has been removed, the floor being kept spotlessly clean, and every unnecessary article of furniture taken away, and every curtain or bang- ing, that may collect dust, taken down. The room should have a cheerful appearance, nevertheless; nothing should be left a moment therein that may taint the atmosphere; and such a thing as a slop-pail should never be seen inside the door. A plentiful use of disinfectants should be made, and if the illness should be of an infectious character, a screen should be hung before the door, and kept damp with some disinfectant.—Cassell's Family Magazine. DRAWING INFERENCES.—" I liked your sermon very much to-day, with a single exception," said a worthy pastor to a young minister who had occupied his pulpit in the morn- ing. "Well what was the exception ? " "I think you use rather too much technical phrases. You repeatedly spoke of drawing inferences. Now, that was Greek to many hearers." "Surely, almost every one knows what we mean by drawing an inference." "You are mistaken. Ido not believe one-half of my congregation understand the phrase. Now, there is Mr. Smith," pointing out a man just turning the corner "who is quite an intelligent farmer; we will overtake him, and I will ask him if he can draw an inference, and Ido not believe that he will understand me." Accord- ingly, the two ministers quickened their pace, and as they came up to Mr. Smith, the vicar said to him, "Mr. Smith, can you draw an inference?" Well I suppose I could," was the doubting reply. "I've got a team of herses that can draw anything to which they are hitched ; but I shouldn't like to try them on A Sunday." THE OLDEST ALPINE TUNNEL.—Perhaps the oldest tunnel in the Alps in existence is the heading driven by the orders of Margrave Louis 11. of Saluzzo through Mont Viso, and constructed in the years 1472 to 1480. The passes over Mont Genevre and Mont Cenis, which before that time were the only means of communication between Northern Italy and Dauphine, are very difficult. Moreover, they entailed a very heavy expense upon the inhabitants of Salnzzo, and were, besides, frequently entirely closed to them, owing to constantly recurring border feuds. This state of things suggested to the Margrave the scheme of piercing a direct road through Mont Viso, connecting the valley of the Po with that of Queyras, opening on to the Durance. The negotiations entered into with the estates of Dauphine and King Louis XI. of France led in 1477 to a satisfactory arrangement, and the tunnel was completed a few years later by Martino d'Albano and Baltasar d'Alpiasco, at a total cost, including the paths leading to the respective openings, of 12,000 florins. The tunnel has a height of Wt., and an average width of Bft., and at the present time a length of only about 250 ft. It is stated, however, that, in conse- quence of frequent landslips, the openings of the tunnel have gradually receded, and that it may have had when first opened double its present length. The geological structure Of Mont Viso is similar to that of Mont Cenis, and fre- quent irruptions rendered repeated repairs necessary. Dur- ing times of war the tunnel has been frequently blocked, and even walled up; but Napoleon I. gave orders for its complete restoration.—Land. THE SCOTCH Lessm—One day in one of the crowded streets I met a poor young girl, who seemed utterly bewil- dered ; she stopped me to ask if I would tell her the name of the street she was in. Her accent was broad Scotch, and her look and air of perfect simplicity was, I perceived, not assumed, but genuine. I gave her the information she wanted, and asked her where she lived, and if she was in search of any friend's house. She said she did not live any- where in London ; she was but just arrived from Scotland and n , ew nobedv who had any house or lodging of their own in ',len, bet she was looking for a friend of the name of Peggy; and Petzte wea a Scotch girl, who was I. ere within a /rile of the pis** where she lived in Scotland. Peggy was in service in Loulon, and had written her direc- tion to some house in this street ; but the number of the , sat, seem to seemed try a house and the name of the mister or mistress had been for- gotten. The poor girl was deterreined she id every house, for she had come all the way from Scotland to see Peggy, and she had no other dependence. I hopeless ease. I was so much struck with her simplicity and forlorn condition that I could not leave her in this r- plexity, an utter stranger, as she evidently was, to rile dangers of London. I went with her, though I own with. out the slightest hope of her succeeding in the object of her search, knocked at every, door, and made inquiries at every house. When we came near the end of the street, she was

In despair, and cried bitterly -o.ne.--of the last doors opened, and as a footman was surlily beginning to answer my questions, she darted past him, exclaiming, " There's Peggy !" She flew along the passage to a servant girl, whose head had just appeared as she was coming upstairs. I never heard or saw stronger expressions of joy or affec- tion than at this meeting, and I scarcely ever, for any ser- vice I have been able in the course of my life to do for my fellow creatures, received such grateful thanks as I did from this poor Scotch lassie and her Peggy for the little assist- ance I afforded her.—Monoirs of R. div.head: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTICULTURE, &c.
div.p: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, &c.

LORD BICKLEY 2ND.—Among noteworthy facts at the recent Bath and West of England Show may be mentioned that Mr. S. Kidner's commended Devon bull, Lord Bickley 2nd, was stated to have been the eighteenth calf of its dam, whilst that dam also produced the famous Devon ox, which a few years ago took Champion plate at the Islington exhi- bition of the Smithfield Club. THE INSTITUTE OF AGRICULTURE.—The Council has ' established a scholarship which shall entitle the holder to ' free instruction in the Institute for one session. It will be awarded from year to year to that son of a tenant farmer who shall pass best in the advanced stage under the Govern- ment examination for the principles of agriculture in each succeeding Mry. It will be distinguished as the "Robert Brown Scholarship," to commemorate the labours of the late Robert Jeffreys Brown in his earnest endeavours to secure for farmers" sons a cheap education in agricultural science. Applications to be made to Professor Tanner, the hon. secretary of the Institute of Agriculture, South Ken- sington, not later than June 30 next, stating the examina- tion number of the applicant. Candidates for the first election may have been examined in May of this or any preceding year. INTERESTING EXPERIMENT WITH SILOS.—In the early spring of this year it was announced that Lord Tollemache had resolved to erect upon his Cheshire estates four silos, to demonstrate to the farmers of Cheshire the great economical advantages of preserving green fodder by the process of • en- silage for the winter and spring use of cattle and horses. These silos have been constructed upon the most economical plan, with a view to its adoption by tenant farmers, and on Wednesday they were inspected by Lord Tollemache and his son. If the material to be packed in the silos is properly treated—if, that is to say, it be cut into suitably short lengths and bewail compressed so as to exclude all air from it —there need be no fear as to the results when the silos come to be opened in October or November next. The experi- ment undertaken by Lord Tollemache is very important, and if it should prove successful there can be no doubt that it will lead to nothing less than a revolution in the method of agriculture, not only in Cheshire but in other large sections of the United Kingdom. WAYGOING TENANTS AND THE GROUND GAME ACT.—A somewhat novel point.under the Ground Game Act formed the subject of an inquiry lately, and as it refers closely to a point of law which may probably arise in numerous in- stances in the case of outgoing tenants at Michaelmas next, it may prove instructive and useful to agents, more espe- cially as we believe the legal opinion given to be one on which strict reliance can be placed. A tenant has recently left a farm held under the Agricultural Holdings Act; he alleges that hares and rabbits are damaging his waygoing crops, and he asks whether he has the legal right to kill and shoot them. The answer given is that the tenant has still all the rights given by the Ground Game Act to an "occu- pier," and that he can exercise them, presuming that he is entitled by lease or custom to the waygoing crops. In such a case, the law considers him still to be the occupier of the fields in which the waygoing crops are growing. In the words of Baron Parke :—" The outgoing tenant remains in possession until all is done which he has a right to do in respect of that crop."—Land Agents' Record. IMPORTATION OF LIVE CATTLE.-1 letter from Mr. Thornton in The Times says that :—" In Great Britain last year 32,313,371 acres were under cultivation, with 5,807,491 head of cattle. In Ireland, 15,212,390 acres were culti- vated, with 3,986,847 cattle; showing in Great Britain one head to about every a acres; and in Ireland—a country whose soil, climate, and people seem naturally adapted for cattle rearing—has one head to every four acres; while the little island of Jersey, whose cultivated area is 20,550 acres, has 11,299 head of cattle, or about one to every 11 acre. Surely, if it be possible in so small an island as Jersey to raise so large a supply of live stock, it is possible to in- crease our numbers in this country and in Ireland." "Some years ago," says Mr. Thornton "I stated in The Times that every year I sold between 2,000 and 3,000 head of cattle for breeding purposes throughout England and Scotland, and about 200 in Ireland. Consequently my experience among the farmers of the country enables me to state that the opinion of breeders is that the losses arising from foot and mouth disease are the great hindrance to more cattle being bred at home. Directly it attacks breeding herds the milk supply diminishes, and it becomes unfit for food; the cow frequently aborts her calf, and, should the calf be born alive, it grows up puny and delicate; often, too, the cow fails to produce another calf. This season the prices of store cattle, especially in Ireland, have reached unheard-of prices. They are chiefly brought to this country for grazing, the public having no confidence to risk a whole year's profit in breeding. In 1880 the action of the Privy Council had so reduced the disease that for some months it actually ceased. The outbreak which has occurred since then has been clearly and distinctly traced to an importation of cattle from a foreign country in which disease was known to exist. The foreign supply is estimated by the chief authorities at about 6 per cent. to our home supply, and so long as our prices are better than those which can be obtained in foreign coun- tries, the law of supply and demand will regulate their im- portation either in a live or dead state. With a slight in- crease of cattle per acre—of even one and a half instead of one head to every 4- arres—the result would soon be appa- rent in a reduction in the price of beef as well as in butter and cheese,:and of a greater and cheaper supply of milk for our children."

i ABORTION IN EWES.—At a recent meeting of the Lin- colnshire Agricultural Society, it was resolved:—" That in consequence of the loss suffered by farmers from abortion amongst ewes, the Royal Agricultural Society of England be asked to send down a competent person and advise therein." This was brought before the Veterinary Com- mittee of the Royal Agricultural Society, and, on their recommendation, the Council decided—" That application be made to the Royal Veterinary College to allow Professor Axe to make inquiry into the subject, and to report to the Veterinary Committee." . In compliance with the above resolution, Professor Axe has accordingly sent out a series of questions, With a request for answers as full and accurate as possible. Professor IV. A.'s address is Royal Veterinary College, Camden Town, N.W. The following are the ques- tions :

1. State if the land over which your ewes have run, since Sept. last, is high or low. 2. Describe the nature of the soil and sub- soil. 3. State (A) what number of ewes you out to the ram, (8) their breed, (C) their age. 4. When were they put to the ram? 5. On what kind of food were they tipped? 6. Did they suffer from any disease such as foot rot, liver rd. foot and-mouth disease, &c., immediately prior to or utter leaving the tun; and, if so, to what extent. 7. Describe fully the winter feed of the past season, and state if it 'has been in accordance with your cus- tom of former years. 8. Mention the kind of manure employel for your turnip crop. 9. Did your turnips continue sound through the winter? 10. If on roots, state if your ewes "eat their way," or followed other sheep. 11. What percentage of your ewes were barren? 12. It is not the quantity of the meat, but the cheerfulness of the guests, which makes the feast. WHAT SHALL WE PLAT ?—The Mayor.—A-great deal of amusement is often to be got out of the clever replies re- quired in this game. The leader pompously assumes the office of mayor, and calls upon each of the other players to select some trade, business, or profession, and to impress his choice upon his memory. This being done, the mayor ad- dresses, according to his own fancy, any member by the title he has taken, as for instance : "Master Cobbler, I called at your house, but you were not at home. Where were you ? " 'the cobbler must reply instantly, "I was at the tailor's," or any other that he selects. The tailor cries out instantly, "What for ? " The cobbler must at once furnish some suitable reason, such as, " To buy a coat," adding, "But where were you ? " The tailor replies, "At the baker's." The baker must quickly ask," What for?" The game thus continues, compelling everyone to be on the alert, as all failures are punished with forfeits. Any player may say that he was at the mayor's, who must instantly ask, "What for ? " This generally provokes an amusing .reply, and the mayor then starts the round again. HOGARTH AND CALAIS GATE.—The municipality of talaia are carrying out their scheme for levelling the forti- ecattans about their town, and so extending its limits to in- ch:tat the neighbouring and much larger suburb of St. Platte. The deep, surrounding fosses, filled with stagnant, pestilent waters, are also to be removed. At the Peace of Paris of 1815 some Nottingham lacentakers, settling in the then little village of St. Pierre, set up there a tulle manu- factory, which now employs dpwards of 10,000 hands, being one-third of the total suburban population, and nearly equal to that of Calais itself. It is proposed to erect be- tween Calais and St. Pierre a great central railway station or flare, a theatre, and a large hotel de tale. With the de- fences will disappear the old gate and drawbridge which forms a background for Hogarth's "0, the Roast Beef of Old England I" engraved by him and Moseley in the year 1749. Soon after the second Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle ' custody or (1748), Hogarth crossed over to France but his journey came to an abrupt end at the port of landing. Taken into While sketching at Calais Gate, he was led before the ties, who placed him and his sketch-book under a searching examination. They thereupon committed Hogarth to the charge of one Grandsire, his landlord, who undertook that he should not quit his lodgings except to embark for Enßland.—Builder. VEGETABLES. - Onions will require thinning, which should not be done in a haphazard way. It is as well in the first instance to draw all the weakest and those that touch each other. The final thinning may thus be left a few days longer, when all should be removed so as to leave the crop even, and at a distance of 6in. apart in the rows. Those who wish to have a few to draw daily will not have to re- sort to this general thinning. We would point out that there is much mischief done to the onion bed by allowing anyone to draw out of it indiscriminately, as it frequently occurs that everyone makes for the largest at each visit. Onions are easily transplanted, so that if it is desirable to inorease the supply it can readily be done. In transplant- ing, avoid the error of putting them in the ground any deeper than they were previously. Beetroot is also sus- ceptible of being transplanted, and should be drawn with care for the purpose. They must also be inserted their full length and straight down in the ground, and supplied with water immediately after to settle the soil around them. Assuming the rows to be about 10in, apart, the plants in the rows should be Bin. Parsnips, if a foot between the rows, must be Bin. or 10in, from plant to plant in the row; but, unlike onions and beetroot, they do not do so well &Ars- planted ; neither do carrots, and in thinning these we pro- ceed very cautiously, and simply reduce them so as to avoid any crowding. We lose so many, as a rule, through the carrot grub, that we dare not be too venturesome. Broad beans should be stopped, and if part is served so now and the remainder later on, a longer succession will be the result. We make it a rule to stop some as soon as there are signs of the lowest pods forming. If there is an accumula- tion of black fly, usually called "Dolphin," we commit the tops to the fire. Scarlet runners will submit to stopping with advantage where the supports are not sufficiently , long, or otherwise weak at the top. By practising con- tinual stopping at 3ft. or 4ft., they can be grown by the aid of sticks such as are used for peas, and their produce I will be but slightly diminished. The spring-sown Parsley will require thinning, and the surplus, if required, will suc- ceed if transplanted. The plants are best if regulated so that they do not touch each other. THE STRAWBERRY BED.—This will now require attention, and some provision mast be made to protect them from getting gritty through being splashed by heavy rainfalls. We shall enumerate some of the protecting materials used for this purpose, leaving the reader to select that which is most accessible and commensurate with the contents of his pocket. Litter from the stable is the material usually em- ployed, and, where the price does not militate against it, there is nothing to surpass it for cleanliness and durability. Bracken or the common fern dried is used in those parts where it is so abundant that it only requires getting. In wet weather it soon decays. It has one advantage over litter—therelis no fresh supply of weeds introduced into the garden by its use. Bark from the tan-yard answers the purpose so long as the weather is moderately fine. In wet seasons it soon becomes, from frequent vtreading, inter- mingled with the soil, which is very disappointing, as its , services are nil when most required. Spent -bops have fre- quently been called in use, and are on a par with the tan. Small growers have before now used bushy branches of the desired height. These, after being trimmed, are so many forked sticks, and in their auxiliaries the strawberries are placed to rest. The end of the branch should be pointed so as to go readily into the ground. Heather or ling does for the shorter trussed varieties. Birch, or old birch brooms pulled to pieces, as well as the twiggy branches of thebeech, will do for all sorts. If it is requisite to increase the breadth of strawberry plants, all runners from outside rows may be drawn outwards before any material is laid between, and , when they are sufficiently advanced they should be pegged i down or a small stone laid on each to preserve it in its place until well rooted. Plants attended to in this manner will produce a fair crop the following season, if attended to as we shall direct later on. Tax FRONT GARDEN.—Sweet. Williams and wallflowers will now be sufficiently advanced to pridk out. To econo- mise space, they may be inserted two or three inches dis- tant at present. Plants treated in this way grow sturdy and are more adapted to withstand the severity of the winters. Seed from self-sown wallflower germinate and come up abundantly some seasons, and this is one of them. , They are much in advance of those we have sown this ' spring. Myosotis or forget-me-not is:also produced abun- dantly from self-sown seed. So that when once it is intro. duced into a garden there will be always a supply, unless it is deliberately cut up by the hoe or continually disturbed by the rake. Now that the seeds are maturing, cut some shoots off and shake over the surface of the soil in one corner, and insert a stick to indicate their position. They require no covering, but may be gently pressed with the foot. In this way they are more likely to remain uninjured, and they can at the proper time be planted in regular order whenever they are required. Everything should now be done to make the front garden as attractive as possible, for the season of many of the plants is only short. The sur- face of the soil should be kept nice and fresh by hoeing or raking. Remove all decayed leaves and flowers, so as to give the whole a neat appearance.

THE 'Wmpow.—Fuchsias intended for exhibition should have special treatment, so as to have them at their best at the desired time. About eight weeks before the date of the show they should be moved to larger pots, and, in a few days after, the points of the shoots may be pinched by re- moving only the first pair of leaves. Geraniums of the zonale section should have similar treatment, and all the flower buds should be removed until a month before the show. It is obvious that any flowers about to expand now would be over before a month's time, and to allow them to remain is simply exhausting the energies of the plants. The appearance of geraniums and fuchsias at shows leads us to think that this point is frequently overlooked by others who are supposed to be better informed in such matters than the cottager.

There was once an elephant in a circus, and one day a boy said to him, "Want a lump of sugar, old fellow?" The elephant nodded, and felt real grateful, for elephants are very fond of lump sugar, which is what they live on in their native forests. But the boy put a cigar instead of a lump of sugar in his mouth. The sagacious animal, instead of eating up the cigar or trying to smoke it and making himself dreadfully sick, took it and carried it across the cir- cus to a man who kept a candy and cigar stand, and made signs that he'd sell the cigar for twelve lumps of sugar. The man gave the elephant the sugar and took the cigar, and then the intelligent animal sat down on its hind-legs and laughed at the boy who had tried to play a joke on him, until the boy felt so much ashamed that he went right home and went to bed. A SAGACIOUS DOCI.—A neighbour of ours is the owner of a very curious dog, whose appearance does not especially re- commend him, for he is the most awkward-shaped black- and-tan terrier I have seen, but very sagacious. It is the custom of this animal to accompany his master to the sta- tion in the morning, frequently crossing the river with him to Tilbury. When his master wishes to part company with him, he makes a bow and says, "Good morning, Snap," whereupon "Snap" drops his tail and toddles back to the steamer, lands at Gravesend, and finds his way home. In the evening he knows the time his master is likely to return, and will go down to meet him, frequently taking passage in the boat, and awaiting his arrival at Tilbury. He also at- tends his mistress when she goes shopping in the town, and should he happen to miss her, runs round to all the places at which she is in the habit of calling. Should his first "call" not be successful, he will continue his search else- where. THE is appointed head of the family. He may rule by love, but it is his right and duty to rule; and to him, as the monarch'of that little state, must be the last appeal. Hence he appears before his children invested with authority—that divinely appointed representative of law— and if he worthily sways the sceptre over his little realm he develops in his children some of the most desirable traits of character. If love is one of the elements of family hap- piness, order is another; and it is his, in the last appeal, to support order. If the sympathies and affections of children should be developed, so should their spirit of obedience to rightful authority; and it is to develop that spirit. It is undoubtedly desirable to raise the mother's authority to the highest degree, and when the father is what he should be, and does what he should do, she stands invested in the eyes of her children with a power combining indirect reverence for the father, who appears only to sustain material rule, with direct obedience to her own gentle fondness. CRIMINAL INGPsurrv.—The ingenuity displayed in some of the instruments devised by coiners and burglars, often involving the application of elaborate scientific principles, and the patient industry and perseverance with which nefarious schemes are matured and carried out, are qualities which, in their legitimate exercise, would realise for their possessor an income beyond any gains that his unlawful endeavours can bring, even were these devoid of risk and not liable to failure. We read for instance, of a clipping machine by means of which the body of a sovereign is separated from the "milled" rim which encircles it, a thin slice out of the centre, leaving the two faces intact, the loss supplied by an amalgam, and the coin then dexterously put together again, so that the weight nor the " ring " of it is greatly altered. One would imagine that the amount of gold thus obtained would hardly cover the working expenses; at best, the profit must yield a much lower per-centage on the in- vested capital than what it would return in honest business. It is surprising also to note what a charm small frauds have for people not usually included in the criminal classes; and nowhere is this exemplified to a greater extent than in the passion for petty smuggling which seems inherent in the breast of travelling humanity. Men who would scorn to make an imperfectly obliterated postage-stamp do duty a second time, and whose integrity in all other affairs of life is unimpeachable, will plot and plan all sorts of cunning devices by which they may cheat Her Majesty's Custom House, and will even spend more in "tips" to elude the vigilance of the officers in" running" cigars and spirits which they do not want than they would have to pay for legal duty. Possibly the law's delay—or the delay which it occasions —may afford some cause, if not excuse, for this; the weary waiting and vexation of soul attending the baggage-search being the most disagreeable incident of the voyage.— Chamber's Journal.

OUSE OF LORDS.—MomeAT. THE DECEASED WIFE'S SISTER BILL, &C. The Sea Fisheries Bill and the Criminal Law Amendment Bill passed through Committee. Their Lordships in Committee, on the Marriage with a Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, agreed to an amendment providing that marriages under the bill should not be solemnised in churches of the Establishment.—The other amendments which the Earl of Dalhousie had pro- mised to introduce, having been agreed to, Earl BEAUCHAMP intimated that on the motion for the third reading he will move the rejection of the bill.—The Alcester and Wolseley Bills were read a third time and passed. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. SCOTCH BUSINESS.—The PRIME MINISTER stated that the Home Secretary would on Thursday ask leave to bring in a bill providing for the arrangement of Government business in Scotland. SOUTH AFRICA.—The affairs of South Africa were intro- duced by Sir M. Ificits-Baaca, who asked for the name of the High Commissioner to be sent out and for the instruc- tions that would be given to him.—Mr. GLADSTONE ex- plained that since the Government determined to send a Commissioner a telegram had been received which met or anticipated the proposal. The Transvaal Government pro- posed to send representatives to England to consider the subject, and the Government had intimated that they were willing to receive a deputation in London, including the President and Vice-President of the Transvaal. THE TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT.—In answer to Mr. Broadhurst, Mr. Grans-roam said it was the old prac- tice of Parliament at the beginning of the present century to meet some time in May, take a considerable vacatioa at Christmas, and prorogue at the beginning ef June. The question whether they should revert to it was one of con- siderable interest and importance, especially to members of the House of Commons. It had been a good deal discussed in private, but very little in the House. He was not at all sure of the condition of members' minds on the subject, but it was plainly a question for the House, and it would pro- bably be the duty of the Government not to raise it unless they felt well satisfied that the desire of the House was in favour of the change. TEE SUEZ Caßat..—Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply to another question, made an important statement as to the Suez Canal. "A comparison of views" has been taking place between the Government and the Canal Company on all points that are likely to be raised, and in many agreement exists, but there is not yet complete harmony in regard to the "amount and time for a reduction of rates upon the canal." It was im- possible to speak in detail as to this or other points of divergence, but before the Government arrived at any agree- ment they would make a full statement in Parliament, with a view to being put in possession of the information and experience of the commercial community. NEW MEMBER.—Mr. S. Buxton took the oath and his seat on his election for Peterborough. The honourable member was greeted with cheers from the Ministerial side. THE CORRUPT PRACTICES BILL.—The House then re- sumed Committee on the Corrupt Practices Bill, and passed Clause 5 after a prolonged discussion on a proposal by Sir W. Dyke giving the alternative of summary conviction with imprisonment not exceeding four months, and a fine not exceeding £5O. for persons convicted on indictment of Corrupt Practices.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL undertook to consider on Clause 40 whether it was possible to endow a local tribunal with the power of summary conviction.—The amendment was negatived, and the clause passed.—On Clause 6, which declares certain expenditure to be illegal, including payment for conveyance of electors to or from the poll, Mr. H. FOWLER proposed an amendment with the object of relaxing the prohibition against hiring convey- ances for the conveyance of voters to the 'boll, so as to place the less aristocratic candidate on footing and nearer equality with his opponent who could command the use of many private carriages.—After a long discussion the amend- ment was withdrawn.—The Committee was still engaged on Clause 6 when progress was reported. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TITESDAY. The Earl of BEDESDALE proposed to carry out the deci- sion of the House of Commons by passing a New Standing Order permitting railway companies to pay interest out of capital during the construction of their lines.—A debate fol- lowed, but their Lordships determined not to take any action in the matter.—Lord CARLINGFORD stated that Mr. Dobson had by no means given up the hope of passing the Rivers Conservency Bill this session. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. THE INFORMER CAREY.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND stated that although James Carey had written a letter stating that he should take his seat again in the Dublin Town Council, he had not yet received any pardon for the murders of which he had declared himself guilty, and that be might be legally tried for the offences. THE WELSH EDUCATION BILL—The PRIME MINISTER promised that the Welsh Higher Education Bill should be introduced as soon as possible, but held out no hope that it would be passed this session. THE DISTURBANCE AT CURRAGH CAMP.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON, referring to the disturbance at the Curragh Camp, stated that the affair had been much magnified by the newspapers, as no fire arms were used and no men were killed. THE CORRUPT PRACTICES BILL.—The chief business of the sitting was the further consideration of the Corrupt Practices Bill in committee, and with this measure progress was again very slow. Discussion was resumed on clause 6, declaring expenditure on the conveyance of electors to the poll illegal, and an amendment proposed by Mr. Stanton was defeated by 163 to 68 votes. The next point raised was as to payment to electors for the exhibition of ad- dresses, bills, banners, and so forth, and the provision of the bill in this respect having been confirmed, discussion turned upon the restriction of caedidates' committee rooms and the action of political associations. In the end the provision of the bill was again confirmed by a majority of 214 to 122. Then Mr. Cowen proposed to restrict the use of private carriages at elections, and the debate on this point was in I progress when the sitting was suspended. On the House resuming in the evenings count out at once took place. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The proceedings were of an exceptionally uninteresting and lifeless character, and it was with considerable difficulty that a house was kept for a sitting of little more than three hours.—The sccond reV.ing of the Irish Reproductive Loan Fund Act Amendment Bill was moved by Mr. O'KELLY, and was accepted by the Government, Mr. TREVELYAN intimat- ing that he would suggest some amendments in committee. —Mr. ANDERSON'S bill to obolish the imprisonment for debt which takes place ostensibly under commi' tals for coa- tempt of court was withdrawn on the ground that the sub- ject had been more adequately dealt with in the Bankruptcy Bill. The same hon. member also withdrew his bill on the banking laws of Scotland.—Mr. HASTINGS moved the second, reading of the Infectious Diseases Notification Bill, and dur- ing the debate upon it the House was counted out. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIILMSDAY. THE DECEASED WIFE'S SISTER BILL THROWN OUT.— The Lords have thrown out the Marriage with a Deceased Wife's Sister Bill. The third reading of the measure was formally moved to-night by the Earl of Dalhousie, upon which the Duke of Marlborough moved, as an amendment, that it be read a third time that day six months. Three bishops—Winchester, Lincoln, and Exeter—took part in the debate, and when a division was taken there appeared 140 for the third reading and 145 against. The announce- of the numbers was received with loud cheers. The Pri- mate and sixteen of the bishops voted in the majority against the bill. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY. Lord E. FITZMAURICE stated that communications of a friendly character bad been received from different foreign I Powers, in reference to Lord Granville's proposals as to the Suez Canal.—Mr, TREVELYAN, referring to the American statement about the landing of Irish paupers in New York, said there had been a great deal of exaggeration in the matter.—Mr. GLADSTONE intimated that it was the intention of the Government, on Monday next, to ask for the whole of the remaining Tuesday sittings for Government business. He also stated that it was not intended to proceed with the Committee on the Ballot Act Continuance Bill, until the Corrupt Practices Bill had passed through Committee.— The Marquis of HARTINGTON told Mr. O'Kelly that he had no information as to the rumoured attack on British troops on the Afghan frontier.—The House discussed the Army Estimates in Committee.

COLLISION IN THE CHANNEL. TWENTY-FIVE LIVES LOST. A disastrous collision is reported to have occurred on Friday, in the English Channel, between two ships, both belonging to the New Zealand Shipping Company. The Waitara, bound for Wellington, at the Antipodes, with a general cargo and some passengers, sunk shortly after the crash, which was a double one, and twenty-five lives were lost. Most of those on board were happily saved by clambering on to the other vessel, the Hurunni, by which the Waitara was run down. The former vessel, which was bound for Otago, sustained considerable damage. Both vessels had been towed into the Channel, but their respec- tive tugs had cast off prior to the collision. The following official statement in respect to the disaster ha.; been furnished by the New Zealand Shipping Company; "The ship Waitara, K. Webster master, left Gravesend on Tuesday, 19th Inst., in charge of a pilot and in tew of the tug Victoria botind for Wellington, New Zealand, with a full cargo Victoria, 16 passengers, and a crew of 25 hands all told. The tug was let go off Beachy Head, and the ship proceeded down channel under sail at 10 p.m. On Friday, the 22nd inst., a vessel was reported on the star- board bow, and before the course of the Waitara was altered struck her amidships, rebounded, and struck her again in front of the poop, cutting her below the water's edge and causing her to fill and sink immediately. For a moment the headgear of the colliding vessel, the Hurunni, became en- tangled in the mizen rigging of the Waitara, and by this means some of the crew and passengers saved their lives. An attempt was made by the chief officer and some hands to launch a boat from the Waitara, but the ship sank so rapidly that they failed to do so. The Hurunni was brought to immediately, and the boats lowered to pick up survivors. The following were saved; Mrs. Check, W. Noble, L. B. Dale, and 11. G. Russell, cabin passengers; H. T. Middleton, chief officer; H. Self, Carpenter; Hyde boats- wain; Cutten, steward ; Worsley, apprentice Arnold, Davis, Williams, Paterson, Sunderland, A.B's •, and K. Web- ster, master. The following were drowned : Mr. Check, the Misses Haylor, two young lady passengers, and A. Noble, cabin passenger; eight steerage passengers, and 13 of the crew, including Mr. Saunders, second officer; the chief steward, Stock and Cattrell (apprentices). Both ships were owned by the New Zealand Shipping Company, and bo th were bound for New Zealand, and left Gravesend the same day. The Hurunni is being towed back to London."

[l33f ANGLO-SCOTUS.) If I recollect aright, Newtonian" in one of his letters complained of The Examiner compositors leaving a space out between two of his words, and so damaging the sense. I will not charge him with being too particular, so will re- late an incident of the "leaving out" order that may con- sole him. Only the other day a journal devoted to insurance matters gave an account of a trial for arson, in which a couple of females, one of them being a widow, were con- cerned. One of the witnesses, whose evidence is reported in full, should have been made to say "that he had seen a light burning in the window all night." But the composi- tor left a consonant out of the sentence, and the consequence was that there duly appeared in print a description of a candlestick such as human beings had possibly never before seen or heard of. Beloe, in his " Anecdotes of Literature," states that the book which is distinguished by the greatest number of errata on record is that containing the works of Pica Mirandula, printed at Strasburg in 1507, by a printer of the name of Knoblouch. The errata of this volume occupy fifteen folio pages. The elder Disraeli records how, in connection with the criticism of a polyglot Bible, edited by Abraham Ecchel- lensis, the omission by the printer of the first o from the word " oculo," in a letter written by Flavigny, moved the first named to accuse the last named individual of "an enormous crime;" and they straightway began to apply to each other such epithets as "impious," "obscene," Sac. I don't want to wring anyone's withers, but I may as well confess to " Newtonian " that the influence of the satanic imp was very nearly making me assert the existence of a most wonderful kind of pasture, the admittance to which would have gladdened the heart of the celebrated Newton cow. The P.D., we know, made " Newtonian " assert that "he liked an etnetic, if not too strong." The P.D. also made it appear as if I suggested that staid Newtonians should " thump " the Devil with the body of a rooster. A person who liked an emetic, or one who took tricks (meta- phorically or otherwise) by thumping around with the. body—dead or alive—of an old rooster, would indeed be a novelty. But I am digressing, and must bark back, in case I make a hash of my subject But there, I fancy I hear some of the readers of The Examiner sarcastically saying that as a rule Scotchneen are good at a hash, either in its concoction or consumption. Possibly the compositor in question went to sleep on a sup. per of stewed giblets, and woke up the next morning slightly fowl-foggy after dreamitig all night about cock-lore. The influence of the male rooster certainly is considerable, so the comp.'s fog is excusable. A cock assured Themistocles of his victory over Xerxes. Aristophanos tells us that roosters reigned supreme over Persia before the time of Darius and Megabazus. Numa Pompilius was inspired by a cock, and Romulus was influenced by the same bird in his decision as to the site of Rome. It was sacred to Mars, Apollo, Mercury, and lEsculapius. Mohammed found a huge representative of the bird in the first heaven. The Moslem doctors say that Allah lends a willing ear t 3 him who reads the Koran, to him who prays for pardon, and to the cock, whose chant is divine melody. I don't know about the "divine melody;" nor can I vouch for the assertion that when cocks cease to crow the day of judgment will be at hand. But I am not surprised to find metaphorical allusions to the bird bothering printers, seeing that it is on record that an African tribe complains bitterly that it was all through the cock that they have remained black, and different from the rest of mankind. The great creating Spirit, it is said, set himself during the daytime to model the human race. By sundown he had fashioned about fifty different figures out of clay, but they were all more or less brown, and some of them were quite black. He set them up in a row, and then it appeared that they would look better if they were white. So he mixed a pot of whitewash, and set about daubing them by the light of the moon. But he did not get on very fast, and when he had a score or more to whiten, day dawned, and the cock crew. He came to the conclusion that the rest mast remain as they were. And so it has come to pass that some of the races of mankind are red and brown, while the poor negro has remained quite black—and all through a trouble- some cock, who would crow when he was not wanted. Moral :—lf the negro does not complain about being done out of his share of the whitewash, why should "Newtonian" or I grumble at the omission of a space, or the substitution of one letter for another.

P.S.—Since the foregoing was written I find that some of the sporting prophets have become inoculated with the P. D. spirit. As the Newton races are just over their "difference" may prove interesting to readers of The Examiner. 4' Pegasus," of the News of the World, says:—"The sporting writer in Truth and the compiler of 'notions' in the Referee have afforded their readers a little novel amuse- ment. I reprint the foliowing for the edification of our country readers. The Referee, haviir, commented upon the supposed withdrawal of Tristan for the Orange Cup—a race for which he could not have been entered, foreign ownership. being a bar to his admission—Truth came out with the fol- lowing :—" There are some writers on turf subjects who, ap- parently, desire to obtain a reputation for discernment by spelling everything backwards.' One of these pretentious twaddlers indulges in an elaborate sneer against Mr. Lefevre for not having run Tristan against Barcaldine for the Orange Cup. If the writer who censures the withdrawal of Tristan had taken the trouble to read the conditions of the stake, he would have discovered that Mr. Lefevre's *horse was never engaged." Having thus freely expressed himself, the Truth "blunderer" remarked that "he hoped that nothing would occur to prevent the meeting of Barcaldine and Tristan in the Goodwood Cap." Had the Truth writer concluded with this "hope" his ideas would probably have met with general approval, but evi- dently sorry for having made such a "fussy" reference to the Referee error, he made ample amends by committing a blue- der in the very opposite direction, as follows :—" It is un- fortunate that Border Minstrel has not been entered fdto the Goodwood trophy, as he would then have an opportunity of showing whether he is really a great horse. There was no- thing iu his Vase victory to justify the extravagant eulogies of which he has since been the subject." If the Truth writer had "taken the trouble to peruse the entries and con- ditions of the Cup," he would have discovered that BORDER MINSTREL is entered for the race, and I shall take this early opportunity of suggesting that the "eulc;gies of which he has been the subject" are net "extravagant," and I shall not be surprised if he lowers the colours of Tristan and Barcaldine over the 4-- miles at Goodwood, Border Minstrel being in re- ceipt of 2st 51b from the former and 2st 2113 from the latter."

div.head: SAD SUICIDE NEAR NEWTON.
div.p: SAD SUICIDE NEAR NEWTON.
DROWNED IN A RAIN-TUB.

The suicide of William Hindley, a retired farmer residing in Bolton-road, between Newton and Lowton, which took place on Sunday morning last under circumstances of a sad character, has given rise to many expressions of sorrow on the part ot the residents of the neighbourhood. It seems that the deceasd, who was 73 years of age, was married for the second time some three years since, but his wife died about eight weeks ago. Since then the old gentleman has been in a very desponding state of mind. The only occu- pants of the house were himself, a son (the latter only two years old), and a housekeeper named Betsy Hindley Howard, and when the deceased retired to bed about half-past nine on Saturday night last he appeared to be in his usual health. He occupied a bedroom alone, and nothing further was heard of him until the following morning. Shortly before half-past five Miss Glover, residing in a neigLbouring house, looked through her bedroom window, and, to her surprise, saw a man with his head and shoulders in a tub placed against the house-side for the pur- pose of catching the rain-water. Two tubs were standing to- gether,and the deceased was laid over the top of one and had his head and shoulders in the other. She hastily called a neighbour named Mat. Wainright, coachman to Mr. Nichol, and he proceeded to the spot and pulled the body out of the water. It was found _to be that of Mr. Hindley, and it was carried to his home. Or. Worsley, of Golborne was sent for, but of course his services were unavailing, as the poor fellow was quite dead.—An inquest was held at the Bull's Head, Lowton, on Tuesday afternoon, before Mr. T. W. Barker, the district coroner. The following evidence was given :—Betsy Hindly Howard stated that she had been the housekeeper to the deceased for the last three months. She noticed nothing strange about him when he went to be bed about his usual time on the previous Saturday night. She heard nothing of him again until his body was brought home a little after five o'clock on Sunday morning. He was partly dressed and had on part of an old suit of clothes. She had no doubt he committed suicide..—Miss Glover stated that she resided near the house of the deceased, and at a quarter past five on Sunday morning she looked out of the bedroom window. She saw a man, who afterwards turned out to be the deceased, leaning over one of two water-butts in the yard and his head and shoulders were in the other, which was full of water. She immediately raised an alarm and , called Matthew Wainwright, who came at once and pulled , the deceased out of the tub. He was quite dead.—Tbe jury ' returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased committed 11 suicide while in a state of temporary insanity.

PALMY DAYS (Cassell and Co., Limited).—This is the title of the extra holiday number of Cassell's Family Magazine, and its contents will be found suited to a variety of tastes. The lovers of fiction may spend a pleasant hour or two in per- using the numerous stories, not the least interesting being The Bride of a Day ;" for the poetically inclined " Happi- ness" will have its charms ; " Child, amidst the Flowers of Play," cannot fail to give enjoyment to readers possessing a taste for music; and to those who are about to select a resort for spending their summer holiday, we commend the contributions on "Some Pretty Points of Manxland Scenery;" " The Isle of Beauty," and "Third-class through Spain," combined with " Hints about the Summer Holi- day," by a family doctor. We must not omit to mention " We two 'on a Sociable," an article descriptive of the tour of a lady and gentleman on a double tricycle through some of the choicest scenery in England. " Pic-nic Dain- ties" is an appropriate paper, and not less so is " The Life of a Booking Clerk." "Palmy Days" is, on the whole, ex- cellently got up, ani it will prove a good companion alike by road, rail, and the seaside. It fully maintains the credit of this enterprising company.

Seven lives have been lost by the inundations in Silesia, and immense damage has been done to property. The remains of Bishop Colenso were irrerred at Maritz- burg on Friday. The death of the right rev, prelate ap- pears to have caused a profound sensation throughout the colony. Reports of the destructive ravages of the locusts con- tinue to be received from various districts of South Russia, Taurida, and the Don. In Melitopol 9,000 acres have been fired and the crops destroyed by the despairing inhabitants in order to arrest and stamp out the pest. The West African mail brings details of the fighting on the Small Boom river. The engagement at Jalliah appears to have been severe, but our troops. both West Indian and native, when once inside the stockades, made very short work of their opponents, of whom a great number were slaughtered.

TONQUIN.-A telegram to the Standard from Hong Kong states that severe fighting is imminent in Tonquin. The Annarnese occupy entrenched positions and are well armed. The French will attack immediately on the arrival of their reinforcements. The Governor of Cochin China has ex- pelled from the colony the representatives of the Annaraite Government, who are alleged to be in connection with secret societies hostile to France. It is reported from Damietta that out of 42 deaths which occurred there on Monday, 23 were from cholera, and the remainder are suspected to have been due to the same cause. Strict gaarantine is being enforced at Alexandria against all arrivals from Damietta by sea, and railway communication with that port is suspended. Cases of cholera are reported from Mansura, a considerable town on the Nile, and there is much reason to fear that the epidemic will spread.

NEWS FROM THE SOUDAN.—There are several interesting items of news from the Soudan. The native tribes are sub- mitting on all hands to the national troops. The report of the mixed commission appointed by the Council of ,Minis- ters to examine the scheme for the construction of a railway from Suakin to the Soudan recommends that the line should follow the most direct course between Suakin and Berber. The native who some time ago murdered three Europeans has been condemned to death by court-martial, and his four accomplices have been sentenced to various terms of im- prisonment with hard labour. DEATH OF GUSTAV AIMARD.—The death of Gustav Aimard, the author of many well-known works of romance, is announced. He was born in 1818, and at an early age went to America, afterwards journeying through Spain, Turkey, and the Caucasus, where doubtless he gathered *materials for the books of adventure that have made his name so familiar in England. During the war with Ger- many he organised a body of franc-tireurs composed entirely of journalists, and rendered some distinguished services. His numerous novels dwelt chiefly with Mexican and Indian adventures, and were written in a nervous and dramatic style. AN A ISTRALIAN FIRE: A FAMILY BURNT TO DEATH.— Information has just been received by the last Australian mail of a fire which occurred at the village of Sutton, a few miles from Beechworth, by which a whole family of six per- sons lost their lives. According to the intelligence it seems that a miner, named Coupin, and his family resided at Sut- ton, and at three o'clock in the morning the father discovered that his house was in flames. His wife was ill at the time. Coupin brought out of the burning house two of his chil- dren, but they were very much burnt. He then returned to attempt the rescue of two others of his children and his wife, but he did not afterwards come back. When the fire had burned itself out, the charred remains of poor Coupin, his wife, and two children were found. The other two children, whom the father had brought out of the burning building, made their way to a neighbour's house, but one died on arrival. Medical aid was summoned to the other, bat it succumbed to its sufferings soon afterwards. Thus the whole family perished. HORRIBLE CATASTROPHE IN ITALY: 47 PERSONS BURNED TO DEATH.—A horrible catastrophe occurred on Sunday evening in the village of Dervio, near Como. A performance of marionettes was proceeding in a large hall over a tavern situate at the entrance of the village, when some sparks from a Bengal light, used in the intertainment to represent a conflagration, set fire to a quantity of straw and firewood stored doge to the building. The proprietor of the Marion- ettes raised a cry of fire, but no one moved, the audience be- ing under the impression that his object was merely to make the performance more realistic. Shouts of " Fire, fire !" were then heard from the outside, but the people within the tavern, thinking that there was an affray proceeding in the street, instead of trying to escape, barricaded the door by placing a heavy table against it. Before the unfortunate beings had time to discover their mistake the flames burst upon them. On the room being subsequently entered 47 charred bodies were found close to the table amongst others those of the proprietor and his wife. Several other people were injured more or less severely. The audience numbered about ninety persons.

. . THE TRIAL OF LOUISE MicaEL."--The trial of Louise Michel and her associates for inciting to riot and plunder at the demonstration of the Invincibles was concluded on Saturday before the Court of Assizes of the Seine. On the previous day M. Rochefort was called for the defence, but he spoke chiefly of the self-sacrifice which he declared he had seen on the part of Mdlle. Michel in New Caledonia. In a somewhat incoherent speech, Mdlle Michel asserted that she raised the black flag " because that flag is the flag of strikes, and signifies that the workman is without bread. In England the meeting would not have been interfered with. The people are dying of hunger, and are not permitted to say so. I therefore, with black flag in hand, went out to proclaim that the people are without work. That is my crime; judge it as you please." The court pronounced judgment on Saturday, and Louise Michel was sentenced to six years' imprisonment and ten years' police supervision. Pouget, her secretary, was sentenced to eight years' imprison- n-pult and 10 years' police supervision. Moreau to on year's imprisonment, Thierry and Target to two years' ii;,..onment by default, and the remainder of the accused were acquitted.

A FATAL FIGHT AT HAYDOCK. SEQUEL TO NEWTON RACE FRIDAY. The utmost excitement was occasioned in Haydock, on Friday- night and Saturday last, by a report to the effect that a Man, named William Cunliffe, better known as " Billy Pea," had been killed while fighting with two other men at a place known as Double-locks, near Blackbrook. The report quickly spread throughout the township, and also to other places in the neighbourhood, and as is usual in such cases the rumours were greatly exaggerated. It was freely asserted that Cunliffe had been kicked to death during the fight, but it turns out that such was not the case —though it is indisputable that th:. man died—almost in- stantaneously—from injuries he received in the struggle. It would seem that the deceased, Cunliffe, who was forty-eight years of age, and formerly employed as a collier, was a widower, and for some time past had lodged at the house of a Mrs. Margaret Sefton, the tenant of a small " sweet " and "toffee-shop," in a row of houses, en the canal bank near the double-locks. Up to five or six weeks ago, a young man named Patrick White lodged at the same place, but since then he and an elder brother named Michael have lived at the house of a man named Critchley, near Stanley Old Mill, a short dis- tance from the double-locks. Enquiries which have been made in the district have elicited the fact that Cunliffe and the two Whites were together during the greater portion of Friday last, and between them consumed a considerable quantity of drink. In the afternoon they retired to the house of Mrs. Sefton, where Cunliffe lodged, and they there partook of more drink, which they had brought with them. About four o'clock some dispute arose between Michael White and Cunliffe, and as the dis- pute waxed warmer "hard words " were indulged in. It is stated that Michael came out with a remark which exci- ted Cunliffe, and subsequently the two men left the house, and, along with others, proceeded a short distance on the canal bank or towing path to fight. They fought, or rather scuffled and struggled for a time, and Michael struck Cunliffe a violent blow near his left ear, knocking him to the ground. He lay there without moving, and when the bystanders went towards him, to their horror and alarm, they saw that the poor fellow was quite dead. The body was at once removed to Mrs. Sefton' s house and placed on a sofa, while the Whites hastily retired from the scene of the fatal struggle. It is said that Michael White was asked to stay, but he callously replied, "No, let the die." He ac- cordingly proceeded in the direction of St. Helens, and no- thing further was heard of him until he was subsequently apprehended at his lodgings. The matter was reported by some person at the police station in Park-road, Parr, and P.C.' s Radcliffe and Carruthers immediately proceeded to the neighbourhood. Patrick White never left the house after the body of Cunliffe had been conveyed thither, and on the arrival of the police officers he quietly submitted to be taken into custody. He was afterwards taken to St. Helens Town Hall, and for a short time detained in custody until he was handed over to the Haydock police. It was understood that his brother Michael had left the district with the intention of seeking safety in flight, but Sergeant Devlin and P.C. John Tracey, of the Haydock division, displayed unusual vigilance, and with commendable promptitude succeeded in apprehending him at his lodgings. On the afternoon of the following day (Saturday) they- were conveyed to the residence of Robert Houghton, Esq., J.P., at Lowton, and taken before that gentleman on a charge of causing the death of Cunliffe. They were formally charged for the purpose of being re- manded until after the inquest, and after.the facts of the case had been briefly narrated, the two prisoners were re- manded until Tuesday. The prisoner Patrick is a young man of 21 years, while his brother Michael is ,29 years of age. Both are unmarried, and have worked as colliers. The first named is said to be a rather delicate young fellow, and goes not possess very good eye-sight, while Michael is a strongly built and powerful man, and for some years served in the militia. His " dis- charge " speaks of his character as being "indifferent." His brother Patrick was committed for some years to the training ship Clarence, stationed at New Ferry, near Liverpool. Both men have been born and bred at Prescot, and the shocking affair with which they have become so unenviably con- nected has created much interest in that district, where they are well-known.

The new Dean of Windsor (Rev. Randall Davidson) was installed on Monday morning. It is intended to confer the freedom of the city of Edin- burgh on Lord Rosebery, in recognition of his distinguished services to Scotland. On Tuesday, a deputation of the Corporation of Birming- ham had an interview with the Home Secretary on the sub- ject of specially rewarding the Birmingham police for the part taken by them in the discovery of the recent dynamite conspiracy. Sir William Harcourt, we understand, under- took to consider the representation made to him. signor Raggio's marble bust of the late Earl of Beacons- field—the original of the statue in Parliament-square—will, it is hoped, be secured permanently for St. Stephen's Club, the members having started a voluntary subscription for its purchase from the sculptor. The deceased statesman gave Signor Reggio three sittings, the last of them immedi- ately before he was attacked by his fatal illness. Three boys, all under sixteen years of age, were on Satur- day sentenced by the Sheriff of Cupar Fite to receivd cor- poral punishment, and be afterwards detained for five years in a reformatory, for breaking into Captain Scott's cabin on the Mars training ship and stealing certain articles. The lads confessed to having set the ship on fire a short time ago, but they were only arraigned for the minor offence. THE PROTECTION OF PUBLIC BUlLDlNGS.—According to orders issued from the Horse Guards, the guards were on Saturday reduced to the ordinary strength at Buckingham Palace and Tilt-yard Guard, Whitehall. The military guard at the National Gallery, Trafalgar-square, and the sentry at the Irish Office, Westminster, are withdrawn. The buildings will, however, be closely watched by the police. DEATH OF SIR WILLIAM KNOLLYS.—The death is announced of General" Sir William Knollys, Usher of the Black Rod, which took place, on Sunday, at his residence in the House of Lords, from intermittent fever. The de- ceased knight, who was a son of General Knollys, whe claimed to be Earl of Banbury, was in the eighty-sixth year of bis age. He held several important appointments in the course of his career, and was at one time Comptroller and Treasurer to His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales. COMMUNION PLATE FOR THE LIVERPOOL CATHEDRAL.— A communion service of gold plate intended for the Liver- pool Cathedral, when built, is now on view at the rooms of Messrs. Elkington and Co., Liverpool. The service has been manufactured on the order of the late Mrs. Lawrence, a lady who contributed very handsomely to the endowment of the sae of Liverpool, and consists of fifteen pieces. It is of Gothic design in repoussd work. Messrs. Elkington and Co. have themselves contributed an alms dish. The whole service has been designed by Mr. W. C. Cadman, of London.

POTTED MEAT AND HORSE FLESR.—At the Bradford Borough Court, on Tuesday, Benjamin Thompson, potted meat manufacturer, 93, Hoxton-street, Bradford, was com- mitted for two months for having in his possession pieces of flesh which were unfit for human food. A man named Padgett, a dealer in horse flesh, sold to the defendant on the 7th inst. 361 b. of horse flesh for id per pound, and in the afternoon of the same day a sanitary inspector, on v:siting the defendant's premises, found the defendant boiling the horse flesh, which was seized, condemned, and destroyed, as being unfit for human food. WORK OF TILE NATIONAL REFORM UNION.—A report was laid before the execntive committee at its last meeting showing that during the past season the total number of lectures delivered, and meetings held, under the auspices of the Union was 237, as against 211 in the preceding season. Of these, 79 have been delivered in Lancashire; 36 in Yorkshire ; 61 in thE northern counties, exclusive of York- shire and Lancashire ' • 27 in the eastern counties ; 7 in the midland counties ; 20 in the counties south of the Thames; 4in London and its suburbs; and 3in Wales. During the past half yeAr 21 new branches have been formed, of which 5 are in Lancashire; lin Yorkshire ;11 in the other nor- thern counties • 2 in the southern counties ; 1 in the London district; and lin Wales. The total number of associations and clubs now affiliated and subscribing to the Union is 300. Ms PARCELS POST.—it is stated that some delay is likely to occur in bringing the parcels post into operation, and that after all the scheme may be postponed for a few weeks after the Ist August, which is the date fixed for its introduction. At the beginning of June the Post Office issued a circular to the public requesting that they might be apprised of the probable extent to which the parcels post woulii be taken advantage of. Replies to this inquiry have so greatly exceeded the expectations of the Postmaster- General that very considerable additions to the facilities of transit will have to be made by Mr. Fawcett, who is very anxious that wMn the system is finally introduced it may work without any hitch, and he has therefore, we understand, reluctantly agreed to the postponement at the urgent solia- tation of the officials who are oompleting the necessary arrangements. AN ELOPEMENT FRUSTRATED.—On Saturday morning a scene of great excitement was witnessed at New-street station, Birmingham, when a runaway daughter was cap- tured by her mother, just as she and a young married man with whom she had designed to elope to America, had got into the early morning train for Liverpool. The pair of run- aways had seen their luggage put into the guard's van, and then the man went to get the tickets. While he was so en- gaged an elderly and highly exclted lady was observed run- ning along the footbridge, and, getting on the departure platform, she took a hurried survey of the persons on it. Catching sight of the girl, she rushed at her and, shouting repeatedly," Oh, you wicked laussey ! " laid hold of her and threatened to give her into custody if she did not go home. The daughter at leny,th consented to go home with her mother.

OBSTRUCTION IN THE GRAND COMMITTEE—On the Attorney-General on Tuesday moving the Grand Committee on LAW to abandon the Criminal Code Bill, Mr. Monk gave expression to the general feeling as to the conduct of Mr. Warton in deliberately obstructing the measure, and was strongly in favour of reporting the matter to the House. But the committee generally was opposed to anything of this kind, and when Mr. Buchanan insisted upon a division on his proposition to formally report that obstructive tactics had prevailed, he was defeated by 30 to 7. Ilia further progress with the bill has been rendered impossible through the action of two or three members of the committee is well known, and if the conduct of these gentlemen had been re- ported, the House would have been compelled to waste a considerable amount of time in censuring or punishing. them. This the Attorney-General wished to avoid, but it is to be hoped that the strong dissatisfaction that is felt at the con- duct of the obstructive members will not fail to restrict obstruction to Grand Committees.

TIIE CIIMIGE OF THEIFATENING A BISHOP.—The charge of sending a letter signed an Invincible," to the Bishop of Norwich, threatening to murder him and his family and to destroy his palace and cathedral, preferred against Joseph Bette, commission agent, Northumberland-street, Norwich, was further heard on Tuesday, before the Mayor, at Norwich Guildhall, the town clerk prosecuting. The Rev. Sidney Pelham, son of the Bishop, deposed to receiving the threat- ening letter in the absence of his lordship, and handing it to his father. William Henry Wright, a printer, who had done several jobs for the prisoner, not only stated that the threatening letter was in the prisoner's handwriting, but produced documents which he had seen the prisoner write or he had brought him to print. Mr. George Smith Inglis, of Red Lion-square, London, an expert in handwriting occa- sionally employed by the Treasury, stated that he had made a careful analysis and critical examination of the threaten- ing letter and the documents produced by Wright, and a comparison of different words showed them to be the same handwriting. Witness pointed to strong peculiarities in particular words in support of his conclusion. The prisoner was committed for trial at the assizes. During the hearing he persisted in asking questions of witnesses that were perfectly irrelevant and once told the town clerk , to sit down.

Gus AND GAME LICENSES —The popular provisions re- specting gun and game licenses foreshadowed in the last budget statement are now fully provided for by Act 46 Vict., cap. 10. The date of expiration of all licenses to kill game, hitherto expiring on the sth of April, is altered to the 31st of July. Licenses now in force or those that may be granted during the current year will hold good up to the 31st of July, 1884. This applies to gun licenses expiring 31st March. The occasional shooting licenses at £1 each, hold- ing good for 14 days, must prove highly popular. The manner in which they are to be issued leaves little to be de- sired. The days covered will run cbnsecutively, and are inclusive of the days when the license commences and ter- ' minates ; but they may be taken out at any time, and the I date of commencement made to count from any future date named. For instance, a gentleman about to proceed on a holiday tour may Obtain one of these licenses before start- ing, and have it so as to cover any period of 14 days he chooses to name. One thing, however, must not be lost sight of. The present act abolishes the present privilege respect- ing repayment of gun license duty where a game license was afterwards taken out. It was understood, of course, that a surrenderdd gun license could not form payment of £l, but after the 31st October next, as regards £3 licenses, too, no allowance or repayment of any kind will be made. PRIVATE CLUBS: ABUSE.—Attention has from time to time been called to the existence of drinking and gam- bling clubs at which intoxicating liquors are sold at all hours of the day and night. These clubs have flourished and multiplied, though both the licensed liquor trade and the temperance party are strongly opposed to them. But a case has now been raised which may seriously interfere with their success in future. A workingman's social club exists at Stalybridge, to which entrance has hitherto been gained by the payment of twopence to the "steward." Cards, dominoes, and other means of amusement are provided, two papers are taken in, and there are said to be 1,000 members. The subscription of twopence, in addition to securing mem- bership for a month, entitles the member to a certain amount of "refreshment," and the business of the society is mainly transacted on Sundays, when the house is opened at six in the morning. Under these circumstances it is not surpeis- ing that nearly every Sunday men are locked up for being drank in the street after leaving the club, and the police have at last prosecuted the " steward " for selling drink without a license. The defence of course, was that the place was a club, with a duly defence, committee, rules, and all other legal requisites; but the magistrates considered it only a colourable club, and imposed a fine. A case was asked for and refused, and for the defence it was said that the proceedings would be carried further. It is to be hoped that this threat will be carried out, and that a guiding deci- sion may be finally arrived at. Co-operation is a good thing, but the remark scarcely applies to co-operative drinking. It is necessary, daring hot weather to avoid beverages likely to heat or stimulate the system. Cocoa, deprived of the super- fluous oil, and gulranteed absolutely pure, is a rn,s's soothing, , sustaining, and refreshing beverage. Be sure that you get Cadbury's Cocoa Essence when you ask for it, as imitations are often pushed by shopkeepers for the sake of extra profit. Makers by special appointment to the Queen.—Advt.
