div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Mr. J. Greening (chairman) presided at the usual meeting of the Board, held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday. There were also present—Rev. G. F. Roberts, Major Cartwright, Messrs. Cooper, Darbyshire, Brown, .Appleton, Harrison, Blackhurst, Forster, Humphries, Caldwell, Worthington, Hunt, Waimealer, Siddeley, Swinton, Greenall, Kilshall, Grange, Gibson, W. Houghton, and J. C. Sutton (clerk), Mr. Basil Cane (Inspector of the Local Government Board), was also present.
ANOTHER FURNISHING INCIDENT.-THE EXPENDITURE AT THE SCHOOLS.

- The minutes of the Schools Committee stated that the Committee mat on the 26th inst. The Committee having examined the applications and testimonials of candidates for the offices of industrial teachers and mothers for the homes, had selected the most suitable couples to appear be- fore the Board for election, third class railway fare and 2s each to be allowed to persons from a distance. Mr. John- son, cabinet-maker, appeared before the committee with samples of furniture for the committee-room. Upon the motion of Mr. Darbyshire, seconded by Mr. Wm. Houghton, the committee recommended that Mr. Johnson's tender for one table at £9, one dozen chairs at 50s. each, 'one chair- man's chair at £4 10s, one vice-chairman's chair at £3 103 ; one linoleum at 2s lOid per yard, with border at 2s 4d per yard, be accepted. The committee also recommended that Mr. Johnson's tender for decorating the committee-room and for furnishing the office and waiting-room be accepted. The doctor reported all the chil- dren to be in good health.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved, and Mr. HUNT seconded, the confirmation of the minutes.—Mr. HARRISON said it would be very interesting to know what the cost of this establishment will be. It struck him very forcibly, from present indications, that it would be an estab- lishment rivalling in annual expenditure the House. He was afraid it would. He only wished Mr. Winstanley, the late chairman, had lived to see what the first year's expendi- ture will be, for he very boldly said, and pledged his credit, that after mature consideration cf all the circumstances it would not impose upon the ratepayers more that id. in the £. He was afraid Mr. Winstanley was very wide of the mark.—Mr. APPLETON asked if the members did not think the cost of the chairs was exorbitant.—Mr. HARRISON : should certainly not give £2 103. for a chair for my dining- room.—Major CARTWRIGHT, although a member of the Schools' Committee, said he did not happen to attend the meeting on Tuesday. If he had done he should certainly have opposed the minutes. Therefore, he thought, without any disrespect to the committee, he had a perfect right to make any remark on the question. He understood some time ago that the furniture was absolutely ordered, and on visiting the com- mittee-room he saw furniture there, but whether there was sufficient he did not know. But if the Guardians recollected, some time ago, when furniture was purchased for use in the House, there were great complaints about the cost of it. The order was given in such a way that it was very awkward to get out of it, and the furniture was con- sidered at the time to be excessive, as no doubt it was. Well, when therewere so many complaiLts about excessive expenditure on that furniture' he thought there was just cause of complaint in regard to the price named in the minute book for furnishing the committee's room. He thought the committee-room might he furnished for at least one-half the amount mentioned, and very well fur- nished indeed. He did not see that they needed to go to an expenditure of £5 for a chair for the chairman to sit in —(hear, hear)—nor £3 10s. for a vice-chairman's chair, nor as:much as 50s. each for chairs for the committee to sit upos. He was quite of Mr. Harrison's opinion that the cost of the schools was very considerable, and that they would find out, as he had always said, and he thought it was high time to check it if possible. He must say he had done his best to check it—(hear, hear)—there was no ques- tion about it. But he had been opposed all through his calculations, but he knew what it would cost. What was the result? The expenditure came to exactly, or even more than he anticipated [Mr. HARRISON: Considerably more.)—or what he stated to the Board. He told them, and told them unhesitatingly, when they had got the whole of the work completed and the full number of officials, that the expenditure connected with that establishment would not come very much short of 7s. per bead when the place was fully oaccrlf,i by 200 children. When he knew that to be a fact w•' ".? was stating he thought it was his duty cs r": '‘ 9 the ratepayers to do his best to p:f f• • • • -- s-xpenditure. He had called i! r .F, 2,1 ' and it had been. f • • I J.:. They would have

C.l `.3 when the appointments —.:ung to the list he had seen. How rney, pray, when the whole of the chil- vat the House? How many officials were there Lo look after the whole of the children they had now get at the schools Three. And he ventured to say the children were as well cared for as any children in any other workhouse in the kingdom. The children were as well cared for, as well educated, and as well turned out dur- ing the time the whole of them were at the House as they had been since, and at far less cost—at half the cost or ' thereabouts. • That was saying a great deal, but it was true. What had they now in the institution? Why, upwards of 120 or 130 deserted children—deserted by their parents, who had encouragement absolutely given to them to leave their children behind, because they knew the children would be maintained in such a manner that they themselves could not equal. The Board would have a case before them that day—a very extraordinary case—of a man who had gone away to America, and left his family of five or six children here. He had left them without a copper. and his brother, he was told, had found the money to ship this man, who had left six children chargeable to the :Union, because the man knew as well as possible both his wife and family would be cared for far better than he could care for them. The sooner they took steps to ship children off, as other unions were doing, to where they were wanted, the better. His impression was that the moment it was known they were going to send the children out of the country they would have less children at the schools. The parents would come and take their children out of the schools before they would allow them to be transported, as it were. But here people left their children—The CHAIRMA.N : If the Major would just allow me, I think he is going a ULM _ CARTWRIGHT said it was quite true. He was just stating his reasons for opposing what be considered was reckless expenditure. Far be it from him to cut down ex- penditure so low that the children could not be educated. He would do it to the letter, but he would net go to the ex- pense they were going to. He might tell them that the very institutions that they had copied were now sick of the system. It cost the sum of Bs. 6d. per week to maintain children in the south of England in similar institutions to the one they had at Padgate. Therefore he opposed the ex- penditure, although it was not very large, and he op- posed it on principle because he thought it was an expenditure to which the Board should not go, and that the sooner they curtailed it the better. He moved as an amendment that the minutes be referred back to the committee for further consideration. —Mr. HARRISON was not aware that it seemed an un- gracious thing to return the minutes to the committee for re-consideration and he could not help thinking the gentle- men who had ad the settlement of the question in reference to the furniture had perhaps been to some degree misled. They had not perhaps sufficiently thought over the various sorts of expenditure that were being entailed upon the Board, and he could not help thinking furniture of a much less expensive kind than that would do very well. For instance, in that very room but a few years ago, the chair- man's chair cost 205., and he could not held think- ing that to go and spend £5 for a chair , for an institution which as only auxiliary to the house did seem a somewhat lavish expenditure. He thought arm-chairs such as there were in the country Guardians' room were quite sufficient for all reasonable purposes. Let them act in matters of this kind as if they were acting for themselves. If any one of them had an office which wanted furnishing he was sure they would not go to the expense suggested for furnishing the committee- room. He had, therefore, great pleasure in seconding the amendment proposed by Major Cartwright.—Mr. BROWN said the committee only assented to the furniture on the condition that the room was considerably improved—decor- ated and made suitable to receive it. At present it was utterly unworthy of the furniture which the committee had recommended should be purchased. He supported the amendment.—Mr. APPLETON also supported the amendment.—Mr. BLACIEHURST said he endorsed all the committee had done, and he should sup- port the minutes. He did not think it was absolutely necessary they should furnish the committee-room worse than the room they then sat in. He remembered when they had gone on deputations to asylums, schools, Sze., they were generally ushered into a room of some pretensions as to furniture. They should finish the committee-room off in a manner that would make it the most important room about the building, and not furnish it in a shabby way which would reflect upon the Union. It was a well known fact he did not encourage extravagance in any way, and it was because he thought in purchasing the furniture they were not approaching to extravagance that he supported the minutes.— I —Mr. HARRISON said supposing they could separate the seats on which they were sitting, what did they consider each seat would cost? Why, not Li; and those were good enough for the Board.—The CHAIRMAN asked if Mr. John- son had sent in an estimate for the decoration of the room. —Mr. HARRISON: IS it contemplated to decorate the room to suit the furniture ?—The CHAIRMAN: Yes.—Mr. DARBY- SHIRE said the room was without a cornice, and was left in the rough plaster.—Mr. HARRISON: You can be as eloquent in a room without a cornice as with a cornice, can't you ? Mr. CALDWELL said the original cost of the chairs was 15s. each. They did not want eloquence but business, and they could do business as well on a chair which cost 15s as one which cost £5. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. DARBY- SHIRE in reply, said one reason why Mr. Harrison recom- mended that the minutes should be reconsidered was that he thought the :committee had not done justice to the matter. Now he could tell the Board that the subject had been considered for the last six or seven weeks. The Com- mittee had bad it before them in all shapes and forms, and they had spent a great deal of time on it. He, therefore, hoped thAt the Board would not refer the minutes back to the committee ; they could not do more than they had done. In regard to the allusion .to the furniture supplied to the House, he did not remember that there was any particular fault found with the furniture, and they must bear in mind that that furniture was for officials, while this furniture was for gentlemen round that board. I (Hear, hear.) The price might appear excessive, but they were eak oh tirs, seated well, and would last 50 years, and ' be a credit to the Union and an ornament to the committee
rn

which recommended them. He hoped the Board would see their way to support the committee. They could not see their way to put office furniture into the committee room , for the Guardians to sit upon. As to the chairs in the country board room he was tired of sitting upon them, and , he did not think it right to ask the Guardians to go and sit four or five hours on a wooden bottomed chair. What they did was for the benefit of the ratepayers, and the ratepavers ought to provide them with comfortable seats. (hear. hear.)—On the vote being taken the amendment was carried by seven votes.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE: I hope you will find another school committee. We can't get on any longer, and I hope you will find another committee.—Mr. BLACKHURST said it was perfect nonsense to refer the matter back to the committee—Major CARTWRIGHT : I am very sorry my friend should be so put out with so little a matter, because if he had had half the experience I have had at this Board he would have said nothing.—The CLERK said he had per- mission to make a statement respecting what the late Mr. Winstanley said. When they paid principal and interest on this expenditure, the money in hand being sufficient to cover the furniture mad everything else, they paid £424 10a ()id half yearly, and :Ad in the £ produced £-620. When •Mr. Win;tanley spoke of it not costing Id in the £, his recollection was that he referred to the cost of the building, because if they con- sidered they would see it would be absurd to say they could maintain 200 children and officials, and keep up the institution at Ad. in the X. The statement would only refer to the cost of the building.—Major Cartwright rose, and the CHAIRMAN said he (lid not think they need go into the matter. He granted the clerk the privilege to make the statement.—Major CARTWRIGHT : Therefore I ask for my right to be heard.—Mr. HARRISON submitted that, inasmuch as the clerk was permitted to make a statement, he ought to be permitted to say he had a very distinct recollection indeed of what Mr. Winstanley said. He distinctly stated it would not cost the ratepayers any additional expense beyond what would be covered by Ad. in the X. He did not apply to any particular branch, but he said it would not increase their pecuniary responsibility more than Id in the £. That would cover all additional expense as far as building the schools at Pad- gate.—Several Members: That is what the clerk save.— Major CARTWRIGHT said they must do justice.—Mr. WIN- STANLEY was under the impression at the time he made that statement, which Mr. Harrison and he recollected as well as possible, that £G,OOO was to be the whole outlay on the institution. But it got to £B,OOO before any contract was made or anything, and instead of that it was costing nearly £15,000, which made it more than double the amount originally stated, and did they wish to tell him -;d. in the £ covered the expenditure ?—The CLERK said it did indeed.—Mr. HARRISON: Look at the servants we employ.— The CHAIRMAN : Twelve months time would tell.—Major CARTWRIGHT : You shall have it in'the course of 12 months if I live that long. We can't mix it up now.—The subject then dropped

THE SURCHARGE AGAINST THE EX-CHAIRMAN. The CLERK said he had a letter from the Local Govern- ment Board, dated 13th June, with reference to Mr. Black- burst's appeal against the disallowances and surcharges of the sums of £33 and £33, which were made by Mr. Basle- hurst, district auditor, at his audit for the half year ended at Michaelmas, 1882, of the accounts of the Guardiaus of the Poor, for the purchase of furniture for the workhouse. The letter concluded as follows :—" The Board accordingly con- firm the auditor's decision with respect to the disallowances and surcharges. They are prepared, however, in the present instance, to remit the disallowances and surcharges in the exercise of the equitable jurisdiction conferred upon them by the 11 and 12 Vic., cap. 91, sec. 4, and they enclose a cartificate to that effect in pursuance of the 29 and 30 Vic.. cap. 113, sec. 5. The Board trust, however, that expendi- ture which has not been properly incurred by the Guardians will not again be charged in the Guardians accounts. The cheques and receipts forwarded to the Board are herewith returned."—The CHAIRMAN: Very good.—A MEMBER : It is very satisfactory.—Major CARTWRIGHT : I know to somebody it EROWN : It would be to anybody. AN EXPLAN' The CLERK road the following letter : _ . _
AN EXPLANATION.

The Hollies, Latchford, 25th June.—Dear r. Greening,-9.1- though I am much better in health than I have been, and hope soon to be ab e to regain my former state of activity. I am advised to rusticate a little longer; and my object in writing to you is to say that my attendance at the various meetings in connection with the Board of Guardians may still be irregular and uncertain for some little time to come. I shall feel obliged if, when occasion requires, you will kindly make this explanation to the Board.—Believe me, &Ir. Mr. Chairman, yours faithfully, CaAs. BROADBENT.—John Greeni, g, Esq.

div.head: MASTER'S REPORT.
div.p: MASTER'S REPORT.

The MASTER reported as follows :—" I beg to inform the Board that the children from this institution joined the pro- cession of Sunday school children, and marched to church. Along the route I was several times complimented upon their appearance by people of all ranks and grades. In the afternoon we took them to Overton Hills, where they enjoyed themselves thoroughly, returning home well pleased with their day's enjoyment."
SCHOOL SUPERINTENDENT'S REPORT.

Mr. MINES, superintendent of the schools, reported : "Our festivities in connection with the Sunday schools' anniversary held on Friday last, have passed off satisfac- torily. We are indebted to Mr. Joseph Houghton for al- lowing the children to play in one of his fields, and alsa to the Rev. W. H. Williams for a quantity of fl.wers and a bundle of illustrated papers (Graphic and illustrated London News). The cemented yards have during the past fort- night been relaid by Mr. Macleod, of Manchester. I find however, that some of the cemented floors inside the building are beginning to give way, and the continual ac- cumulation of dust and litter on their surface somewhat impedes the general cleanliness of the hcrmes."

Shoemaker and mother: Mr. and Mrs. R. H. Powell, Everton, Liverpool ; Mr. and Mrs. William Farrell, Sand-street South, Liverpool. Handicraftsman and mother: Mr. and Mrs. Samuel Mealor, Williamson's-terrace, Warring- ta;. alrg;, v%e,ftrUol3i „gre qae,Pr2OLVMtd Board, and eventually Mr. and Mrs. Reynolds, Mr. and Mrs. Powell, and Mr. and Mrs. Bailey were appointed to the positions for which they applied. This was all the business of general interest.
WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT, -- THURSDAY—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge.

A WARNING TO SECONDHAND FURNITURE f3U-YEII-S.- I In this case Samuel Gough, general dealer, 8, Aikin-street, Warrington (for whom Mr. S. Yearsley appeared) was plain- I tiff ; and George William Reynolds, provision dealer, Priestley-street, Warrington (for whom Mr. T. J. Ridgway appeared), the defendant.—Mr. Yearsley said the action was brought to recover possession of a wringing machine which was hired by plaintiff by agreement to one William Cox, Robson-street, Manchester-road, at a rent of is. 3d. a week. Shortly after that agreement was entered into, Cox found himself wanting money, and he disposed of the machine to a furniture broker. The broker conveyed it to an auctioneer's sale-mom, where it was sold to the defendant, who was taking the machine away on a cart when the plaintiff recognised it as the machine he had hired out to Cox. Plaintiff afterwards applied to the defen- dant for the machine, but he refused to give it up, and the present action was brought to recover the machine, or £3 35., its value.—Evidence in support of this statement bay- ing been given, Mr. Ridgway asked his Honour whether he had any case to answer after the cross-examination made by him, and the plaintiff's admission that he was aware this machine was taken under a distress for rent and sold under such distress ; and also whether plaintiff had sufficiently identified the machine as being the one that he sold. A machine, or furniture, let out under an agreement for hire was not legally protected from a distress by the landlord ; and as plaintiff had admitted that he knew the machine was sold under distress for rent he submitted defendant had a good title to it, and was entitled to hold it even against the person who originally let it out.—His Honour: Who do you say plaintiff has a claim against P—Mr. Ridgway: Against the hirer, because there is a breach of agreement, no doubt, by Cox.—His Honour thought he must have some clearer evidence than he had at present that there was a sale under distress.—Mr. Ri Igway pointed out that plaintiff admitted there was, or that it had been ascertained, there was.—James Smith, bailiff, 23, Green-street, was then called by Mr. Ridgway, and he deposed to taking possession of the goods and furniture at the house of William Cox, 23, Robson-street, on the 28th March last. Amongst them was a wringing machine. The distress he made was on behalf of the land- lord—the Earlestown and Newton Building Society—for rent. The machine was sold by Cox to a man, named Cun- nington, and he (witness) was paid out.—Elijah Cunning - ton, furniture broker, Kerfoot-street, stated that on the 28th March last, Cox called him into his house, where he saw the last witness, who Cox told him was there for rent. He purchased the wringing machine and other articles.—Defel. dant said, on the 20th March last, he bought the machine at Mr. Pike's sale-room, and it was delivered to him on the following day. The first demand made for the machine was on the 26th May.—Mr. Ridgway submitted that the machine was legally distrained, and seeing the bailiffs still waiting for their money there was a proper and legal sale of the title to the defendant. —His Honour, in summing up, said Cox selected goods that did not belong to him, and sold them in order to save the rest of his property. That was not a sale under distress in the common course, and as he considered the machine suffi- ciently identified, he gave judgment for the plaintiff for £3 3s, the value of the machine, the amount to be reduced to 5s on the return of the machine.—Mr. Ridgway obtained leave to appeal.

RE ESTATE OF EDWARD EIISTANCE, WATCHMAKER.— Mr. Walton, barrister (instructed by Mr. Percy Davies) ap— peared in this matter for the trustees under the liquidation (Messrs. Lewis Voisey and William Tulford Brown); and Mr. Mulholland, barrister (instructed by Messrs. Haynei Son, and Co., Liverpool) appeared for the re- spondents, the West Lancashire Building Society. Mr. Walton said the petition was filed on the 17th May this year, Mr. Voisey was appointed receiver, and entered into possession on the same day ; and the question to be decided by his Honour was as to the rights ef the Building Societ:y under a seizure which they made on tli.?f. H following day, the 18th May, under a deed, to the .termso which he should presently call his Honour's attention. e

did not think that there were any facts in dispute. &for the seizure was made it was admitted that the Building Societydid receive a letter giving them notice that the pat. tion had been filed. An interim:injunction was obtained at the instance of the receiver, and the application that day was for a declaration that the society was not entitled to seize as against the trustees, and that the property seized was the property of the trustees as against the Building Society. Tkeir rights depended on the terms of a deed of mortgage dated 7th December, 1881, made ween the debtor and lad the Building Society, of the dwelling-house of the debtor, which was called Latchford House. That was a mortgage securing an advance of £l,OOO. lie did not know that it was necessary to refer to the terms further than to the one proviso under which the Building Society entered, and under which he understood they coihnad to be entitled to the chattels. The £l,OOO was to be repaid in certain instal- ment and he read the proviso which was to the effect that the mortgagor covenanted with the Building Society that so often as the repayments should be in arrear, wholly or partly, it should be lawful for the society to enter a distraint. He admitted there were payments in arrear.—His Honour: To what extent ?—Mr. Mulholland : We have distrained for £76.—Mr. Walton said on the 18th May, after receiving notice of the Bang of the petition, the Building Society entered upon the mortgaged premises, and there claimed to distrain upon the household furniture and chattels upon the premises. It was a rnortgage on the land, and the right to distrain was an additional security given by the deed. These were the facts. Toe receiver went into possession on the 17th, and remained in possession ; and since the interim injunction was granted someone had been in possession representing both the receiver and the society. The question was simply whether or not the Building Society had a fight to , distrain as against the trustees. He submitted on various I grounds they had not. There was no doubt if there was rent due the land:ord could distrain even at the cemmence- ment of liquidation. His point was that there was no rent at all due, that there was no rent under this deed, at any rate, so far as it gave any rights of seizure of chattels or a bill of sale, within the meaning of the Bills of Sale Act 1878; and further that if there was no rent due the goods were clearly in the ordinary disposition of the debtor at the time the petition was filed.—After hearing the arguments, his Honour said this case seemed to him to turn upon the question whether it was a license to take possession. He thought on the arguments it did not come within the terms of section 6 of the Bills of Sale Act, 1378. The only question really, he thought, was whether at the time that this entry was made the goods were in the ordinary dispssition of the debtor, and whether this clause of the deed was a. license to Lake possession so as to render it necessary to register it under E the Bills of Sale Act. In regard to the goods being in the ordinary disposition of the debtor the evidence showed they were at the time of the filing of the petition in his ordinary disposition : and he thought they must hold that the power to seize was inralid as against the trustee because the deed was not registered under the Bills of Sale Act, 1878.

Mr. John Bright has written to a Birmingham corres- pondent, sympathising with an agit, tion to dispense with the viewing of bodies at inquests, and promising to mention the matter to the Attorney-General. The Exchequer returns from April 1 to June 23 show--- Receipts, £19,224,582; expenditure, £17,358,168 ;' balances, £7,913,050. Corresponding period last year—Receipts, £18,476,034 ; expenditure, £17,209,636 ; balances, .£6,012,648. The Prince and Princess of Wales visited Winchester on Wednesday, and were enthusiastic illy received. After in- specting the Royal Counties Agricultural Show, the Prince and Princess visited the Minster and other places of interest in the city, after which they returned to London. THE SECRETARY OF STATE FOR SCOTLAND. - There is said to be almost a general expectation among Scotch mem- bers that Lord Rosebery will consen-t to return to office as Secretary of State for Scotland. probably with a seat in the Cabinet. Failing the noble Earl, it is thought in some quar- ters that Lord Dalhousie may be offered the posttion. CRUSHED TO DEATH BY A TOMBSTONE —Mr. Smith, a mason, of Ayr, was engaged on Tuesday dressing a tomb- stone, when the stone fell from the platform on which it stood and crushed Mr. Smith so severely that he died in a few minutes. The stone weighed upwards of half a ton. Mrs. Smith was a witness of the occurrence, but could do nothing to assist her husband, the stone being heavier than she could move.

A GOOD" CoLLEcTioN."—Rowland Hill once preached in aid of a certain meritorious institution. At the conclu- sion of the sermon, just before the plates were handed round for the collection, he made this E.hort address to the congre- gation :—" From the great sympathy I have witnessed in your countenances, and the strictattention you havehonoured me with, there is only one thing I am afraid of—that some of you may be inclined to give too much. Now, it is my duty to inform you that justice, though not so pleasant, yet should always be a prior virtue to generosity; therefore, as you will all immediately be waited upon in your respective pews, I wish to have it thoroughly understood that no person will think of putting anything into the plate who cannot pay his debts." It is needless to say that these remarks pro- duced an overflowing collection.

LANCASHIRE CONGREGATIONAL CALENDAR. - The Lan- cashire Congregational Calendar, which is published under the superintendence of a sub-committee of the executive of the County Congregational Union, has just been issued for the present year. The changes introduced last year are continued, and the result is a very useful and comprehen- sive handbook of the denomination in Lancashire. The list of churches shows that in the Blackburn district there are 51 places of worship, with 25,935 sittings; Liverpool 70 churches, 33,325 sittings; Manchester 134 churches, 75,412 sittings; Preston 42 churches and 13,140 sittings; a total of 297 churches, with 147,812 sittings. Reports of the annual conference are given, together with a mass of information relating to the benevolent, religious, and other societies connected with the denomination.

THE RUNCORN DRAPER AND ins DOGS.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Robert Roberts, draper, Bridge- street, was summoned for keeping, on the 29th May, two dogs, when he was only licensed to keep one. At the last court, the defendant stated one of the dogs was under six months old, and the magistrates adjourned the case in order that he could bring proof of that fact. He now stated that Mr. ,Powell, from whom he had purchased the dog, had mislead him. The dog was over six months old, but had he known that he should have been sorry to keep it with- out obtaining a license.—The Bench fined the defendant lOs and costs, 12s 6d. • POACHERS AND THEIR PARAPHERNALIA AT RrI•TCORN. Joseph Forster and Robert Jannion, young men, were brought up at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday to answer a charge of being in possession of nets for the pur- pose of taking game.—P.C. Egerton said on Sunday, the 17th inst., when he was near Frodsharn Bridge, he met the defendants coming along the highway. Knowing them to be poachers, he stopped them and searched them. Janni- on had eleven nets wound round his body under his shirt, and in a bag concealed in Forster's trousers he found a ferret. The nets were wet, with fresh soil attached. The ferret's feet were also wet. Each defendant was fined lOs and costs. DILUTED LIQUORS AT RUNCORN.—James Knlwles, grocer, Church-street, was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of having on the 30th ult. sold to P.C. Bossons a pint of vinegar which was not of the substance and quality demanded.—The defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined 10s. and costs £1 4s. Sarah Abrams, keeper of a public-house in Hatton-road, was charged with selling P.C. Bossons a pint of adulterated rum on the 30th May. The analyst had made an examination of the liquor, and certified that it contained 30 per cent. of water, being five per cent. more than was allowed by Act of Parliament.—Defendant stated she was ill in bed when the officer called, and her neice mixed the furn.—She was fined 108. and costs £1 63. COUNTY COURT BUSINESS IN RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. —ln reply to an address of Mr. Norwood, M.P., dated the 6th of June, 1883, a return from every County Court in England and Wales was issued on Saturday last giving the total number of plaints, :tc.. entered for trial, with the sums sued for, costs, and fees. We give that part referring to Runcorn :—ln this court 1,260 plaints were entered for trial, representing the sum of £3,172. Of these 853 were determined, and judgments obtained for £1,676, ex- clusive of costs (L 243 and fees (£470). The moneys re- ceived to the credit of suitors was £1,693, and the amount paid to them £1,681. There were 240 judgment summonses issued, 152 heard; 54 warrants of commitment issued, 7 debtors imprisoned, 267 executions against goods issued, and four sales made. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN GENTLEMAN.—MT. G. J. Knight, accountant, of Runcorn, met with a painful accident at Manchester on Tuesday :afternoon. Mr. Knigt.t was descending the steps of a building where he had been transacting some business, when, owing to their awkward construction, his foot slipped, and he fell forward on to the landing. He experienced intense pain in the left knee, and he lay on the floor in a helpless state until assistance arrived. He was then conveyed to the Infirmary, where it was found that the knee cap was broken, and the injured limb was atteaded to. Fortunately Mr. Knight was able to travel, and he took the train for Frodsham, where he was met by a cab, and arrived at Runcorn in the evening. Much sympathy was expressed for the injured gentleman, who bill probably be confined to home for several weeks.

RCJNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The usual fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also present—the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, John Lock- wood, Messrs. C. Reynolds, J.P., J. Ashton, John Highfield, J. G. Claudet, John Mclntyre, John Cballoner, C. Rigby, J. Darbyshire, J. G. Hamilton, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), J. G. Bride (medical officer), and Farrington (inspector).—Tenders for the making of the Halton main sewer were read from William Worrall, Five Crosses, Frodsham, and John Littler, of Frodsham. Each of the tenders amounted to -£loo.—On the motion of Mr. Challoner, seconded by Mr. C. Rigby, Mr. Littler's tender was accepted.—A precept was ordered to be served upon the overseers for the amount.—The Medical Officer reported a case of scarlet fever at A ppleton. DAMAGING PROPERTY AT WIDNES.—John Kelly, Patrick Riley, and Cain Shields were charged, at Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, with doing wilful damage to a win- dow, the property of Mr. Hargreaves.—Mr. T. J. Peters prosecuted, and remarked that a gang of ruffians seemed to be organised for the purpose of damaging property, and asked the Bench for an exemplary sentence.—Adam Green, living in Pier-street, said about four o'clock, on the after- noon of the 17th inst., a heavy blow was given at the wall of his house, loosening the mortar and filling the house with dust. He went out and saw a gang of about a dozen young men, among whom were the defendants. They had bricks in their hands. He afterwards saw them pushing bricks and slates through the whole in the wall. They also did damage to the sash of the window.—Mr. S. Owens, agent to Mr. Hargreaves, estimated the damage at 303. —Riley, who could not be identified, was dismissed. Kelly and Shields denied their guilt, and the former called a wit- ness named Roger McDonald who said Kelly was at a wake at the time he was alleged to have been doing the damage. —By Mr. Peters: The house where the wake was held was near the residence of Green.—The magistrates then dis- missed the charge against Kelly, and fined Shields 103 and costs, and ordered him to pay 10s towards the damage.

A VIOLENT FELLOW AT RUNCORN.—Before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. C. Reynolds, at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, William Roach, a rough-looking young fellow, was brought up in custody, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Brunswick-street; with assaulting P.C. Kelly, and also with wilfully damaging the window in the cell at the police station, by breaking twenty panes of glass, worth 6s. 81—The prisoner pleaded guilty to all the charges.— About eleven o'clock on Saturday morning, the prisoner was lying on the footpath in Brunswick-street in a state of drunkenness. P.C. Kelly went to him and requested him to get up and go about his business. The prisoner said he would go when he liked, and the constable took him into custody. He several times kicked the constable in a violent manner, and the latter knocked him down and handcuffed him. In Church-street the prisoner again kicked him, but P.S. Whalley came on the scene, and between the two officers, the prisoner was taken to the police station. A short time afterwards, the prisoner was served with dinner in his call. After ha had consumed it. be amused himself by smashing tbe cell windows, with the can which had held it. For drunkenness, the defendant was fined 103. and costs; for the assault, 20s. and costs, and a similar penalty for the wilful damage; or in default, ten weeks hard labour. The prisoner went to gaol.

UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WlDNES.—Crowded congregations assembled in this plane of worship on Sunday, on the occasion of the annual sermons on behalf of the Sun- day School. Mr. James Bramwell, of Liverpool, occupied the pulpit morning and evening, and preached two excellent sermons. In the afternoon a children's service was held, and the Rev. J. Billington, of Runcorn, delivered an ad- dress to the scholars. The choir had prepared special music for the occasion, and under the conductorship of Mr. J. Bet- ney, sang during the day the anthems " Praise the Lord," "The Heavens are telling," and the Hallelujah chorus." The collections amounted to £26 ss. On Monday evening the scholars further celebrated the anniversary by giving an en- tertainment in the chapel, which was well filled. Mr. R. Webster presided, and delivered an address. The Rev. J. billington also addressed the meeting, and in the course of his remarks gave a few facts regarding the school. The income for the past year amounted to £27 14s 2d, and the expendi- ture to £26 17s 2td, leaving a balance of 18s OP in the hands of the treasurer. The school library contained 249 books, and the 26 ,members had borrowed 786 volumes during the year. There was a balance of .£l. 19s in hand on the library account. The children went through an excellent programme iri good style. At the close of the entertainment a collection was made, and realised .€.3 4s. Hid, making the total collections £29 8s 6d. RUNCORN OPEN AIR CONCKRTS.—On Thursday evening the Mill-brow Brass Band played the following programme on the market ground :—March, "Khedive" (Snowdon) ; selection, "Napoleon" (De Lacy); march, "Sunny " (8.M.); chorus, "Great is the Lord" (Frost); march! "FOOLISH DRUNK" AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, John Radford, a labourer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Friday night. About ten o'clock the prisoner was lying on Dell Bridge, bleeding from a wound to his head, and P.C. Smith raised him up and attempted to take him home. The prisoner, however, became so rough that he was locked up, and the magistrates fined him 20s. and costs. In default of paying that sum he went to gaol for a month. STAR OF WIDNES LODGE, I.O.G.T.—The members of this lodge intended to hold an out-door demonstration on Wednesday, but owing to the inclemency of the weather they were unable to do so. They, however, headed by the Star of Temperance brass band, marched to the Public Halt in Hutchinson-street, where a public meeting was held, under the presidency of Bro. T. Bold, who delivered an address. W.T. Bro. Clark and Captain Elmes, of the Blue Ribbon Army, also delivered speeches. ROBBERY FROM A RUNCORN PAWNBROKER.—At Runs corn Police Court, on Thursday, Hannah Radford wa- brought up on remand charged with stealing two frocks on the value of 5s 3d, and a girl's tunic worth 9d, the property of William Craddock, pawnbroker, Church-street. On Sat- urday night a girl saw the prisoner and another man enter the prosecutor's shop. The prisoner took a parcel from the counter, and then left the shop with her companion walking along Brunswick-street and Mount Pleasant. Mr. Crad- dock was informed of the robbery, and gave information to the police. Subsequently P.C. Norris apprehended the pri- soner. The prisoner was remanded until Monday. ATTEMPTED ROBBERY FROM A TILL AT WIDNES. Before Mr. G. Pilkington, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Edward Davies was charged with attempting to rob the till of the Arch Hotel, which is occupied by Mr. J. Calligan. On the previous day prisoner was served with a pint of beer by Mrs. Calligan, who afterwards went to another part of the house. Whilst there she heard the jing- ling of money, and retarning quickly to the bar she found the Prisoner on the counter with his hand in the drawer. The prisoner decamped, but the landlord being informed of the circumstances by his wife, gave chase and succeeded in cap- , turing him. P.C. Barker afterwards took him into custody. I —The prisoner was remanded. TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TlCKET.—Yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. H. S. Hall, Daniel Sutcliffe, who described himself as an engineer from Macclesfield, was charged with travelling from Liverpool to Widnes on the London and North-Western Railway without having paid his fare.—Mr. Smith, the stationmaster, said the prisoner arrived at Widnes by the 11.40 train from Liverpool on Thursday night. On being asked for his ticket he could not produce one, and said that he had only 3d in his pocket. 'This statement proved to ba true. He informed the magis- trate that he had respectable relatives who would pay the costs of the proceedings if he was set at liberty.—The pri- soner was remanded to Wednesday, but it was understood that he would be admitted to bail on his friends entering into sureties for his appearance. ROBBING A HEN COOP AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, Elizabeth Ogden, a woman of bad cha- racter, who had been 17 times previously convicted, was charged with stealing a tame fowl, the property of Mark Walsh, a labourer, residing in Nelson-street. About five o'clock on Monday afternoon Mrs. Walsh fed the poultry in the back yard, the stolen hen being amongst them. Quarter of an hour afterwards she missed the hen, and whilst in search of it the prisoner passed her.--A labourer named Thomas Graham was standing at the end of an entry in the neighbourhood when the prisoner came up to him, and he saw the feet of a fowl "peeping" beneath her shawl. He seizei hold of her and took the hen, but the prisoner made her escape in the direction of the "Van Tromp" public- house. Subsequently Mrs. Walsh captured the prisoner, and gave her into the custody of P.C. Collier.—The prisoner was committed to Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial. BRUNSWICH SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY RUNCORN. —The anniversary services of Brunswick Sunday School will be held in St. Paul's Chapel, on Sunday, the Bth July, when the Wesleyans will have the opportunity of hearing the Rev. Robert P. Downes, who is one of the most able and eloquent preacher in the Connexion. In a biographical sketch of the rev. gentleman, the Christian Globe says— " The noble thoughts which teem from his poetic mind, and the intense earnestness of the man make at all times a deep impression on his hearers. Whatever his subject may be, his treatment of it is as exhaustive as his language is sub- lime and his manner impassioned. He is never at a loss for thoughts and words, by which all who hear him, be their views negative or positive, may well profit, and which can- not help but command the attention and reverent admiration of both the educated and uneducated classes." On Monday evening, the 9th July, Mr. Downes, will preach a sermon in St. Paul's Chapel as a substi;.ute for the President of the Conference, a fact which testifies to the confidence reposed in his oratorical powers. THE " DEGRADED DOCTOR " AT RUNCORN.—Before Mr. Bankes, at Ruecorn Police Court, on Thursday, James Tids- well Asken, who describes himself as a doctor, was charged with drunkenness and riotous behaviour—P.C. Bossons said about 7-30, on the previous evening, he was on duty in Bridge-street. The prisoner was there in a state of drunkenness, and creating a great disturbance. The prisoner was in the habit of getting a few glasses of beer, which made him very silly, and the boys run after him in , the street. They did so on the present occaeion, and the prisoner struck a bay four years of age on the head with a stick he was carrying. The prisoner went into every public. house in Bridge-street. About ten minutes previous to this time witness had told the prisoner to go to his lodgings.— The prisoner said he was exceedingly sorry; but he had been much annoyed by loafers at street corners. Because he prescribed they had given him the appellation of "quack doctor." He went from one house to another prescribing for illnesses, and only charged 3d. or 4d. for a prescription. He had held himself "too cheap," and had consequently become degraded.—Superintendent William- son remarked that the prisoner had been in the town nine months.—The prisoner said lie had been staying in the town to get work and better clothes; but at 60 years of age he thought be could not improve his position. He should be glad to leave the town.—Mr. Bankes: Apparently it is drink that has brought you to what you are. You are a Idisgrace to yourself, and a nuisance to the town. The best thing you can do is to leave the town. You were convicted in May last for riotous conduct in a church. You will be fined 103 and costs 5s Bd, or in default 14 days' hard labour. —The prisoner went to gaol. RUNCORN BRUNSWICK SUNDAY SCHOOL: PICNIC TO CHESTER AND BEESTON CASTLE.—On Tuesday, the teachers ! of the Brunswick Sunday School held their annual picnic. This year the place selected was Beeston Castle. One half I • of the party took the 9-10 train in the morning for Chester, I and after enjoying themselves on the Dee for a few hours, were joined by the rest at Chester station, and proceeded by the two o'clock train to Beeston Castle. They were but 30 in number, owing to the unsettled state of the weather, a steady downpour damping the spirits at the time of start- ing in the morning; but in the course of an hoar or so it became delightfully fine, and the ulsters and other wraps that had at first been serviceeble soon became an incum- , brance. Through the kindness of Lord Tolle- ' mache, the party were permitted to go through Peckforton Castle. Everyone was struck with the sturdy character of this new castle, built in the old fashion. Its massive masonry, both within and without, gave one a . sense of security, if not of the luxury and home comfort ,of modern mansions. After admiring the paintings and I furniture which the various rooms contained, the party returned to Beeston Castle, where tea had been provided. The rest of the time was spent in exploring the well- preserved ruins of the castle. The view from the castle is most extensive, comprising many square miles of level , meadow land, with glimpses of the Dee and Mersey, as ! the rays of the setting sun danced upon their surface. A well, 365 ft in depth, proved a source of attraction to the party, who looked with great interest as the atten- dant lowered the candles to The surface of the water. The , return journey was made by the way of Crewe, where, after la stay of half an hour, the London express took the party safely hoine by 9-30. Rineconet REFRESHMENT HousEs.—At Runcorn Petty iSessions, on Monday, John Dutton, refreshment house • keeper, Church-street, was charged with keeping his house open during the time when by law it ought to have been closed.—P.C. Noden said at a quarter past eleven, on Saturday, the 16th inst., he visited the defendant's refresh- ment house in Church-street, and found three persons at the counter. The defendant's wife was serving them at the counter. In another room two other men were eating re- freshments. Witness asked the defendant's wife if she knew the house ought to be closed at 11 o'clock. She re- plied it was not stated on the license, but witness told her that the time was nevertheless 11 o'clock, and he should make a report on the matter.—Defendant pleaded guilty.— Mr. Bankes: There is no suspicion that the house is being' used for an improper purpose.—Supt. Williamson : No. I am sorry to say that the refreshment house keepers have got it into their heads they could keep open as long as they liked, and I instructed the sergeants to inform them that they could not do so.—Mr. Bankes: They have been cautioned before, then ?—Superintendent Williamson: Yes, sir.—Mr. Bankes said it was the defendant's own fault that he was in this position and would be fined ss. and costs.--John O'Dah Bancroft, keeper of a refreshment house in Church-street, was charged with keeping his house open during the time it ought to have been closed. P.S. McMichael said at ten minutes to twelve on Saturday night, the 16th inst., he visited the defendant's refreshment house, where he found a boy and a girl. The defendant was serving the boy with some potatoes. Witness asked defendant if his sister had informed him that he had called on Thursday night, and cautioned her to close at 11 o'clock. Defendant replied that she had, and he then asked him why he had not closed. He then commenced to argue with a7itness about other places keeping open, and was very impert;umt. Witness said he had nothing to do with other places. His time for closing was sane as that of public-houses, and he would be reported.. —Defendant was fined ss. and costs, 9s. Od.

THE EXAMINER, SATIT RI)AY, JUNE 30, 1883. RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT r RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- RUNCORN. SIONERS. A meeting of ratepayers was held in Bethesda School- room, on 't hursday evening, for the purpose of electing tbree members of the Burial Board in the place of Messrs. El. Coleburn, Geo. Rhodes,•and W. Littler, who relired but were eligible for re-election. The Rev. Canoe Barclay, viatar, occupied the chair, and there weie also present— Messrs. W. Handley and W. Whittaker (overssers), James Handley, T. Norman, F. Fairhurat, H. Co!et)urn, G. Moss, J. D. Jmes, W. Brookes, W. Littler, Adams, 0. Leak,Brindley, D. Blebrown, A. Darbyshire, J. Gleaves, and W. utton (assistant overseer.—Mr. FAIRHURST pro- posed the re-election of Mr. Coleburn as a member if the Burial ',Board.—Mr. NORMAN secamied the :motion with pleasure. He did not think a better man than Mr. Coleburn ever sat on the Burial Board. He had been a member six years, and during that time he had never missed one single meeting. It was his (Mr. Norman's) opinion that men who would attend to the office were the men that ought to be put In, and he had great pleasure in seconding Mr. Coleburn's nomination.—The motion was carried unanimously.—On the motion of Mr. FAIRHURST seconded by Mr. J. HANDLEY, Mr. G. Rhodes was unanimously re-elected.—Mr. W. Littler was also re-elected, on the motion of Mr. COLE- HUHN, seconded by Mr. W. WHITTAKER. The next business before the meeting was the follow- ing resolution, which been- placed on the not.ice paper at the instance of the Waterloo House Committee "That in the opinion of this meeting it is expedient that the offices of the overseers be removed to Waterloo House, and the overseers are hereby empewered to remove from their present offices, No. 5, Alcock-street. to Waterloo House, at a rental of £3O per annum, including rates, gas, coals, and cleaning, subject to the approval of the Local Goverment Board."—There was no member of the com- mittee present to move the resolution, and Mr. NORMAN observed that as the Commissioners were going to move to Waterloo House, it was essential that all the public offices should go there also, and at the same time, because one expense would then be sufficient.—The CHAIRMAN: Are the rooms convenient that you propose to give the overseers ?-eMr. NORMAN said he supposed so. He was very sorry that Mr. Meadowcroft or Mr. Shaw was not present. He had, however, great pleasure in moving the resolution.— Mr. 0. LEAK seconded the motion.-In reply to Mr. Fairhurst, Mr. Surrow said the rooms at Waterloo House would be a pound a year cheaper than the overseers' present offices.— Mr. W. HANDLEY made a statement at the request of the chairman. He said some few weeks ago the overseers re- ceived a communication from Mr. Brookes asking the over- seers to meet the Waterloo House Committee at Waterloo House with the object of inducing them to have the over- seers' office there. The overseers pointed out that they had no power to take offices or remove from their present ones, as they were held under an order issued by the Local Government Board at the instance of the ratepayers; and that the ratepayers themselves must melee in this matter. He (Mr. Handley), Mr. Whittaker, and Mr. Sutton met Mr. Shaw and Mr. Meadowcroft last week, and went through the house. The rooms they offered the overseers were the drawing-room and a small room at the side of it, which would have an entrance frcm Egerton- street, to make it convenient as a hall or waiting-room for people going there to pay rates. When the question of rent arose, Mr. Shaw at first asked £35 a year, but subsequently reduced it to £3O, including coal, gas, taxes, and cleaning. The overseers pointed out to Mr. Shaw that the resolution would have to be very definite for that meeting, and that it would be necessary for a member of the committee to be present and support it. If it was the wish of the ratepayers that the overseers remove, of course they would do their best to carry that wish out as soon as possible.—Mr. MEADOW- cRoFT, who had just arrived, said he thought there was some misapprehension in regard to the rent of the offices covering the rates. Mr. Shaw informed him that day that the rent was not intended to cover the rates. The incon- venience and confusion likely to arise if each set of offices paid their own rates was pointed out, and Mr. MEADOW- caorr said that could be easily met by increasing the amount of rent payable. He did not see why the overseers should ask for better accommodation in every respect than they had now for a less sum of money. He moved an amendment that the rent be £35 a year including rates, &c., and the committee to do the structural alterations.— Mr. BROOKES seconded the amendment, which, on being put, was lost by 9 votes to 7.—Mr. 13xacKniEs then move,' that the rent be £3l, and Mr. IlAnitgit having described what structural alteration would be necessary, Mr. D. Brs- BROWN seconded the motion, which was also lost.—Thr original motion was declared carried, and a vete of thank( to the Chairman concluded the proceedings.

div.head: DREADFUL ASSAULT ON A CHILD AT
div.p: DREADFUL ASSAULT ON A CHILD AT
RUNCORN.

Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. William Bankes, George Curling, about 30 years of age, was charged with having,on the 23rd June an 4 on other days,committed a rape on Mary Dodd,ll years of age.—Elizabeth Dodd, wife of John Dodd, engine driver, living at 69, Shaw- street, said the prosecutrix was her daughter. The prisoner came to lodge at her house on Saturday, 15:11 June. He was an engine driver. From something she saw on Monday, the 25th cost, she questioned her daughter. who said she had been assaulted by the prisoner. She informed the police. She had left ;the prisoner and the girl in the house together on several occasions. The prisoner was sober on each occa- sion. The prosecutrix, a little girl of light complexion, said she remembered the prisoner comirm to her father's house. The first night he came, the 15th June, she was left alone with the prisoner. Her mother had gone out, and the other children were in bed. Soon after her mother had gone out, the prisoner, who was sitting on a chair in the kitchen, said " Come here." She went to him, and he seiz,d her and committed the offence with which be was charged. She asked him to let her go and see if her mother was corning. He released her, and she went out. He followed her and broue•ht her in, and gave her a half-penny, telling her that she must not tell her father and mother what bad taken place. Last Friday, the 22nd instant, she was again alone in the house with the prisoner, her father having gone a walk with her mother. He - assaulted her again that evening, and again the even- ing following when her mother was at chapel. He gave her a penny, and asked her not to tell her father and mother; but on the Sunday night she told her mother what had taken place. The prisoner said he would "give it her" if she told her mother, and that was the reason she did net do so before. The prisoner was sober on all these occa- sions.—Dr. MacDougall having given evidence, P.S. Whalley deposed to apprehending the prisoner, who, in answer to the charge, said "Ye', I had been drinking spirits, and I did not know 'what I was doing."—The priso- ner was formally committed to take his trial at the next Chester Assizes.
ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN BRIDGE COLLECTOR.

Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, sen.' and Mr. G. Pi!king- ton, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Monday, a young man named James Dixon was charged with refusing to give up his ticket on Runcorn Bridge, and also with assaulting the collector, John Alderson.—Mr. Appleton, stationmaster. Runcorn, prosecuted on behalf of the Railway Company.— John Alderson, the collector, said on Saturday he was on duty in the ticket office at the Widnes end of the bridge. About a quarter-past four the prisoner passed him without giving up his ticket, and witn3ss followed him and asked him for it. The prisoner said he had already given up his ticket, but witness again demanded the ticket, when the prisoner struck him and pushed him down, his head coining in contact with the fence. At last the prisoner gave up his ticket, but it was with difficulty witness succeeded in releasing himself. The prisoner, who was under the influence of drink, continued to he very violent, and challenged witness to come into the street and fight him. During this time a number of people were passing over the bridge, and many were waiting for tickets. He was consequently compelled to let the prisoner go, but subsequently he locked the office up and went in search of a police officer. He afterwards gave the prisoner into the custody of P.C. Barker.—lnspector Barnett stated that the prisoner was drunk when brought to the police office.—Wm. Farrell, brickmaker, Runcorn, deposed that he witnessed the assault. The prisoner had the ticket in his hand at the time, and when he gave it up he seized the collector in a violent manner, saying be would take him to the police station. After knocking the collector against the rails the prisoner struck him several times.—The prisoner, in defence, alleged that he was never asked for his ticket, and that the collector handled him roughly without reason. wMr. Gaskell said it was the prisoner's duty to give up his trcket whether it was asked for or not. The collector oc- cupied a very responsible position, and he must be protected. A bye-law of tbe company sanctioned by Act of Parliament ' authorised the magistrates to inflict a fine of £5, and they felt bound to make an example of this case to show that conduct such as the prisoner had been guilty of could not be tolerated. They were bound to give protection to men occupying such positions as the collector, and they could not do less than sne the prisoner 40s. and costs, or in default one month's imprisonment with hard labour.—The prisoner asked to be allowed to pay the money by instalments, but the Bench refused to show him any leniency whatever as the case was a serious one.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.—The scholars and teachers of this school had their annual treat on Monday, when they went by train to Frodsham, and spent a pleasant day on Overton Hills, the weather being fine. The Revs. J. Pickwell and D. Schofield, and the super- intendents accompanied the party. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, RUNCORN. After being closed for about six weeks, the above chapel will be re-opened to-morrow (Sunday), when the Rev. W. Dawkins, of Helper, will preach two sermons; while on Tuesday ser- vices will be held in the afternoon and evening. On the latter occasions the Rev. J. Adcock, wh3 is a well-known and eloquent preacher, will occupy the pulpit. In the hands of the joiner and decorator the interior of the sacred edifice has undergone a most pleasing metamorphosis. The ugly straight-backed pews of a Puritanical generation have dis- appeared, and varnished pitch-pine benches of handsome appearance and comfortable construction meet the eye as one enters the charch. The church has gained much in brightness and airiness of aspect, and we are sure the ordin- ary worshippers of the place will conduct their devet:ons with equal reverence and more comfot under this improved state of things.

div.head: CHAIRMAN ON' HIS POSITION.
div.p: THE CHAIRMAN ON' HIS POSITION.

I TllO CHAIRMAN, on taking his seat, was warmly applauded. He eaid : Gentlemen, before we proceed with the business of the meeting, I think I ought to say a few words in refer- ence to my position here to-day. I was absent fiord town last week, and from the meeting of Vue 'Board at which you were good enough to appoint Ite to this position. Conse- quently, I was precluded from expressing my acknowledg- ments for the honour you have done me in placing me here; and, therefore, I take this, the first opportunity, to thank you for the distinction you have conferred upon me, as well as the confidence you have shown in me. I cannot say that this is a position to which I ever aspired, nor is it one which I ever hoped or thought to occupy. Indeed, my dis- position shrinks from it, but after the representations. and I may add congratulations, and further, greatest of all, the spontaneous expression of goodwill and regard which you have shown to me in placing me here, which inspire within me some hope and encouragement that I may be able to discharge the duties which devolve upon me, I feel that it would be a somewhat ungracious act on my part to refuse the honour which you have sought to do me. But I must say that I don't regard the event as one of import- ance to myself, but rather as an honourable and laudable advance on the part of this Board in the conception of just and liberal principles‘in so far that I understand it to mean the interment—the perpetual interment—of those traditional jealousies and exclusive sentiments which have prevailed for so long a period in regard to this office and the manage- ment of the matters at this Board. (Hear, hear.) I should also like to say another word in reference to a subject which was alluded to at the last meeting, because it has taken a somewhat prominent position in the discussion which toek place in reference to my representative character. Now it is quite true that I represent large interests, but I claim that these interests contribute very materially to the pros- perity of Runcorn,—(hear, hear)—and that, apart from the large amount of rates which are contributed directly by those interests, they also contribute indirectly a very large sum to their employes. There if you abstract those two factors from the ratepaying and wealth producing power of the town, you really create a serious gap in the present pic- ture of the welfare of Runcorn as compared to what it would be if that state of things existed. I do think that these interests are very beneficial interests, and should not be considered as a disqualification to the enjoyment of the full rights and privileges of membership of this Board, and particularly when it is borne in mind that many gentlemen, and I say it in all respect, have been returned to this Board and occupy their seats simply by one or two votes. Therefore, Ido think that some consideration should be given to interests which exist. I hope, as I said before, that any appointment signifies the interment, or rather ex- tinguishment, of those musty ideas which prevailed some 30 years ago—(hear, hear)—and I trust we shall all co- operate in the policy because it is a wise and sound policy, a policy which con:anemia itself to all intelligent men, that it is best to cultivate, to encoarage, and to develops as far as we consistently can any interest or any industry which is likely to bring benefits to the town. (Hear, hear, and applause.) That being so, I appeal to you to extend to me your cordial support and your sympathy in the discharge of the duties which appertain to this high office—(hear, hear)—because it must be apparent to ion, as it is to my- self, that I cannot hope to discharge those duties with credit to myself or to you, and with advantage to the town, unless I have your co-operation. (Hear, bear.) it is on that ground that I ask you to extend to me it, and I can assure you 9aat no individual effort shall be wanting to promote the interests of the town, and further, I may say, sustain and hand down to my successor the dignities and privileges of this position as unimpared and as untarnished as I have received them. I again thank you, gentlemen, for the honour you have done me in placing use here. (Ap- pla Use)

The business of the meeting was then Proceeded with. A short discussion took place with respect to what the reporters had to publish; and as negotiations were still progressing, it was intimated to the reporters that they must not publish the clauses.—Mr. LIGHTBURN, as chairman of the Ship Canal Committee, then narrated their proceedings at London, and pointed out what concessions they had succeeded in ob- taining.—A desultory discussion ensued. Mr. SHAW re- marked that before the Board separated they ought to put some limit on the expenditure of the committee, which caused Dr. MacDougall to rise indignantly to his feet. He considered it most ungenerous treatment to limit the com- mittee's expenditure, which he was sure would not be very extensiyc.—Mr. SHAW observed that he should he quite satis- flA if the doctor would agree to pay them. !Subseqaently the meetirg was adjourned until Friday morning, and the membns rose.

div.head: CAPTURE OF AN ALLEGED IRISH CONSPIRATOR AT WIDNES.
div.p: CAPTURE OF AN ALLEGED IRISH CONSPIRATOR AT WIDNES.

Secret societies, it is well known, include among their members considerable numbers of the Irishmen of Widnes, and when at the beginning of the week Government detec- tives were observed searching the town, rumours were rife that they were on the track of the pereotretor of some ont- rage. This surmise proved to be correct. The detectives conducted their movements with the greatest secrecy, and at midnight on Tuesday, Sergeant O'Brien, of the Royal Irish Constabulary, who was one of the detectives, accom- panied ley Inspector B irnett and Sergeant Robinson of the Widnes force, together with a number of constables, visited a dwelling-house in Elizabeth-street, Moss Hank. This house is used as a lodging-house, and is occupied by Mrs. Condron. The officers knocked at the door and demanded admission. Their presence, however, was unheeded, the occupants evidently having retired to rest. At length the landlady was aroused, and opened the door. She was con- siderably startled when P.C. Pitt stepped into the entrance, followed by several other tall dark figures, but sumin med up sufficient courage to ask their business. In a matter- of-fact tone Pitt replied that they were in search of a man who was charged with neglecting his family. Mrs. Condron replied that she was -convinced there was no one in the house they could want for such a purpose, and desired the officers to enter. They accordingly did so, and the Irish detective and Inspector Barnett questioned her as to her various lodgers. Among the latter WAS a man of the name of Smit'e, on hearing which name Sergeant O'Brien, from information in his possession concluded he was on the right track, and accompanied by several of the officers he went upstairs Here there seems to have been a difficulty in recoSising the culprit, for Mrs. Condron alleges that the policemen remained in the bedroom an hour. Smith when aroused stoutly. denied that be was the man wanted; and refused to acknowledge that Rogerson, the name by which Sergeant O'Brien accosted him, was his proper cognomen. Sergeant O'Brien then said "Come, that won't do; I knew you very well in Ireland and am sure yen are the man.' Smith at trois seemed confused, stepped frem his bed and dressed himself, without further attempting to deny his identity. As we have stated an hour elapsed from this point before the officers descended from the bedroom, and what took place there is a mystery to the occupants and lodgers of the house. However, when they did emerge, Mrs. Con- dron, who, in common with the other inmates of the house, had regarded Rogerson, alias Smith, as a quiet, inoffensive young Irishman, demanded: "Are you quite sure you have got the right man ? " No doubt seems to have lingered in the minds of the officers on that point, for they conveyed their prisoner without further parley to the cells at Widnes Police Station. The arrest had been conducted with such secrecy that until half-past six on Wednesdayevening when Sergeant O'Brien conveyed his charge (whose clever capture is deserving of handsome recognition) by the London and North-Western Railway to Manchester, where Rogerson will be detained until he can be handed over to the Irish authori- ties. The prisoner's real name is stated to be John Rogerson. He is 22 years of age, and the son of a farmer residing at Culler, near Ballyfoden, Ireland. He is described as a tall, Nein young man,with light hair,of common-place appearance and quiet inoffensive manners. He seemed to know some members of the Irish community in Widnes on his arrival, but he received very few visitors at Mrs. Condron's, where he had lodged during his stay in the town. He never re— ceived any communications by post. To his fellow-lodgers he appeared to be an ordinary character intent upon making an honest livelihood, although he was always very reserved regarding his past life and connections, and at times seemed so gloomy that they fancied he had something preying on his mind-. There was, however, nothing in his actions to lead anyone to suppose that he was a desperate character. He is stated to have been a good Catholic and tO have at- tended mass at Father Clarke's church in Lugsdale with regularity. It is alleged that Rogerson is one of the prin- cipals in a dynamite outrage committed at the residence of Mr. John Rosman of Weston House, Ahascragh, county Galway, who is a fended proprietor and a partner in the firm of Messrs. A. Guinness and Co., of Dublin, the celebrated brewers. The outrage was committed on the night of the 20th of March, 1882, by a band of Moonlighters. The prisoner, with about ten more men, laid a large quantity of dynamite against Mr. Rosman's house, while the family and domestics, with the exception of Mr. Rosman, were in bed, and the effects of the explo- sion were the destruction of the whole of the windows and irreparable injury to a large quantity of valuable furniture. Fortunately none of the inmates were injured, as the dyna- mite had been ignited in an unscientific manner, else the place would have been entirely demolished, and its inmates killed. It is said there was sufficient material used to have blown up the Tower of London. Six men are already com- mitted for trial for the offence, and this prisoner makes the seventh. It appears the outrage was committed at the in- stance of a man who farmed under Mr. Rosman, and who was distrained upon for several years' arrears of rent. It has been proved that he instigated the geng to commit the heinous offence. The police authorities have reason to be- lieve that another dynamitard has been recently in Widnas, and was a fellow lodger with Regereon. His name was Barnet Garritty, and he worked as a labourer at Messrs. Pil- kington's chemical works, where Rogerson also was employed. He lodged at Mrs. Condron's for twelve months, but left the town about two months ago without hinting in the vaguest manner where be was going.
