The Greenock police yesterday entered premises in Crawford-street and seized an illicit still and 20 gallons of whiskey. Thomas Welsh and Catherine Kelly, who were caught in the act of distilling whiskey, were brought la:. fore the mac-istrates and fined £3O and £5 respectively. A COUN l'Y COURT JUDGE ON MONEY-LENDERS. Mr. Woodforde, county court judge at Hereford, during the hearing, yesterday, of a case against a Birmingham money-lender, said he should be glad to see these thieves (money-lenders) exterminated. They were the curse and ruin of the working classes. THE DECEASED WIFE'S SISTER BILL.

The 42 Peers who voted for the second reading of the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill were absent on Thursday night, while the 17 who were then absent now voted in favour of the third reading. The 35 Peers who opposed the second reading were absent, while the 22 then absent now voted against the third reading. The Daily News says :—The Deceased Wife's Sister Bill having 1)&11 defeated by the vote of the bishops, thus nullifying, a clear majority of the temporal Pee-s, arrange- ments are atnut to Da mane tor noicllng meetlngs in varioue eris of tb noeiotry to call for the removal of the bishops iron, Ow House of Lora.
A: YOUN LADY CO N VIC OF R )11BERY : PAINFUL CASE.

Mary Boocott, 19 years of age, of ladylike appearance, and the daughter of highly-respectable parents at Nottingham, was, at the Birmingham. Quarter Sessions, yesterday, found guilty of stealing a purse containing £5 from the Misses Yrk's Ladies' School, Bristol-road, Birmingham, and sen- tenced to four months' imprisonment. The girl was on a vi&t to some friends in Birmingham, and visited the school respecting a situation as governess After her departure the purse was missed, but prisoner was not in the slightest degree suspected until the police found that she had committed the theft. The accused, and several of her relatives who had attended from Nottingham, wept bitterly upon bearing the verdict of guilty and the sentence.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT,
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT,
HOUSE OF LORDS.

Lord Alcester's and Lord Wolseley's Grant Bills received the Royal assent.—Lord STRLTRNAIRN called attention to the system of recruiting for the army. He said the short service system had broken down. Lord MORLEY defended the short service, under wnieh they got 30,000 recruits per annum, while under the long service they had a difficulty in getting 15,000. The subject dropped.—The report of amendments on the Criminal LEM Ameadment Bill was agreed to, and the House adjourned.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

A SECOND SUEZ CANAL—Mr. BOURKE gave notice that at the earliest opportunity he should move that no arrange- ment for making a second Suez Canal would be satisfactory which d:d not provide for the reduction of tolls and adequate representation of British shipping in the administration.
'CHOLERA IN EGYPT.—Lord IiARTINGTON intimated that every care would be taken to protect British troops in Egypt from the cholera. There was nothing at present to cause apprehension. _ . _

THE Coma= PRACTICES BILL.—The House went into Committee on the Corrupt Practices Bill.—On clause 6, Mr. COWEN proposed that any person wlao should lend his own carriage, or provide other carriages to convey voters to or from the poll, shall be guilty of illegal practice, but this should not prevent any person using his own carriage for the conveyance of himself or other persons in company with him to vote.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL consented to modify the clue in order to prevent horse borrowing or using hired carriages let out for hire. He proposed to allow a candidate to hire a carriage for himself, but not other persons, and to accept voluntary offers.— After some discussion, Mr. COWEN wish( d to withdraw his amendment in favour of Mr. Leake.—The amendment, however, was negatived.—Mr. LEAKE then moved an addi- tion to the clause, which provided that no person should lend a carriage to an election committee or agent, or to any othor person for conveying voters to or from the poll, and every person so borrowing or lending should be guilty of an illegal practice.—The ATTORNEY•GENERAL could not accept the proposal—On a division, there voted—for addition to clause 54. against 244. Mr. SHEIL moved the omission of subsection 3, which pro- vided that where it was ordinary practice for an elector to let house, land, or building for exhibiting bills or advertise- ments' such practice should not be deemed corrupt practice, but that he should be deemed to be employed for reward and not entitled to vote. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL objected to the omission of that proviso.—Mr. STAVELEY HILL hoped the proviso would not be struck out.—The pro- posal to omit the subsection was withdrawn.—Lord R. CHURCHILL thought the subsection ought to be re-cast, as it would not meet the object intended—that of putting a stop to the hiring of shop windows for exhibiting bills at election times. He moved the omission of the first two lines of that sub-section.—Lord B. Churchill's proposal was agreed to.—Mr. LEWIS moved the omission of the last por- tion of the sub-section which deprived an elector from vot- ing where he was engaged under the sub-section for hire or rewards.—After discussion, the proposal was rejected, and the clause was agreed to.—Clause 7, which made the ex- penditure of money over the amount provided in the bill an illegal practice, was then proposed.—Lord G. HAMILTON moved an amendment for limiting the time for election ex- penditure—After a long discussion the amendment was withdrawn, and progress was reported; and the sitting was I suspended.

The House resumed at 10 minutes past 9. EDIICATION.—Sir J. LUBBOCK called the attention of the House to the fact that the minster whose duty it was to bring forward the educational estimates in the House had never any power of appointing the officers to whom the administration of the votes was -en trusted. He moved that in the opinion of the House the time had arrived when there should be a separate department of education.—Lord LYMINGTON warmly supported the proposal. LEFT SITTING.]

div.head: WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.
div.p: THE WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.

1 The 4epositions of the old man William Baron, clogget, 5, Barn-street, Widnes, who is lying at Widnes Hospital suffering from a broken leg, were taken is the presence of the prisoner, Timothy Leonard, on Saturday morning. The magistrate was Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, junr.—The prosecutor said the prisoner went to his shop on Saturday night, the 18th inst., for a clog which he had been clogging for him. The prisoner asked the price and he told him &I. The prisoner said 7d. was enough. Just previous to this some boys had been annoying him in front of the shop, and he went out to drive them away. As he was coming back he saw that the prisoner was trying to get away with the clog. He seized the prisoner by the coat and called for the police. The prisoner put his band on his shoulder, raised his foot, and kicked him on the hip. He "smashed him on the ground with his foot." The prisoner, when he kicked him, said, "take that," and then ran away. He (prosecutor) then found that he could not lift his right leg, and had to be carried into the shop. He did not give the prisoner the least provocatian.—Cross-ex- amined by Mr. Knowles (who appeared for the prisoner) witness said it was the prisoner's weight, and the vengeance with which he kicked him that broke his leg. He bad never offered to settle the matter for £2O. He did not bear the prisoner any malice. Some of the prisoner's friends had been to him and he had told them that if they would pay the damages," settle the police," and make all square, he did not want him to be sent to prison.—Dr. O'Kedle said the prosecutor was suffering from a fracture of the neck of the thigh bone. Being an old man he would not like to pronounce him out of danger. There was a good deal of swelling but no appearance of a kick. It was his opinion that the leg had bees broken by a fall.—Evidence which has been previously given having been rep,!atfd, the pri- soner was taken to tba police station and formally com- mitted to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

div.head: Tattero to tte editor.
div.p: Tattero to tte editor.

"THE PLAY'S THE THING." Sir,—When the public are once satisfied that a nuisance mast be removed, their readiest means of protesting against is through the public press. Warrington is fast becoming one of the largest Lancashire towns; its working-class recreations should be of a healthy and vigorous kind. The public-house, circus, theatre—all are catering largely for a share of that surplus capital the workman may have to spend. As a rule, the public-house is provided with com- fortable and inviting bar rooms, where a few hours each evening may be happily spent in spite of all Sir W. Lawson may say to the contrary. But what shall we say of the circus and theatre? Each in its way plays a paltry part locally. To the theatre remains all the possibilities of a grand educational scheme; to the stay of the future will our children look for desirable relaxatton. Managers, when blamed for placing immoral or suggestive pieces on the boards, at once retort by saving that they meet the public demand. From the days of Wycherley to the present time this may have been so. Before education became compul- sory a higher life was unknown to the people. Either a narrow debasing cant, termed religion, or, on the other hand, a desire for all that was low and obscene, was all that was placed before them. Both were but the outcome of ignorance. Surely our children, who are now being edu- cated at almost railway speed, will not be satisfied with such a state of things as this. For men to sit listening to a lot of stupid and ignorant talk from Salvation lasses may be possible for a time, but this will give place to something vastly better p If to eburch and chapel the people must go, it will only be to hear men more learned thal themselves. A feast of reason must be spread before them. And now, Mr. Editor, what shall we say of the building in which all this is to take place? In all conscience no fault can be found with the buildings that minister to the .wants of the upper and middle classes; but where do the lower classes meet? The street corners compete with the fields and lanes. Stewed up in an unhealt by workshop all the week, the more sensible seize the opportunity when it comes of getting a whiff of fresh air, and who ;hall blame them? But during the week there are times when the mind wants a little change, and the body forthwith sallies out to obey this natural call. If to the theatre fancy Jack Robinson asking his wife and family to accompany him to Scotland-road theatre to see Henry Irving in "Much ado about nothing." Why, she would think either herself or our leading actor was going to be insulted. In fact, I think I ought to apologise for linking the mere name of Irving with our grand local Thespian in- stitute. Nothing of a modern and civilising character should dare to intrude itself upon that relic of the past. There it is—cold, damp, draughty, egress and ingress, fit monuments of our forefathers' wisdom, a nuisance of which the caloric part of nature seems to be entirely unaware. There are some buildings that have come down to us from the past, upon which we look with respect and veneration; the vandal's hand must only touch them after careful in- quiry has been made, but the building I refer to has but one venerator, and he is all-sufficient, all-powerful. I almost expect he will place a notice board up at each end of Scot- land-road, warning lovers of the beautiful off. He himself being such a lover of the old and ugly will be found striking a proper attitude and crying Builder spare that pile, Touch not one single brick, Warrington, June 27, 1883. CLIFFORD DIX.

For twelve months sin e the date mentioned in the summons she had been an inmate of the Workhouse, and her husband had not contributed to her supp >A for 15 months. The family had ill-used her shamefully, and she alleged that the defendant was concealing his brother at Widnes.—Superintendent Wil- liamson observed that the woman was being badly treated The police had a warrant for her husband for not contributing to her support. He was in hiding at Widnes.—Mr. Bankes said the complainant could not wish to press this case after the lapse of 18 months, and asked him if he would withdraw it.— The complainant declined.—Mr. Bankes said his action looked like vindictiveness, and under the circumstances the Bench dismissed the case. OLD OFFENDERS.—John Hewitt, who had been 20 times pre- viously c3IIVICted, was tined 15s and costs for drunkenness; and J ,hn Finney, who had been cmvicted 15 times, was fined lOs and costs for a slmilar offense.—Robert Bradley, a lodging- house keeper, whose 12th appearance it was, was fined. 203 and costs also for having been drunk and desorderly on Sunday. CHIMNEY ON FraE.—John Wailing was fined Is and c'sts for having allowed his dwelling-housa chimney to be on fire in Frederick-street on the 13th inst.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
ACEON GRANGE

At the Liverpool Police Court, on Wednesday, James Bradford, wholesale milkdealer, of Acton Bridge, was fined 20s. and costs for sending to Liverpool for sale a quantity of new milk containing ten parts of water to every 100 parts of milk.

div.head: ALTRINCHAM.
div.p: ALTRINCHAM.

ALLEGED ATTEMPT TO PASS BASE COlN.—CleMelltilla Weever, who was staying with some relative at Altrincham, was charged at Sale, on Monday, with attempting to pass a base half-crown. The prisoner, it is alleged, attempted to pass the coin at three shops, bat did not succeed. She was committed fer trial. COUNTY COURT BUSINESS IN ALTRINCHAM.—III reply to an address of Mr. Norwood, M.P., dated the 6th day of June, 1883, a return from every county court in England and Wales was issued on Saturday last, giving the total' number of plaints, Sze., entered for trial, with the sums sued for, casts, and fees. We give below that part referring to Altrincham :—ln this court there were 1,989 plaints en- tered for trial, for sums amounting to £5,023. Of these 1,072 were determined, and judgments obtained for £2,690, exclusive of costs (£322) and fees (£739). The moneys received to the credit of suitors was £2,846, and the amount paid to them £2,885, During the year 744 judg- ment summonses were issued, 4613 heard; 207 warrants of commitment issued, 16 debtors imprisoned, 427 executions against goods, and 10 sales made. CROFT.

CHRIST CHURCH.—On Sunday the annual sermons on be- half of the Sunday School and Choir in connection with the above church were preached morning and evening by the Re. William Wilson, vicar of Burtonwood. The com- munion table and window ledge had been tastefully de- corated for the occasion, by a few of the lady members of congregation, with choice ferns and flowers. There were good congregations at each service, which was full choral; special hymns being sung by the choir. The solo and quartette "Incline Thine ear to me"(Himmel) was given at the morning service, and the anthem" Oh give than!rs unto the Lord" (William Jackson, jun.) in the evening. The bass solo in the morning was creditably sung by Mr. Thomas Marsh, and the alto solo in the anthem was sung with taste by Miss Annie Green. The choir performed their part of the services in a most satisfactory manner, led by Miss Kirk- man. Mr. F. W. Ball the organist and choirmaster presided at the org-,ati with groat abiJUT. Tho eollootione amnnnted to £lO Os 11d. The weather proved unfavourable in the evening, and no doubt prevented many friends from at- tending from a distance. CULOFIETIL

ANNUAL SERMONS AT RISLEY PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH. —On Sunday two sermons were preached in the above church by the Rev. W. D. Fairbairn, M.A., of Eccles, in aid of the funds of the chnrch, and to liquidate the debt on the new harmonium. There was a good congregation at the afternoon service, but only a small attendance in the even- ing, in consequence, no doubt, of the weather being very un- favourable. The collections amounted to £4 14s. FRO DSHA ISL

A SLEEPING WAGGONEIL—SamueI Hunt, Frodsham, was at Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, fined Ds. and costs for being asleep whilst in charge of a waggon and three horses at Acton Grange, on the 2nd inst.—Sergeant Booth said defendant had the reins tied round his legs, and WAS in great danger of falling off the waggon when he was awakened.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

GOLBORNE TRIP TO BLACKPOOL.—The cheap trip from Golborne to Blackpool, arranged in connection with St. Thomas's - Church (Golborne, and St. Mary's Church (Lowton), proved to be very successful. The " special " left Golborne about 6-30, and called at Bampurlong and Wigan. About 510 persons were conveyed by it, and the day was very pleasantly spent. The various attractions of the famous seaside resort were visited, the return journey being commenced about eight o'clock. TREAT TO SCHOLARS AT GOLBORNE.—The Congregational Sunday School scholars received their annual treat on Fri- day afternoon last. Over 200 assembled at the chapel, and after singing a few hymns marched through the town. At the residences of Mr. R. Yates, Mrs. Travis, Mr. Mitchell, and Mr. Davies, hymns were sung, and on returning to the school the scholars sat down to their annual tea' which was greatly enjoyed. They afterwards proceeded to afield kindly lent by Mrs. Burchall, and here they pleasantly spent the remainder ef the afternoon.

CHURCH SCHOOL TREAT AT GOLBORNE.—The scholars attending St. Thomas' Schools, Golborne, were regaled with their annual treat on Friday last, and, as in former years, spent a very enjoyable afternoon. They met at the church shortly before one o'clock, and a short service was held, iu which the rector, the Rev. C. T. Quirk, and the Rev. W. Thorpe (curate) took part. On being formed in proces- sional order they paraded the grounds attached to the Rectory, and sang two or three hymns. They were after- wards led by the Golborne brass band through the streets of the town to Mr. Brewis' house, where nuts and oranges were given to the band, while the teachers had other re- freshments. At the school they were regaled with a capital tea, at the conclusion of which they adjourned to the cricket club field and amused themselves until dusk. The band played several selections of music in a creditable manner.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST SCHOOL TREAT AT HAYDOCK.— The scholars attending the Primitive Methodist Sunday School, Haydock, were regaled with their annual treat and field-day on Friday afternoon last. About 60 attended at the school, and on the way to a field near Pewfall, kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. B tlharry, sang at the residences of Mr. James Tarton, Mr. William Alker, Mrs. Cunliffe, Mrs. Briscoe, and Mrs. Forshaw. The tea was an excellent one, and was partaken of by all present with evident relish. Afterwards the scholars enjoyed themselves in playing the customary games and sports until dusk put a slop to the enjoyment. HAVDOCK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL SCHOLARS' TREAT. —The annual treat to the scholars attending Haydock Wesleyan Sunday School took place on Thursday after- noon last week. The scholars, to the number of nearly SOO, assembled at the schoolroom about one o'clock, and were formed in precessional order. They proceeded to the resi- dence of Mrs. Evans, who had kindly granted them per- mission to walk through the grounds, and here milk, buns, were supplied to the scholars, Mrs. Evans generously defraying the cost. On leaving the Heyes, the scholars , walked to a field at Garswood Park, and on the route thereto Isang various hymns at the houses of Mrs. Cunliffe and Mr. William Alker. The field had been kindly placed at their disposal by Mr. Hurst, and everyone thoroughly enjoyed themselves. Daring the afternoon the scholars were treated to their annual tea, after which games, races, &c, were heartily indulged in until dusk. HA (DOCK CHURCH CHoirt ANNUAL PIC-NlC.—The choirs of St. James's Ch lamb, and St. Alban's Mission Church at Haydock were treated to their annual pic-nic or outing on Friday last. The whole of the arrangements in connection therewith were made . by the Rev. H. Mason

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 30 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 30 1883.

(curate), and it is to that gentleman's credit that everything passed off as successfully as it did. About 40 members of the choirs (including a few friends) assembled at the Gars- wood station, and they proceeded by the 6.40 a.m. train to Southport, at which place they arrived about nine o'clock. The company afterwards broke up into different narties, and while some were enjoying a walk to the water or a sail thereon, others were strolling about the pier, promenade, Sze., or paying a visit to the Botanic Gardens, the Winter Gar- dens, and other attractions of the popular sea-side resort. At half-past three in the afternoon, the whole of the com- pany assembled (by previous arrangement) at the Botanic Gardens and together partook of a most enjoyable tea. The journey home was commenced at 7 o'clock, and everyone arrived " safe and sound" after the day's outing. Notwith- standing one or two slight showers, the day was very pleasantly spent.

at the point, he ran for assistance. The nearest place at which assistance could be procured, however, was the Red Cat public-house, about a mile dis- tant from the scene of the accident. Lathom there found a , young man named John Carrigan, who ran back with him and went into the water and brought out the body of deceased. An inquest was held on Monday by Mr. Barker, county coroner, relative to the affair at the "Original Red Cat" public-house.---After evidence to the above effect had been given the Coroner said that was a very sad affair. It seemed a pure accident, deceased having acme into the cold water while in a heated condition, and had probably been seized with cramp. The only thing occurring to him (the coroner) was that it appeared to be a thoughtless act on the part of Lathom to run away when by stepping into the water, which was not deep, he might have saved the poor fellow's life. But he seemed to have been paralysed with fear, and thought it best, under the circumstances, to run for help.—The jury were of opinion that deceased, who it appeared was a good swimmer and had often bathed in the same pool before, had been seized with cramp and con- seqaently became helpless. A verdict of "Accidental death" was therefore returned. _
WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

Mr. T. Sutton Ticamis, the chairman, presided over the monthly meeting held at the Board-room, Victoria—road, on Thursday. There were also present Revs. Fathers Fin— negan and Clarke, Messrs. J. Brock, H. W. Deacon, R. Shaw, W. Hartland, R. H. Davies, H. Brunner, G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: HITYTON.
div.p: HITYTON.

HUTTON ENGINEER VOLUNTEERS. - The officers and men of the corps of volunteer engineers recently formed at Huvton, in connection with the 2nd Lancashire Engißeer Volunteers, had their first battalion drill on Saturday after- noon. They proceeded from Huyton to St. Helens by train, and marched from the station to the Drill Hall, Croppers Hill, where they were formed in battalion, along with their St. Helens comrades, and in the subsequent drill went through various movements in a very smart and satisfactory manner. The Huyton contingent numbered five sergeants and 97 men, and were under the ccmmand of Captain Campbell, of Prescot. The other officers present were— Lieutenant-Colonel Rothwell, Captain and Adjutant Curry, Major T. Wilcock, Captain Craik, and Lieuts. Lyon, Pendia- bury, and Rothwell. HUTTON QUARRY.

ALLEGED INDECENT ASSAULT AT HUYTON QUARRY.— At Prescot, on Thursday, three men named McCann, Robinson, and Fleet, were brought up in custody before Mr. T. Pilkington, charged with indecently assaulting Margaret Lester. The prosecutrix is a girl about 14 years of age, and it was stated that last Tuesday evening she went to the Huyton Quarry Ironworks with some men's suppers, and while passing through a shed on her way out of the works was laid bold of by the prisoners and indecently assaulted. The prisoners were apprehended by P.C. Hall.—The magistrates committed them for trial. KINGSLEY.

REMOVING PIGS WITHOUT A LICENSE.—John Oultram, shoemaker, Kingsley, was at Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, fined 3s. and costs for allowing three pigs to be removed from his residence into another township without a license.—William "Lindley, who was charge with removing the pigs, was dismissed. KNOWSLEY.

THE CROPS.—Our Know9ley correspondent, reviewing harvest prospects in his locality, informs us that wheat when weighed in the balance will be found wanting. Oats will be short in the straw. The rains which have fallen and are now falling will do the two cereals mentioned good, but will not be of sufficient effect to bring them up to an average standard. Barley has a yellow look, but it is coming round, and an average crop is anticipated. Beans will be a good crop. Potatoes are looking remarkably well. Hay will be as much under the average as it was last year. The district of Knowsley suffered greatly in the month of May from the want of rain, the oats being especially distressed. It may be remarked that the position of the district with regard to rainfall is so peculiar as to be worth investigation. LEIGH.

COUNTY Cotarr BUSINESS irr LEIGH.—In reply to an I address of Mr. Norwood, M.P., dated the 6tla day of June, 1883, a return from every county court in England and Wales was issued on Saturday last, giving the total num- ber of plaints, dm. entered for trial, with the sums sued for, costs, and fees. We give below that part referring to Leigh: —ln this court 2,943 plaints were entered for trial, repre- senting £6,843. Of these 2,150 were determined, ani judg- ments entered for £4,977, exclusive of costs (£169) and fees (£1,197). The amount paid to the credit of suitors was £3,972, and the amount paid out was £3,997. There were 1,023 judgment summonses issued, 753 heard; 252 warrants of commitment issued, 38 debtors imprisoned, 875 execu- tions against gopds, and 29 sales made. LY MIL A NEW BRASS BAND.—A brass band has been formed in connection with the Primitive Methodist Sunday School, Lymm, and nine instruments have been presented by Mr. John Naylor, of Thelwall. ANNIVERSARY SERMONS AT LYMIL—Lailt Sunday morn- ing and evening the 21st anniversary sermons were preached in Lymm Congregational Church by the Rev. W. Reid, of Levenshulme. In the afternoon there was a children's ser- vice, and between £l7 and £lB was realised by the collec- tions. DEATH OF Ma. GEORGE FORREST.—At the good old‘age of 75 years Mr. George Forrest, who has been connected with Lymm for many years, passed away on Sunday morning last. Mr. Forrest was one of the oldest deacons of the Congregational Church, and was highly respected. ;us remains were interred at Hill Cliffe burial ground on Tutl- d ay last. LIVERPOOL CONSERVATIVES AT LYMM. On Monday Lymm was visited by 85 members of the North Toxteth (No. 2) Branch of the Liverpool Workingmen's Conservative I Association, on the occasion of their 7th annual pic-nic. The party were conveyed to Lymm by train from Lime-st. Station, and spent the day in rambling about the pretty grounds of the rector of the parish (Rev. W. Guest) and of Mr. W. Battersby, a prominent local Conservative, and in indulging in various outdoor recreations. The weather, al- though dull and portentious, fortunately kept fine until late in the afternoon, and contributed much to the enjoyment of the plc-ulcers. In the evening the party sat down to a sub- stantial repast at the Plough Hotel. The chair was occupied by Mr. James Warrington (chairman of the branch), and amongst those present were Councillor John Hughes, Messrs. R. Jones, J. T. Metcalf, E. M. Loftus (secretary), I'. Ardern (treasurer to the Lvmm Conservative Association), I'. At- kinson, J. Pratt, J. 'Ellis, T. Foulkes, W. Lloyd, J. Hughes, S. Swift, Szc. After dinner CouncillorJohn Hughes addressed a few words to those present. Mr. William Lloyd moved votes of thanks to Mr. Thomas Ardern, treasurer to the Lynam Constitutional Association, for the kindness he had shown to members during the day, and to the Rector of the parish and Mr. Battersby for having allowed the campany to inspect their grounds. The motion was seconded by Mr. J. Hughes (ex-chairman of the branch), and carried by ac- clamation. Mr. Ardern briefly acknowledged the compli- ment. After dinner the Lymm Brass Band played for dancing in the Assembly Room. NANTWICH.

THE NANTWICH HIGHWAY BOAUD.—The Naßtwich High- way Board have received a communication from Mr. Dolby, Government auditor, surcharging members £630 in conse- quence of what he described as the wilful and persistent neglect of the surveyor to obtain the workmen's signatures to the wages sheets. The board described the routine required by the department as a nuisance, and decided to petition the Local Government Board to remit the disallow- ance. _ _ _

A LADY AND HER GROOM IN PARTNERSHIP.—Mr. T. Hughes, Q.C., has given his decision in a case which has excited considerable interest in Cheshire. Mr. John Cooper, of Nantwich, whose wife was killed in the hunting field some time ago. brought an action against her groam, Mottram, to recover possession of the horse which she then rode, and also the recovery of a sum of money which, he alleged, Mottram abstracted from his wife's pocket as she lay un- conscious. Mottram persisted that the horse belonged to himself by virtue of his partnership with Mrs. Cooper in horse•dealing transactions. The latter portion of plaintiff's case fell through, but the judge ordered the ofendant to deliver up the horse to the plaintiff. NORTH WICH.

COUNTY COURT BUSINESS IN NORTRWICR.—In reply to an address of Mr. Norwood, M.P.. dated the 16th of June, 1883, a return from every county court in England and Wales was issued on Saturday last, giving the total number
of plaints, &c., entered for trial with the sums sued for, costs and fees. We give below that part referring to North- wich :—ln this court 2,421 plaints were entered for trial, _ _

representing the sum of £5,832. Of these 1,541 were deter- mined, and judgments obtained for £3,465, exclusive of costs (£118) and fees £922). The moneys received to the credit of suitors was £2,749, and the amount paid out £2,797. There were 432 judgment summonses issued, 318 heard; 137 warrants of commitment issued, 7 debtors im- prisoned, 723 executions against goods, and 3 sales made. ATHLETIC SPORTS.—This annual festival was held on Saturday, in Winnington Park, Northwich. The weather being very fine there were several thousand spectators. The competitors numbered about 150, and came from all parts of tke northern counties. The following were the principal events :—Two miles bicycle handicap: 1 S. Nabb, Bury, 230 yards; 2F. W. Parry, Shipbrook, 250; 3 E. Bramall. Allostock, 400. One mile bicycle handicap: Final heat-1 S. Nabb, Bury, 110 yards; 2 F. W. Parry, 130; 3 S. Shaw. Shipbrook, 200. One mile flat race: 1 P. Pierpoint, War- rington, 100 yards; 2 Richard Broome, Appleton, 115. 100 yards flat race handicap: Final heat-1 E. M'Evoy, War- rington, 111 yards; 2 A. Baks Beechwood Harriers, 10; 3F. Lee, knutsford, 10. Half-mile fiat race handicap: William Waring, Widnes, 60 yards, and John T. Elsby, Sandbach, 75, ran dead heat for first place ; 3 George Taylor, Crewe, 72. Quarter-mile flat race handicap: IF. A. Hart, Knutsford, 40 yards; 2 James Riley, Crewe, 33; 3 G. H. Cross, Altrincham, 20; 200 yards flat race: Final heat-1 J. H. Fair, Warrington; 2H. Wren; 3J. M‘Mahon. The prizes were subsequently distributed by Mrs. Mond, Win- nington Hall. OVER.

On Sunday, the annual sermons of the Chester-road Primitive Methodist Sunday School were preached by Mr. Miles Parks, of Norleston, who being a popular United Free Methodist local preacher attracted a good congrega- tion, resulting in replenishe 1 funds. These were further increased on Monday by a public meeting, presided over by Mr. William Dodd, when the choir and the scholars sang, recited, and gave dialogues very successfully. The collec- tions came to £5.

div.head: RAINFORD.
div.p: RAINFORD.

SAD DROWNING CASE AT RAINFORD.—On Saturday, a sad accident occurred at Rainford whereby a young man named Martin Duffy, a labourer, lost his life. Duffy, it appears, and another young man named Lathom were going home from work on Saturday at noon, when they stopped beside a pit of water, and deceased, who told his companion that be could do several good tricks in the water, undressed and went into the pit. He swam about three-parts of the way across when Lathom observed him to fling up his arms and diaappear beneath the water. Lathom at first thought deceased was doing one of his tricks, but as he did not rise again, be seems to have lost his presence of mind, and instead of making an attempt to rescue his unfortu- nate .companion, which he might perhaps have done, as the water was less than four feet deep

div.head: UPHOLLAND.
div.p: UPHOLLAND.

THE RESTORATION OF THE CHURCH.—The Earl of Lathom, on Monday, opened a bazaar at Upholland, near Wigan, which is being held in aid of the fund for restoring the ancient priory church of Upholland. The present rector, the Rev. F. D. Cremer, since his appointment, has been most assiduous in his efforts to restore this well-known edifice, which for many years has been in a dilapidated condition. About £3,000 will be required to complete the alterations and restoration, and nearly .£2,000 has already been promised. Lord Lathom, in his short address, said Mr Cremer deserved every encouragement. The way in w.J3ich he had improved the church from the disgraceful object that it used to lee did him infinite credit, and he per- sonally thanked him for what he had done in that direc- tion. Amongst the ladies presiding at the stalls were the Countess of Lathom and the Countess of Crawford and Balcarres.

div.head: WESTON POINT.
div.p: WESTON POINT.

CAUTION TO BOATMEN AT WESTON POINT.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Robert Brock, a boatman, was charged that he, being in charge of the Emiline on the Weaver Navigation, did on the Bth instant obstruct the passage contrary to the bye-laws made by the trustees. Captain Clark appeared to prosecute. It seemed that the defendant disputed with Richard Shaw, the lock tenter, as to his turn. Because the latter would not allow him to go through the lock, be ran his boat between the gates, which could not then be cl,sed. The lock was blocked for 50 minutes. A fine of 10s and costs (12s 61) was imposed. WESTON CHURCH OF ENGLAND SCHOOLS.—The Rev. J. J. Bryant, M.A :preached sermons in aid of these schools on Sunday morning and evening. In the afternoon a children's service was held.

div.head: WHA.RTON.
div.p: WHA.RTON.

The committee of the Band of Hope connected with the Wesleyan Chapel had appointed Wednesday afternoon and evening for their great field-day, sports, walk, tea, and meeting. Unfortunately the rain stopped the sports and walk, and greatly interfered with the mixed meeting in the evening. The chairman (Mr. John H. Cooke) very ably performed his part, as did the organist (Mr. Singleton) and the chapel choir. We may praise the Union Workhouse children, under the charge of the master (Mr. Howarth), and assisted by Miss Olive Brock. The only drawback to complete success was the wet afternoon and evening. CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS' MEETING.—The meeting of the Sunday school teachers of the Middlewich Rural Deinery took place in the Wharton National School, Winsford, last Saturday afternoon, where the vicar, the Rev. C. Cay, gave out the hymn "0 happy band of pilgrims," and prayed. In addition to the many Sunday school teachers present were the following clergy :—Revs. Cay (Wharton), Hopkins (Moulton), T. W. H. France- Hayhurst (Davenham), Garnett (Delamere), Sturges ( Daven- him), Whitehead (Norley), Arnold (Tarporley), and the Rural Dean (Canon Cooper), who presided. Mr. Sturges read the report of the previous meeting; and in the absence of the Rev. Mr. Chapman (the deputation) consented to give the model lesson (Bible) to a class of girls collected for the purpose. He took "The Good Samaritan" as his subject, which •he handled very successfully. It was afterwards criticised by various teachers andthe clergy very favourably, and a vote of thanks was accorded to the rev, gentleman for the service rendered so willingly. The officers and repre- sentatives for next year were then appointed, which con- cluded the business of the meeting.

div.head: WHISTON.
div.p: WHISTON.

STATE or rue CROPS.—The rainfall has been beneficial in causing the early sown wheat to regain its colour, and assume a more promising appearance, but it is to be re- gretted the farmers have not been able to sow but a very small breadth of what they iutended. Oats are commencing to shoot, but will be as a general rule, very short in the straw. Potatoes late, although some fields are looking re- markably well. Turnips in many cases a failure, and have to be sown a second time. Second years lays, cuts down very thin generally, the rain having come too late. The same applies to clover crops. Altogether the hay crops, will be a long way below the average. Very little barley sown in the district. On Mr. Leatherbarrow''s farm, there is a remarkably fine field of potatoes. WINSFORD.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST ANNIVERSXDIES.—The annual sermons on 11. half of the Primitive Methodist Sunday School, Statinn-road, were preached on Sunday by Mr. Wm. Therm, of I.; verpool. The collection amounted to £5 103.

div.head: -ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
div.p: -ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

William Warbrick, a fitter, of Openshaw, gave himself into custody at Chester, on Tuesday, stating that he had murdered his wife the previous day. Inqiuiries were made, and the woman was found to be at home alive and well. The prisoner's unfounded self-accusation was no doubt due to partial aberration through heavy drinking. NEW MAGIiTRATES FOR CHESHIRE. —lt is understood that at the quarter sessions next week, at Knutsford, several gentlemen will attend to be sworn in as county magistrates. These gentlemen have been nominated by the Duke of West- minster, the new lord-lieutenant of the county. Complaints were made after last sessions at Knutsford at the absence of sufficient jttstices to form a second court, which kept bar- risters in attendance longer than was necessary. This con- dition of affairs will now be remedied. The Wallasey Local Board, finding that the Bishop of Chester declines to consecrate their new cemetery, for reasons he has given, appealed to the Archbishop of York for advice. His Grace states that he cannot interfere with the Bishop's action unlessle has been proved either "legally wrong, or to have wrongly exercised a discretion vested in him." The Board's request, says Dr. Thompson, could only be gratified at the expense of violating two Acts of Parlia- ment, and therefore he cannot move in the matter. COUNTY COURT BUSINESS.—In reply to an address of Mr. Norwood, M.P., dated the 6th day of June, 1883, a return from every county court in England and Wales was issued on Saturday last giving the total number of plaints, &c., entered for trial, With the sums sued for, costs an fees. We give below that part referring to Nantwich and Crewe :—ln this court 2.471 plaints were entered for trial, representing the sum of £6,381. Of these 1,422 were determined, and judgments obtained for £3,087, exclusive of costs (£313) and fees (£908). The moneys received to the credit of suitors was £3,009, and the amount paid out .£2 963. There were 222 judgment summonses issued, 157 heard; 53 war- rants of commitment issued, 10 debtors imprisoned, 551 executions against goods, and 9 sales made. LAYING I'OISON ON A FARM.-At Broxton (Cheshire) Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Joseph Turner, a ratcatcher, residing near Gresford, was charged with having exposed poison on land in the occupation of Messrs. Sadler, Newton-by-Tattenhall.—Mr. Cartwright, who appeared to prosecute on behalf of the police, said that foxes, cats, and other animals having been found dead in the district, the suspicions of the police were aroused, and Sergeant Morgan discovered beside a hedgerow on Messrs. Sadler's farm several quantities of a granular substance which, on being analysed by Dr. Carter Bell, was found to contain 10 per cent. of arsenic. Defendant had been ratcatching for Messrs. Sadler, and one of these gentlemen stated that he saw him putting on the ground the substance picked up.—A fine of £l3, including costs, was imposed.

RAINHILL SPOHTS.—For these sports, which are to be held to-day (Saturday), we believe that more than 250 entries have been received, amongst whom are many of the most noted athletes of the day. ALLEGED THEFT IN A PIICLIC HOUSE.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday, a man named Thomas Prescott was charged with having stolen 5s from the person of Win. Simpson. It appeared that the prisoner, prosecutor, a man named Michael Finn (who had been previously sent to gaol for the same offence), and two or three others, had all been drinking together in the Sefton Arms on the afternoon of the 12th inst. They were all drunk. Simpson told Finn to call for half a gallon of beer and he would pay for it, but before the beer was served Simpson fell a sleep holding 3s in one of his hands. On the beer being served Finn took a shilling out of Simpson's hand and paid for it, and it was alleged the.prisoner took the other 23. Prisoner said he only took as much from the prosecutor as paid for another half gallon which it was his turn to stand, intending to pay it back again.—As it did not appear that there had been'any felonious intent on the part of the prisoner, the case was dismissed.

VIOLENT ATTACK WITH A BRUSH AT ST. HELENS—On Thursday, at the St. Helena Police Court, a man named Laurence Henry Byrne was charged with having unlawfully wounded Patrick Hughes, on Saturday last. —lt appeared that between three and four o'clock on Saturday afternoon live or six men, of whom the prisoner and prosecutor were two, had been lighting amongst each other in Atlas-court, Parr. The police were informed of what was taking place, and P.C.'s Carruthers and Caunce went to the place. On seeing them the party of combatants rushed into a house belonging to a Patrick Kelly, in which they renewed the conflict. The policemen followed them in and just as they got inside the door they saw the prisoner spring from a corner with a long brush in his hand, with which be struck Hughes on the side of his head. Hughes fell to the ground unconscious with blood flowing very freely from his head. He was taken up by Carruther and placed on a table, but did not regain consciousness for several minutes. He was He was taken to Mr. Cotton's, chemist, Church-street, and remedies were there applied to the wound, but as the blood continued to flow he was afterwards taken to Dr. Donnellan, who stopped the bleeding. The blow had also caused a deaf- ness in one of his ears, although that organ had not bon at all affected previous to the fight. He had not been able to work since.—Prisoner was committed to the Sessions for trial, bail, himself in £4O, and two sureties i 1 £2O each being allowed.

div.head: APPLICANTS.
div.p: APPLICANTS.

The District Education Committee reported that during the month of May (four weeks) the number of cases sum- moned before the committee were the following :—Appli- cation for payment of school fees 80, for contravention of Education Act 242, total 322. Fees were recommended to be paid in 67 cases, and 38 persons were brought before the magistrates and convicted.

THE MANAGEMENT. Father FINNEGAN moved the adoption of the minutes of the School Management Committee which contained the following recommendations :—That the committee be au- thorised to appoint a temporary assistant mistress, from July 9th to October Ist, at a salary at th: rate of £4O per annum, to assist in the girls' department of the Warrington- road schools. That the resignation of Mrs. Todd, head mistress in the infants' department of the West Bank Schools, be accepted, her engagement to terminate September 30th, 1883. That the committee be authorised to obtain medals, in order to carry out rule 103 in the rules for the government of Board Schools, at a cost not exceeding 24s per gross.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £437 us 10d. The school fees for May from Simrn's Cross school was £44 is 3d, Warrington- road £2O Is 11d, West Bank £37 2s 61. There had been paid £1,252 Os 8d into the bank. This sum included £1,150 from the oversesrs on account of precept.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. &tem. COOKERY CI•ASSES TO BE ESTABLISHED. _

Mr. B. HOLDEN DAVIES moved the following resolution, of which he had given notice :—" That cookery be taught to the girls attending the Widnes Board Schools, that the School Management Committee be instructed to advertise for—and recommend to the Board a suitable teacher for appointment at a salaay not ex- ceeding LSO per annum, that they be em- powered to provide the necessary fittings, furniture, and utensils, and that the lessons commence in October next." He remarked that the School Management Committee had prepared an estimate of the cost of estab- lishing and maintaining the Cookery Schools, and they had been very desirous indeed that the estimate should not be understated. At the last meeting of the committee a lady, who was one of the teachers of the Liverpool Cookery Schools, was present, and she after- wards visited Sitnms Cross Cookery School and examined the arrangements. From information he had obtained from that lady and from other sources, Mr. Davies was of opinion that the classes could be established at each for about £5O, whereas the committee's estimate was £B4. The CHAIRMAN: You are quite • satisfied that cooking should be taught at each school, and not at a central class? —Mr. DAVIES said he thought it desirable that teaching should take place at each school, because the walking back- wards and forwards of the children would take up almost as much time as the cookery classes.

At West Bank there was no suitable room except the care- taker's room. The caretaker was quite willing to allow the room to be used for the time the Board would require it, which would only be a few hours a week. Of course he would require some little amount to compensate him. He (Mr. Davies) thought that would be the best way, and more convenient than renting a cottage. Then they came to the grants to be received for passes. The amount put down in the estimate was 4s. per head for 150 scholars, and the question might be asked, "Are you quite sure of obtaining the 48. grant for the whole of the 150 ? " His reply was that the code provided 4s. for each scholar attending the cookery classes 40 hours during the year, and he therefore thought they might safely depend upon the estimate being correct. Then there was a grant for domestic economy. This subject was now taught at the Board schools, and last year six scholars passed. The fact that they passed so few pointed to this: that the teaching had been deficient. He maintained that in teaching cookery they were at the same time teaching domestic economy, and would assist the teacher having that subject in hand. Suppose that half the girls who attended the school earned the grant of 4s. for domestic economy, the total cost of teaching cookery would be a sum much less than was estimated. He drew the atten- tion of the Board to these figures to show that the estimate submitted by the management committee was rather over than under the probable cost of teaching the classes. Sup- posing, however, they took the figures given as actually correct, the total cost of teaching was £75 a year. He had learnt that a farthing rate produced £l3O a year, so that the cost would be considerably under a farthing in the pound. One question, which he thought an important one, had cropped up. It was whether the scholars were not already over- worked, and whether the teaching of an additional subject would not be over-taxing the children. Also whether teaching an additional subject and striving to ob- tain additional grant would interfere with the present work, and diminish the grants the Board at present re- ceived for other subjects. He might say that cookery was taught in several Board schools with the greatest success, ! and he did not see why there should not be a similar ! success in Widnes. As to the children being over-taxed he I had consulted a gentleman in Liverpool, who was a mem- ber, and held a high official position on the School Board in that city. That gentleman said that instead of increasing the pressure, cookery lessons had rather the contrary effect, for the change of work was relaxation, and might almost be called recreation. Cookery, too, might be made an ex- cellent aid to intellectual training. A girl in cooking had to reckon up the cost of every item: she had to weigh out all the ingredients for the particular dish she was preparing, and she had a considerable amount of calculating to do. It would be found in working these out that se would have to tax all her stock of arithmetic, which would prove to her !of what value arithmetic really is. (Hear, hear.) He ! thought in considering this matter they ought to consider ; the position of life the girls in the classes I occupy, and the training and education they gave them should be such as would make them better able to fulfil the duties they would have to perform in the future. He had no hesitation in saying that cookery and domes'ic economy would be of greater service that many of the subjects ! taught in the Board schools, inasmuch as they would assist ! them very much. He thought to teach the children how to prepare wholesome food was of not less importance than 1 the task of teaching them needlework. He had great plea- sure in moving the resolution.—Mr. BRUNNER seconded the proposition. He agreed very decidedly and very cordially with what Mr. Davies had said withregard to teaching cookery in the Board schools. He was glad to hear what Mr. Davies had learned since the last meeting with regard to the extra pressure put upon the children. He must confessfor his own part that he was very much afraid that their classes would be considerably below the mark, because he thought it pos- sible that although they might get a grant for teaching cookery, ha did not see how it was possible that they could get it without reducing the grant in other departments. He took it that their children were now fully occupied from Monday morning to Frigay afternoon, and were doing as much as they possibly could. It was difficult for one to understand how they could possibly be got to do more and earn a larger grant in the same number of hours per week. However, he supposed, from what Mr. Davies had said and the experience of other places, they might rest well satisfied on that point Unlike Mr. Davies, he did not think the estimate could be materially reduced, although he granted that in some items it might be. Mr. Brunner observed that it was proposed to erect a kitchen range at Warrington-road school, such as the scholars would probably have in their own homes, for it was not likely they would have a gas stove. Before undertaking a subject of this kind, he though the teachers ought to be consulted, because it was quite possible that although the grant might be increased by the cookery grant, the grant in other subjects might be reduced and the head teachers suffer.—The CLERK: We don't pay by results ?—The CHAIRMAN: To a certain extent.— Mr. BRUNNER : We give bonuses.—Father FINE- GAN : Their parchment also depends upon the report.— Mr. BRUNNER said he would second the resolution with the reservation that the teachers be consulted before it was put in force.—Father FiNEGAN, as one of the committee, obser- ved that he was quite taken unawares by the turn things had taken. His friends, Mr. Davies and Mr. Brunner might have proposed the motion in committee and brought it as a recommendation of the committee, and not leave it.to an in- dividual to bring it before the Board. He understood on the last occasion they met that Mr. Brunner was in opposition to the scheme ; otherwise there was nothing to prevent the motion coming from the committee. Mr. Davies had pre- sented them with a scheme, and if they accepted it, he must admire their faith very much on that occasion, because Mr. Davies had previously brought two schemes before the Board which had not been carried out. He should be ver y glad if Mr. Davies' present scheme, and estimate of the cost was the right one, but he could not let the subject pass by without, in as strong a way as he could, telling the Board his opinion on the teaching of cookery in their schools. No one, be thought, was prepared to deny that the teaching of cookery was of advantage to the person taught, but at the same time this scheme was a very extensive development on the original intentions of the Board. It was only on that occasion that it had been proposed to have three cookery classes. He was not going to say that to establish three schools was not the course to be followed, but it showed that the scheme was a much larger one than they at first supposed it to be. No doubt if they launched into the scheme it would necessitate three schools, and it was, to his mind, a very serious matter. He did not think it would cost less than £lOO a year considering the work, the fixtures. dm They might say that was a very small sum. He knew they had all paid in poor rates—he knew he had paid his within the last few days, and he had found them heavy enough. His farthings and pennies were not so numerous that he wished to see the rate increased even by the small propor— tion mentioned by Mr. Davies. The great difficulty, to his mind, was the operation of the new cede (Mundella's code) which required a third more teaching than the old code. He made this strtement from information he had gathered from the schools, and the question might be asked "Is it fair and prudent, and are we in a position at this time, which may be considered a crisis in the his- tory of education, to adopt this scheme, which would still mere curtail the time of the children, time which, in his opinion, they had not to spare ?" The speaker referred to the remarks of the Earl of Lathom at the opening of the Liverpool Junior Conservative Club on Wednesday, and said he wished to emphasise what Mr. Brunner had said with re- (card to the teachers. He thought it bad been a short- , sighted and almost hasty policy uct to have got the opinion

of the teachers before this time on a subject which would HOP interfere with their teaching so much. He thought the Board ought to obtain the teacher's opinion before they H" legislated on the subject • and contended that as the present Board was on the point of dissolution, the scheme ought to HOP be left for the new Board to deal with.—Father CLARKE said he should certainly vote against the motion, and ob- HOP served that the committee had asked some of the neighbour- ing towns to use the teacher's services, but he believed they 1-1013 were prudent enough to reply that they would not. He LT OP thought some of their neighbours were quite as far advanced in civilization as to adopt in their schools cooking for their op children if Widnes was. He had read in the London papers 11 during the last three or four days letters on the ' or subject of education. One was from a surgeon, who fa. narrated instances where children had died from overtaxa- IROP tion of their brain in school.—Mr. SHAW thought it was clear from what had been said that they were all satisfied la OP that it would be a great advantage to the children to learn cookery, and would also have a good moral eff .ct on their HOP future lives. But they ought to consider whether this good thing would be appreciated. Mr. Davies had told them H°P that in many towns schools of cookery were a great success. He admitted that, but the question was, Would this school, HOP or these schools be a success, and be appreciated by the children in Widnes ? No information had been tendered H.°P upon this point. Many of the gentlemen at that table took 11[ op great interest some time ago in doing what ought to increase the comforts and better the social position of many workman Hop in their employ in commencing the cocoa rooms. (Hear, hear.) They were quite sanguine then that 1 i_l" OP those rooms would be a great boon to the workingmen; that they would be the means of removing them from tempta- HOP tions which were meeting them at every turn. But the workmen had never appreciated that movement, and it had 1101) failed. There was no doubt about the fact that similar rooms had succeeded elsewhere, and had been found to be a HOP great benefit where people availed themselves of them. Therefore he thought the committee ought to get to know 11°P whether sufficient children in their schools would avail 11°P themselves of these classes if they were commenced, and whether their parents would be agreeable. He had no ob- jection to the classes. He was sure they would be a great benefit to the children, but before they entered into the ex- II OP pense, they ought to be satisfied that those for whom it was incurred would appreciate what they did. Then there was HOP another question. Did they believe that the ratepayers of Widnes were so relieved from the burdens which they had HOP been suffering under for a considerable period, that they could bear a heavier tax? He questioned if there was a HOP town in the kingdom where the ratepayers were so heavily taxed as the people of Widnes were, and he H°P did not think this an opportune time for establishing cook- op ery classes. He should be inclined to oppose the reso- lution. Mr. DEACON was on the whole in favour of the or scheme for teaching cookery. It was entirely new to him that day that there was any necessity for having three schools for la o p teaching cookery, but if the School Management Committee was thoroughly satisfied that was the cheapest way of HOP working the scheme, he thought they must take it for granted it was so. It seemed to him that it would probably be cheaper for the children to walk from one school to another, than to permit the teacher to lose time in doing so. But that was a point he should be quite content to leave to the committee. The real question was, What is the object of teaching. It seemed to him that they wanted to give the children such education and information as would probably be useful to them in after life. (Hear, hear.) Now, nothing could possibly be more useful to the to the majority of girls than teaching cookery. Subject to Mr. Brunner's reservation that the teachers be consulted, he thought the eleest thing they coald do for the children, ' was to teach them cookery, even if they sacrificed some part of the grant in some other department. He did not look upon an elemeniary school as a money gaining concern at all. The Board's work was to educate children, not make the schools pay. With regard to Mr. Shaw's question—Will cooking classes be appreciated ?—he should say that it did not matter one rap whether they were appreciated or not. Very likely they would not be appre- ciated at present; they could not expect children of 13 or 14 years to appreciate them. It would be when they were married that they would appreciate the cookery they learned at schocl. He did not think it fair to make a parallel between a cooking school and the cocoa-room movement. They could not say to men go into the cocoa-rooms, drink there, and pay your money; but they had, according to the School Management Committee, 167 children who would go to the cookery school free of any charge.—Father CLARKE : You cannot compel them to go P—Mr. DANsv ; Most certainly they can.—Father CLARKE : It is not a subject you are bound to teach.—Mr. DANRY: You are not bound to teach the extra subjects, but if the Board decide to teach them the children are bound to go.—Mr. DEACON said it s2emed to him that the Board had power to say that the children should go; and it never occurred to him that there was any question about that. He did not think Mr. Shaw's parallel held very much. On the whole, he thought it was advisable to establish cookery classes, subject to the reservation with regard to the teachers.—Mr. Mimic did not think the cost of establishing the classes a matter that they need say much about, as the cost was a very moderate one, and he was certainly of opinion that the value they expected and no doubt would receive from the expendi- ture would be well worth the money. The ratepayers of Widnes, heavily burdened as they were with taxation, would not at all mind the expenditure of £lOO in teaching cookery. A great many parents considered it to be one of the most im- portant subjects that could be taught in the schools, and had expressed themselves greatly pleased at the idea of their children learning cookery. It had been said that the children were already overworked, but Mr. Brock pointed out that a change in occupation or pursuit Was an immense re- lief and, recreation to grown-up people, and would be to children. Eel:dying to Mr. Shaw, he said they could not tell whether the classes would be appreciated until they were tried. In the cocoa-mulls they had to deal with men whose habits were formed, but in the cookery classes they had to train pliant children in a set subject, which would go very far to keep future husbands soosr in after life, because it was intimately connected with the comforts of home.—The CHAIRMAN did not think any money they could possibly spend would be more likely to be at- tended with good results, and he saw no reason why the establishment of the classes should be left to a future Board. It was an open question whether the next Board would be so competent to deal with the question, because we have had three years experience in the management of the schools. He thought it was quite time they should deal with the sub- ject. The object of the Board was not to save money, but to spend their money as usefully as they could so that it would be productive of the greatest possible good. He had no desire to press upon the ratepayers. He fully admitted that the rates were high, and had no wish to take a farthing out of their pctkets that could be well kept in, but he ' thought the ratepayers would thank them fcr the expendi- ture involved in establishing cookery classes. They should remember that their school rate was not in excess of the average for the United Kingdom. The school rate for the United Kingdom was 5 541, and that for Widnes sd. Therefore they could not be called extravagant. A change of occupation .was really relaxation. They could not have two more striking examples than the late Lord Derby and the present Prime Vinister. These two men in the midst of their great avocations found their pleasure in translating Homer, and those of them who had the misfortune or good fortune to lern Greek would know what hard work many would think that—Father CLARKE : It is much easier cutting dawn trees than translating Homer. —After a few words from Mr. Davies, the motion was put to the meeting, when there voted for it—the Chairman, Messrs. Brock, Brunner, Davies, Deacon, and Hartland-6; against—Fathers Clarke and Finnegan and Mr. Shaw-3. The motion was therefore declared carried. DR. O'KEEFFE ABSENTS HIMSELF. The CLERK reported that Dr. O'Keeffe had failed to at- tend six consecutive meetings, and, therefore, had vacated his seat according to the law. The doctor had written ex- plaining that on several occasions he had been compelled to attend Kirkdale Sessions.—The CHAIRMAN said it was com- petent for the Board to elect a new member or re-:4ect Dr. O'Keeffe. As the Board's term was near its expiration, and as Dr. O'Keeffe had given satisfactory reasons for his absence, it would be the better course to re-elect him or ap- prove of his absence. He moved that the Board approve of Dr. O'Keeffe's absence.— Mr. BROCK seconded, and the motion was carried.

ADDITIONAL ACCOMMODATION. The Sites and Building Committee made the following recommendations :—That the Board hire the Oakland-street School Chapel, for the purposes of an infant school, subject to the approval of the Edccation Department, at a yearly rental of £25, in accordance with the letter from the trus- tees, dated June 7th, 1883.—The recommendation was adopted on the motion of Mr. Bltocrc.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE AT ST. HELENS.—Between sixty and seventy parents were summoned before the St. Helens magistrates, on Monday, on account of the irregular atten- dance of their children at school, and in all but a few cases were mulcted in the usual penalty of 54. including costs.

ECCLESTON STEAM CORN MILLS.—We are imformed that Mr. John Melling, proprietor of the Steam Corn Mills, St. Helens, has, at the request of a large number of friends, decided to form a Limited Liability Company for the pur- pose of taking over and working the above-named corn mills. The prospectus will be issued in a few days.

DAMAGING VOLUNTEER PROPERTY AT ST. HELENS,—TWO lads named John McQuire and George Cotton were charged at the St. Helens Police Court on. Fri4ay with having da- maged some railings, the property of Colonel Rothwell, of the 2nd L. EN., the damage being estimated at is 6d. Both of the defendants pleaded guilty.—Sergeant-Major Burns said that considerable damage was done to the railings in question almost every Sunday by a number of lads, and these cases were brought forward to act as a warning._ Each of the lads was fined 6d damage, and 4s Od costs.— John Lamb, anotber lad, was fined in a similar amount for doing damage to a field, the property of the St. Helens Col- liery Company. PUGILISTIC ENCOPNTERS AT ST. HELENS.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, two youths, named John Marsh and William Johnson, were charged with having committed a breach of the peace at Parr.—An officer said that at nine o'clock on the night of the 12th instant, he was called out of his station by a man who said that a prize fight was going cu down the road. On going down he saw a crowd in a tie', in the centre of which were the defen- dants with their jackets off and striking at each other. His attention had been called to a fight between the same two the night btfore, and be then warned their parents.—They were each bound over to keep the pens for three months, themselvel. ja £5 and one surety in £5.

INFECTIOUS DISEASES IN PRESCOT UNION. [BY A RESIDENT.] The Guardians and local authorities of Prescot Union are in a difficult and unpleasant position. In more than one of the townships composing the Union infectious diseases of the worst type have made their appearance, and nowhere in the Union, except at the Workhouse and in St. Helens, is an 7 Provision in existence for dealing with them effectively. St. Helens has a hospital at Peasley Vale, but Widnes, the next largest township, has none, and Prescot has none. The Other townships—Rainford, Huyton, Rainhill, Woolton, and .18° "—being for the most part little more than country „."iBtrietis with separated and small populations, can hardly "Pected to provide hospitals, nor in all probability i'w,..ould the hospitals they could afford to maintain be worth ving• St. Helens, as I have stated, has a hospital, and :th°ugh at present it is conducted on principles and with I tariff which go a great way to negative its utility, no 4°414 in such an emergency as an epidemic would produce, these artificial barries would be broken down, and the public ;444' would be consulted regardless of other considerations. 'What is the position of Widnes? In 1881, when the piect teas urged upon them by the Guardians, the Local ed of that town promised as soon as they got rid of 4tner pressing business" to establish a hospital; but p etlaer they have forgotten their promise or the other ej,ese,ing business has not yet been despatched, or whatever tit's rias been operative with them, the Widnes hospital con- , tles as unsubstantial as a chateau d'espagne—an airy t-vbitxhing without name or local habitation. The reason of as ma Y not be far to seek. Perhaps it is given in a ; Ketence which occurs in the letter from Mr. Hartley to the .A..."mal Government Board, and read to the Rural Sanitary pluthority on Thursday. Discussing the difficulty expe- -I.,,enced hi discriminating between pauper and non-pauper the clerk to the Guardians says " most of the ap- Vt'eations for admission to the workhouse infectious hospital 0 Made by, or on behalf of, those who have not previously in receipt of parochial relief. The applicants in most 85, nevertheless, are destitute, and relief in the shape of order for admission into a workhouse hospital is afforded 41)" the recommendation of the district medical officers, who tVmost instances—it may be unfortunately—are also ,Ical officers of health." Unfortunately, doubtless, for ac; ; fortunately for the township. The Guardians, sto;7,4ing to law, provide a hospital for destitute fever and hot2E patients, and the difficulty of discriminating paupers and non-paupers practically lays them la, et the obligation of opening its doors to all corners. ehs,erefore the course of the medical officers of such a town- as Widnes where there is no hospital, and they are also to the medical officers of the Union, is as plain as the way Parish church. The patient at once gets an order for ejassion to the workhouse hospital, and is admitted there, the township is relieved of the cost of care and maintenance; while the Guardians the the Local Government Board are ascertaining btra Precise point at which to split the technical tl e upon the accurate division of which f:e-: Il""s the patients' status. Having so easy a method of being itself of cost, trouble, and responsibility, it is no k I,llder that Widnes finds it convenient to protract its eutlsing business to the exclusion of the hospital 'On. The case of St. Helens is only a modification of f r" et ste Wide Ie order that the pockets of the borough p, es • • *he Yers may be spared, the hospital is closed to all those hetly cannot pay about ten shillings a week for their main- thies in it. A moderate wage earner may afford to pay leoe et the support of an afflicted wife or child, and doubt- e'.l. is a blessing that he has a chance of doing so instead i4l44loved one being sent to Whiston ; but when he is ' ser,i prostrated, and consequently deprived of wage I elioang Power, what is he to do? Obviously, unless the , inti:iltY of his friends defrays his hospital expenses, he I the' fail back upon the district medical officer and go to thernrkhouse hospital under his warrant. As to Prescot, tb was some time ago an infections diseases hospital in 4t to the er yin. lam not, however, sufficiently acquainted with oitmlcurnstances under which it was provided and after- Ptes:s abandoned to offer any remarks upon it. But I th.not has seldom failed to send a fair share of patients to 6:workhouse hospital, and within the last six months it l''tontributed 30 cases. Other townships have sent their 4 tie4° na, and the result is that the hospital has been for some bot too overflowing. The significance of this fact isi the ObSetirelv hinted at in a remark made by I the clerk 'Z'f thd guardians at the meeting of lo t, Rural Sanitary Authority already referred to. tio4m,e course of his statement of the result of the depnia- that the Lend Government Board to ask the consent of it ,I,oard to the expenditure by the Guardians of £7,000 teicating ne general hospital for the Union. The de- h Eta " pointed out to the Local Government Of be ivardians would not take the responsibility ing tdmittcd to the hosnital suffetinz from one eur!tr,,c Ing another, and dying perhaps from a refer", NI, hat does this mean? It might be supposed to its eeT a future possibility ; but in some if not the whole of laet44out, it relates to accomplished facts. As a matter of ' within the last few months the hospital has been so sro°awilled that it has been impossible to separate fever from Of t), Pox cases, and persons brought in suffering from one arh,"°Be diseases have contracted the other. As to whether , tec" them have died of a third I cannot speak with cer- 1 104', but there is no need to add to the ghastliness and hotpii.,s,"leness of the picture which the facts suggest the ofol;vie image of death in order to demonstrate the urgency niete technicalities, legal subtleties, and questions of con- hs local local interests being at once set aside while compre- host;e measures are promptly taken to provide adequate ot,et' (al accommodation. In reality the question whether Nesgeneral hospital should be established at the joint ex- by ine(ls the Union,or separate hospitals shoeld be maintained tsatte Ividual townships or combination of townships is a it ie of detail which it ought not be difficult to decide,and theri,t9 be hoped that the projected conference of local i.i- arisel.Lles will speedily be held, and issue in the immediate ioration of the present very grave posture of affairs.

A meeting of " Anglo-Indians " was held in London on Monday to protest against Mr. Ilbert's Criminal Jurisdiction Bill. A resolution denouncing the proposal to place European British subjects under the criminal jurisdiction of native magistrates was passed. Judgment was given in the Court of Appeal, on Monday, in the protracted litigation which has arisen out of the visit of Madame Bernhardt to the Blackpool Winter Gardens. The company sued Madame Bernhardt's mana- ger for breach of contract, and obtained a verdict. The defendant moved for and obtained a rule absolute for a new trial. Against the issue of this rule the company appealed, but the Court gave judgment against them, and there is to be a new trial. The shareholders of the Winter Gardens Company will receive the intelligence with much interest. COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN WALES: Two MEN KILLED AND TWELVE INJURED.—A serious explosion occurred at the New Duffryn Colliery, Rhymney, late on Monday night, killing two married men named Micheel Farrell and Elias Thomas, and severely injuring twelve others'. The explo- sion produced great excitement and consternation in the im- mediate district, as there were 100 men in the pit at the time. The works are the property of the Rhymney Iron Company. The force of the explosion was terrible. The men were blown across each other twenty yards away, and huge stones were swept a great distance. The colliery is worked with naked lights. The coal is somewhat friable, and this caused a fall. The cause of the disaster was a fall " of a roof and the ignition of gas at a naked light.

Although unable to witness the ceremony, the inhabi- tants of Runcorn did not fail to show their respect for Cap.' tain Hazelhurst, whe is very popular in the town. Flags 11,ated on the Town Hall and tower of the Parish Church, and bunting was displayed from innumerable points. Cam- den's works was gay with parti-coloured emblems which flattered on every imaginable part of the establishment, and at the time fixed for the marriage to take place the workmen fi-ed cannons in quick succession, while the bells of the Parish Church merrily rang an answering peal. The roar of the cannons and the music of the bells could be heard alternately all the day through. To-day (Saturday) we understand the workmen are to partake of a substantial tea in the Public Hall, where they will afterwards have the pleasure of witnessing a miscellaneous entertainment. When Captain Hazlehurst returns from the honeymoon the volun- teers intend to hold a full dress parade, when the officers, non-commissioned officers, and men will present him with a handsome sword and a beautifully illuminated address.
