THE CORPORATION, THE TRADERS, THE WATER- WORKS CO., AND THE PROMOTERS.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee of the Warrington Corporation, on Monday, the Town Clerk re- ported that the Waterworks Company had petitioned the House of Commons against the clauses and agreement entered into between the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal and the Corporation and traders of Warrington.— The Committee accordingly passed a recommendation that the Town Clerk take all necessary steps to defend the clauses and agreement against the opposition of the Com- pany.—At the meeting of the Town Council, on Tuesday, the terms and conditions upon which the Corporation have agreed to withdraw their opposition to the Ship Canal Bill will be submitted, and no doubt agreed to, after which the Council will pass a resolution to authorize the affixing of the com- mon seal of the borough to the agreement entered into with the promoters. The heads of that agreemept were publish( d in The Examiner a month ago. In order to conciliate the opposition of the traders of the town, another agreement has been entered into between the promoters of the first part, the Corporation of Warrington of the second part, and the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited, Rylands Brothers, Limited, the Whitecross Wire, Iron, and Steel Company, Limited, the Tanner's-lane Tanning Com- pany, Limited, Monks, Hall and Company, Limited; James Fairclough and Sons, corn millers; Roberts, Dale and Com- pany, chemical manufacturers; Henry Kenyon and Com- pany, proprietors of spelter works; Winser and Company, proprietors of chemical works; and Joseph Crosfield and Sons, soap manufacturers; being firms or persons carrying , on business in or near the borough of Wairington, of the , third part. By this agreement it is provided :- 1. The company shall either provide the necessary funds to enable the Corporation to divert the sewage of Warring- ton, which is now discharged into the river Mersey above the proposed lock and sluices at Bank Quay, mentioned in the said clause, and for that purpose to provide and construct a new outfall sewer or sewers with proper connections with the town sewers, such outfall sewer to be carried to, and its contents discharged into, the river, at some point below the said lock and sluices, to be approved by the Borough Sur- veyor or the engineer of the Corporation, and in the event of the river at or below such point becoming silted up, or otherwise becoming useless for the purposes of the said sewage discharge; and shall provide the necessary funds to enable the Corporation to provide another outfall for such sewage, as suitable and effectual as that at present existing or the company may apply to Parliament for, and if so shall use thaJAeary poweisw eublt!ii.rn to execute and do the tore4oing works and thin _.;o instead of the Corporation, and if they obtain such now ere, shall themselves, at their own expanse, execute and do the same accordingly. The said outfall sewer or sewers so to be constructed shall, if constructed by the company, be completed three months at least before the completion of the said proposed lock and sluices at Bank Quay ; or if the same are to be constructed by the Cor- poration, the necessiry ifuLds therefore shall•be provided by the company six months at least before the completion of the said proposed lock and sluices at Bank Quay.
THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

THE WARRINGTON WATERWORKS CASE. The evidence on behalf of the London and North- Western Railway Company was continued on Monday, before the Ship Canal Committee. Mr. Stephenson, the chief engineer, said be had examined the promoters' esti- mates, and in his opinion they were far too low. He fixed the total cost of the undertaking at £10,500,000, against £6,300,000 given in the bill. Other points in the estimates were unfavourably criticised by Mr. Rendel, the Tees dock engineer, and Mr. Barry, engineer to the Metropolitan District Railway. At the conclusion of this evidence, Mr. O'Hara interposing, with the consent of Mr. Pope, asked permission to address a few words to the Committee upon a new case which had arisen. The Corporation of Warrington, be stated, had petitioned against the bill, as had certain other persons who got water from the Mersey, but luring the progress of the incieiry a negotiation had been going on between them and the promoters of the bill. The result of that negotiation had been embodied in an agree- ment, the terms of which it had been arranged should, if possible, be scheduled to the bill if it became an Act The Warrington Water Company, for whom he appeared, on reading the terms of that agreement found themselves re- luctantly—for they had no wish to in interpose in the pro- ceedings—obliged to offer opposition to the insertion of that agreement in the bill. They had no objection to the canal so far as the Company were concerned, but conceived that this agreement would injure their interests, and they objected to their rights being interfered with inci- dentally in the progress of a case like this by an agreement such as this. That agreement was only arrived at last week or at the end of the previous week; the Company held a Board meeting, and presented a petition to Parliament, as they had power to do, against the bill. They had, of course, been deprived of all the advantage of cross-examination of witnesses, but of that they did not and could not complain. All they asked, him. was that before the Committee decided en the preamble they wow(' allow um. witnesses, in order to show how the conditions which it was sought to make a statutory agreement would prejudice the Company in the exercise of their rights as a water-supplying company. Those conditions, if sanctioned, would give power to the people who were to be authorised to keep in the canal to become a rival water company in Warrington, and , while not objecting to the bill, they desired to present their case against this agreement. The conditions contained in the agreement were the conditions upon which the Warring- ton Corporation had withdrawn their opposition to the bill. The Chairman said this seemed to him to ha a matter, not for the preamble, but for clauses. Mr. O'Hara submitted that that was hardly the case. The question to be decided was whether this canal should be made or not, and whether the bill should be passed or not. Incidentally to the making of the canal, and previous to the water of the Mersey entering the canal between Run- corn and a certain place, the Corporation of Warrington were to receive—or rather the Canal Company were to de- liver-7,000,000 gallons of water per day to the towa. That was a condition precedent to the utilisation of the canal imposed upon the Canal Company, and if the committee passed the bill subject to that which the Water Company said ought not to be allowed, they would do the company an injustice and establish a rival water company. If they were to.allow this agreement to be scheduled to the bill, and the bill were passed into law, they would not be heard by any committee. Mr. Michael said this was a matter which did not in any way appear in the preamble, but when the preamble came up his learned friend would be entitled to object to any such clause in the bill. Mr. O'Hara replied that as a condition of the preamble being passed this agreement would be agreed to, but the Company asked the Committee not to insert this agreement as a condition to passing the preamble. The Corporation had opposed the preamble of the bill, and the condition of their withdrawing their opposition was that an agreement should be scheduled to the bill. The Chairman said the Committee were in no way partio to that agreement. Mr. O'Hara replied that the promoters and the opponents had agreed to ask the Committee to put the agreement into the bill. If the Water Company were not here, the Com- mittee would most probably do se, but the Committee were asked not only to do that, but to confirm the agreement, for the words were " prior to the admission of water from the River Mersey, from Runcorn into the proposed tidal cat between Runcorn and the Lock at Walton, the Company shall obtain all necessary powers" to do a certain thing. The Chairman : There may be a dozen agreements of that kind in the bill, of which we are not cognisant. Mr. O'Hara contended that if the Committee were to sanction the bill, they must cover everything connected with it. The Chairman : If that agreement goes into the bill, yo.r clients can say they are damnified by it. Your objec- tion does not touch the preamble at all. It is an objection not to the preamble but only to the schedule. Mr. O'Hara replied that what he wanted was that the Committee should not decide upon the preamble until they had decided upon the objection of the Water Company to this agreement. Mr. Michael asked Mr. O'Hara to show any words which would damnify him. Mr. O'Hara said the question was not the technical read- ing of the preamble, but whether the agreement should be allowed to go in. The room was then cleared, and the Committee having consulted for a few minutes, the Chairman announced that the Committee were of opinion that this was a question for clauses and not for the preamble. The Committee then adjourned until Thursday as pre- viously arranged. After a brief interruption the Manchester Ship Canal Committee resumed its sittings on Thur day at Westminster, when the London and North—Western Railway Company's hostile evidence was continued. Sir J. Bailey was informed by counsel that the Company could not finish its case before this afternoon, and as other railway and public interests have yet to be heard, the anticipation once indulged in that this week would see the end of the inquiry appears to have been a great deal too sanguine. The North-Western Com— pany's opposition is mainly in reference to proposed devia— tions of lines near Warrington and the increase of gradients which a high—level bridge would necessitate.—Mr. Findlay, the general manager, stated that to increase the gradients at Warrington, where the line was now practically level and bore an enormous traffic, to 1 in 114, as suggested, would cripple the carrying capacity of that section by 30 per cent.

2. Prior to the admission of water from the river Mersey at Runcorn into the proposed tidal cut between Runcorn and the lock to be constructed by the company at Walton, the company shall obtain all necessary powers to enable them at any time after the admission of the said tidal water into the said tidal cut, to supply for the use of the manu- facturers and traders, from the river Mersey, water as free from chlorides and otherwise as suitable for the business purposes of the manufacturers and traders as that .now ob- tained by them from the said river' in quantity up to, but' not exceeding, 7,000,000 gallons per diem. In the event of the water in the river Mersey at or near Bank Quay being prejudicially affected for the business purposes of the manu- facturers and traders by any of the works of the company, the company shall, within four months after the receipt of a written notice from any of the manufacturers and traders, who shall together use at least one-half of the water for the time being taken from the river Mersey by the whole of the manufacturers and traders for business purposes, requiring them so to do deliver such quantity of water as free from chlorides and otherwise as suitable for the business purposes of the manufacturers and traders as that now obtained from the said river as shall from time to time be required by the manufacturers and traders for their business purposes up to but not exceeding seven million gallons, and such quantity of water shall be delivered by the company at their own expense for the use of the manufacturers and traders at such point near Bank Quay as shall be approved of by the Borough Surveyor or engineer,and with such necessary con- nections or otherwise as shall in his opinion be requisite for the convenient pumping of the same by the manufacturers and traders now using the water of the said river 3 Prior to the admission of water from the river Mersey at Runcorn into the proposed tidal cut between Runcorn and the lock to be constructed by the company at Walton, such analyses shall be made at the cost of the company by such chemist of such samples of water to be taken from the said river at such point, at such times, and under such cir- cumstances as may be agreed on between the engineer of the company and an engieeer to be appointed by theXor- poration, and in case of difference between such engineers, then as shall be determined by an engineer to be nominated on the application of either of those engineers by the pre- sident for the time being of the Institution of Civil Engi- neers, and the result so obtained shall be deemed, and is herein referred to, as "the standard analysis," and shall be the standard of quality in any question hereafter arising lse- tween the company and the manufacturers and traders as to the water in the river Mersey being so prejudicially affected as aforesaid. A copy of the standard analysis shall be given to the company, and also to the town clerk of Warrington, and a third copy shall be deposited with the Clerk of the Peace for the county of Lancaster, and shall be kept by him pith and as a part of the deposited plans. 4. In case of any such notice being given, the burden of proof that the water in the river Mersey has not been so prejudicially affected shall be on the company. • 5. Upon the failure of the company to provide such supply of Water, as aforesaid, for the use of the manufac- turers and traders at the time and in manner aforesaid, the company shall fully compensate the manufacturers and traders for any injury from time to time sustained by them, or any of them, by or in consequence of any such default, or during the period interveniug between the service of the said notice and the time of affording such substituted supply. 6. If any difference shall arise between the company and any of the parties to this agreement as to the rights, duties, or liabilities of any party under this agreement, such differ- ence shall, if not otherwise agreed, be determined by an engineer to be appointed as arbitrator by the president for the time being of the Institution of Civil Engineers on the application of any such parties, and the decision of any such arbitrator shall be binding and conclusive, and the cost of the arbitration shall be in his discretion. 7. The company shall if necessary make application to Parliament in a future session for any further powers that may be necessary to enable them to peform this agreement, and the Corporation and the manufacturers and traders will support such application. 8. The Corporation will, at the expense of the company, give all reasonable facilities in their power to enable the company to carry this agreement into effect. 9.—Upon the execution by tbe promoters of this agree- ment, and upon the insertion by then in the Bill of the laid clause, the Corporation and the manufacturers and traders who petitioned as aforesaid shall cease to appear upon their petitions, and shall not, either directly or indirectly, in either Rouse of Parliament, oppose, or sanction, or support any op- position to the passing of the Bill, or any amended or varied form thereof, provided that any amendment or variation shall not be at variance with the said clause or with this
YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
HOUSE OF COMMONS, Friday.

This morning, Mr. G. FINDLAY, general manager of the London and North-Western Railway Company, was further examined on behalf of the case of his company in opposi- tion to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. On the question of the possibility of bringing South Yorkshire coal by the pro- posed canal, so as to compete on the Mersey with South Wales and Lancashire coal, he said it would not be possible to bring coal from South Yorkshire to the Mersey for less than 4s. per ton, against is. lid, as the rate from Wigan, and Is. 9d. from St. Helens. As to the steam coal from South Wales, the Baynsley steam coal would not be able to compete with it, because it was 25 per cent. dearer. On the question of the interference with the working of the traffic
agreement; but if any such amendment or variation is pro- posed in either House, then the Corporation and the manu- facturers and traders shall be entitled to take all necessary
measures for opposing such amendment or variation, in so far as it is prejudicial to their rights and interests, as aforesaid.

• 10. Within three calendar months after the Royal Assent shall have been given to the Bill, the promoters shall pro- cure the company to affix the seal of the company to this agreement, and to adopt the same, and thereafter this agree- ment shall be read, construed, and take effect as if the com- pany were a party thereto of the first part instead of the promoters. The company shall not cpmmence their works until they have sealed and adopted this agreement, and I until the company have so sealed and adopted this agree- ment, the promoters shall be jointly and severally responsible ito the second and third parties hereto for the due perfor- mance and observance of this agreement, and be liable in \damages for every or any breach, non-observance, and non- performance thereof respectively. 11. This agreement is made subject to the sanction of Parliament, and shall be scheduled to and confirmed by the , I Bill.
12. All the stipulations hereinbefore contained are to be considered as conditional on the said Bill (with or with out amendment) receiving the Royal Assent in the present Ses- sion of Parliament.

- The Standard hears that the promoters of the Man- chester Ship Canal are very sanguine that they will suc- ceed. That their bill will pass appears to be certain, and they are confident that the necessary capital will be found. The new standing order of the House of Commons which per- mits Acts to pass empowering the promoters of new under- takings of this class to pay interest out of capital-mill, if it is confirmed by the House of Lords, no doubt materially help the Manchester people in this respect, and the local feelirg against the railway monopolies is so strong that many people will subscribe moderate amounts without much regard to direct returns for the money invested.

div.head: DISTURBING THE SALVATION ARMY.
div.p: DISTURBING THE SALVATION ARMY.

Wm. Locke, a respectable-looking young man, described as a stonemason, and residing at 34, Wellington-street, was charged at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with having been drunk and disorderly at the Slivation Army Barracks at ten minutes past eight o'clock on Saturday night; and also with having done damage to the amount of ss. to his cell door on Sunday morning.—Prisoner pleaded guilty to the first charge, but not guilty to the second.— P.C. 16 said that at the time stated he was called into the Sal- vation Army Barracks, and found prisoner there creating a disturbance. He had his hat on, and in answer to his (wit- ness's) requests to leave the building, he said he would not go out for a-- man like him. He had then to put him out by force, and to bring him to the police station.—A member of the Army said prisoner began to create a disturb- ance, and he told him that if he did not conduct himself in a proper manner he should call in a policeman. Prisoner said that before a policeman should be called in he would go out. On going towards the door he said "If you want anything come outside, and I will fight you." As he continued the disturbance witness had to send for a policeman.—P.C. 12 (Jones) said that during Saturday night prisoner was very disorderly, and tried to get out of his cell. He broke the iron produced off the door.— Prisoner denied this, but admitted he was "tight."—The Chief Constable: Yes; that was tight, but you loosened it. This was the -first man who had been brought up for dis- turbing the Salvation Army at Warrington, and he felt it his duty to ask the Bench to deal somewhat severely with persons who were brought up for going to the Army drunk and conducting themselves there in a disorderly manner. The police had exercised great patience in the matter. After prisoner was brought out of the Barracks he had an oppor- tunity of going home quietly, but he would not do so, and he had to be locked up.—Alderman Pickmere : I am sur- prised to see a man like you here.—Prisoner : I am very sorry for it. It is the first time, and it shall be the last.— Alderman Pickmere said it was his opinion that if anyone went to the Salvation Army Barracks and created a disturb- ance, it was as bad as going to any ether place of worship and creating a disturbance. Prisoner would be fined 20s and costs for being drunk and disorderly, and would have to pay ss, the amount of damage to the cell door, or, in de- fault, go to prison for five weeks.

div.head: PROSECUTION YESTERDAY.
div.p: PROSECUTION YESTERDAY.

William Jolley, jun., a young man, residing in Challoner- street, was summoned at Warrington Borough Court, yester- day, for having on the 17th inst. been guilty of riotous and disorderly behaviour at a certain place used for religious worship duly certified under the provisions of the statute of the Act of Parliament, called the Salvation Army Barracks. —Defendant pleaded not guilty. Lieut. Frances Cannon said on Sunday, the 17th inst., at three o'clock, after an open door service, they entered the Salvation Army Barracks. When they got in she was informed they were likely to have a rough meeting because several of the rough class had got in the building. The man who told her there was one par- ticular man present who was likely to cause a disturbance aiked her if she would have the man put oat. She said "No, we will not have the man put out. We will see if we can deal with him without putting him out." She got on the platform and reminded the congregation, as they had to do some- times at the meetings, that there were notices u„ „,.., r. _ hl i wnrghin and that people were not to leave the Barracks except when they sang. This they did frequently—every five or ten minutes—so that people could come in or go out, as they did not let persons go out when they spoke, read, or prayed. During the whole of the afternoon defendant repeatedly shouted out such words as "ticket," and others she cauld not catch, and his behaviour was disgraceful, so much so that respectable people got up and walked out of the Barracks. Repeated warnings were given, but things got to such a pitch that they were compelled to call in an officer to turn defend int out. When the officer came in, about half-past four, she said to him "1 give this man into custody;" and then defendant created a dreadful disturb- ance in the hall. She was sure his behaviour to her as a woman, and to the treasurer of the corps, was perfectly dis- graceful. She never in her life received similar treatment front a young man. She believed defendant had had drink, but he was quite capable of conducting himself pro- perly.—James Dickinson, a private in the Salvation Army, said he asked the defendant to keep quiet, but he came out with several oaths. He again asked defendant to keep quiet, but defendant cursed him. He then sat beside the defen- dant to keep him quiet, and defendant told him he would give him a "wringing" when:he got him outside. Defendant shouted out "ticket," and thus disturbed the meeting.— Frank Aspinall said: On the 17th inst. he was assisting to conduct the service at the Salvation Army. Several dis- turbances occurred, and daring the meeting he hoard the word" ticket" shouted out, which caused the people to turn round to see whence the disturbance came. The lieutenant asked who made the noise, and he went to see who had caused it. The previous witness pointed to defendant, and he (witness) told him he had no right to make a noise, and he had better be careful or he would get himself into trouble. They then sang, and a man wanted to go out, bat they told him to sit down by Jolley in the seat vacated by Dickenson. Jolley then got his elbow in the man's ribs, and said if the man did not go outside he would push him out, and continually used bad language. A man afterwards sat between them and defendant gave vent to a hideous " scrike," and they called in a police officer.—The Deputy Mayor: Did he say he wanted to go out ?—He never mentioned a word, sir.—Supposing he wanted to go out, could he have gone out ? Yes during the singing.—But dgring the speaking? We should not let them out then as it Interrupts the proceedings. Was the door locked? No. —Was any one in charge? Yes, two persons ; one inside and one out.—George Samuelson also gave evidence in sup- port of the summons.—Defendant then stated that the "young woman" told the congregation that on Sunday afternoons yang men came to the barracks to mock them, and he simply said " Hear, hear." Robert Fairbrother, wire worker, called by defendant, stated that Jolley did not interrupt the service. He heard another man shout "chicken," nut did not hear anyone shout "ticket."—P.C. Pace said he was called to the -Bar- racks, but he did not hear defendant say anything except "Hear, hear." Mr. Aspinall and three or fonr others• had the defendant by the collar when he was called in, and there was uproar in the building. The people were all standing. He got defendant's name, and then asked them to open the door and let him out. Defendant said if they had done that before there would not have been a disturbance ; he wanted to go out, and they would not let him.—P.C. Neill also spoke of the commotion at the Barracks when he got there, and said when Jolley got outside he ran along Academy-street very quickly. Major Cartwright said there was no doubt defendant bad misconducted himself, and a young man like defendant ought to know better than that. People must be taught that they must conduct themselves properly when they go into the Barracks of the Salvation Army. He found the penalty was very heavy—Ls, or not exceeding two months' im- prisonment. They were not going to punish the defendant to that extent, but as a warning to others they must punish him. They had come to the conclusion to fine him what he considered was a very small amount indeed-10s. and costs (total £1 25.). or in default, 14 days' imprisonment, and the magistrates hoped it would be a warning to defen- dant and others for the future.—Defendant paid the money.

A PRODIGAL'S RETURN AT ST. HELENS.—The eccentric conduct of a man named James Bibby, who resides with his widowed mother and brother at 58, Grant-stregt, St. Helens, has during the past week caused those persons in- terested in his welfare to feel considerable anxiety on his behalf. Mr. Bibby, it seems, like many other people, is in the habit of taking a walk on Sunday mornings, the green lanes around Denton's Green being the favourite scene of his peregrinations. On Sunday morning, at the early hour of seven o'clock, he left his home, apparently for his accus- tomed stroll, but did not return either on that day or the next. His relatives naturally felt much alarmed at this, and although they were not aware of his suffering under any of those evils such as the pangs of despised love or the law's delay, which are said to lead men to think of making away with themselves, they had a pool of water near Denton's Green-lane searched on Tuesday, without however finding his body. All fears, however, were happily dispel- led early on Wednesday morning by the missing man him- self walking into his home. The only reason he vouchsafed for his strange absence was that ho had been in the direc- tion of Liverpool and got "lost" Those who are not satis- fied with this somewhat vogue explanation generally set the occurrence down tu The disturbing influences of the holidays.

div.head: WARRINGTON NEWS.
div.p: WARRINGTON NEWS.

KEEPING A DOG WITHOUT A LICENSE.—Thomas Howell, Battersby-lace, was charged, on Monday, at Warrington Police Court, with keeping a dog without a license,—The case was proved by Mr. Costello, an officer of the Excise, and defendant's wife said that owing to moving about a great deal lately they had forgotten the proper date on which the license ought to have been taken out, and thought it was some time in August. The dog had now been de- stroved.—Defendant was ordered to pay 12s. 6d. and costs. MESSRS. ItyLiams' TRIF TO BLACKPOOL—The annual excursion of the employes of Messrs. Rylands Bros. will this year be to Blackpool. This watering place seems each year to become more popular, and is a capital town for a flying visit, possessing as it does such varied attractions. Blackpool has good boating and bathing, splendid piers, charming winter and other gardens, aquarium, and menagerie, and is within easy distance of other watering places rapidly rising in public favour. Tile trip will take place on Monday next, and arrangements have been made by which the excarsionists can visit the several pleasure resorts at reduced rates.

A FIGHT BETWEEN Guns. At Warrington Police Court, on Monday, Bridget McDonough, Cropper's Brow, and Celia Ward, of the same place, each 17 years of age, were charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in St. James-street, on Sunday night, the 17th Inst.—P.S. Spinks said that about 11 o'clock, on the night in question, he received intimation that defendants were _

fighting in St. James-street. He went to the place and found McDonough in a fit with a large lump over the eye. ' An hour elapsed before she recovered from the fit. He afterwards charged the girls with fighting, and they both admitted it.—Each defendant was ordered to pay the costs and to be bound over to keep the peace. ANOTHER ASSAULT BY A BEGGAR.—William Allen, last from Wigan, was on Monday charged at Warrington Police Court with being drunk and assaulting Hannah Ward, a married woman, on Saturday night.—P C. 33 (Smith) said that on Saturday night Hannah Ward complained to him that prisoner had assaulted her. He followed him down Bridge-street, and saw him go to some women who were sitting on some steps and insult them —Hannah Ward said
that on Saturday night she stood at the end of her yard when prisoner and another man came to her. Prisoner

asked her for some money. She refused, and he then got hold of her in an indecent manner. She told him to keep his hands off her, when he got hold of her by the throat and was about to strike her, but he was prevented from doing so.—Prisoner was fined 103. and costs for the assault, and 10s. and costs for being drunk, or, in default, one month's imprisonment. MAKING FALSE DECLARATIONS AT WARRINGTON.—At Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Joseph Bradburv, pig dealer, Wilderspool-causeway, Latchford, was charged with having, on the 3rd May, made five declarations which were false in certain material particulars, in order to obtain licenses to remove pigs from Latchford to Crowley, Preston- on-the-Hill, and Hatton.—Mr. Thurnam appeared for the defendant, and pleaded guilty. He mentioned the particu- lars of the case which came up at the previous Petty Sessions, in which the defendant was charged with a similar offence, and submitted that defendant had already under- gone substantial punishment for the mis-statements which he certainly acknowledged having made: but assuming— and he believed it to be correct—that no licenses were needed in the cases in which he applied for them, then no infringe- ment of the law could result from those mis-statements.— Inspector Williamson said licenses were required in these cases, as the pigs were sold in the market.—Defendant was fined 15s. and costs in each of the five cases. ASSAULTING A WIFE. JUDICIAL SEPARATION. On Monday, at Warrington Police Court, Joseph Ellis, plas- terers' labourer, 12, Buckley-street, was charged with having, en the 22nd instant, assaulted his wife Letitia.— Complainant stated that on Walking Day she was watching her children in the procession, when her husband came to her, assaulted her and nearly tore all her clothes off her back. She was ashamed to stay in the streets, and she went home. After she had been there a -short time her husband came in, got hold of her by the throat, dragged her about, and was about to " punch " her when a police-constable she had sent for came in. Her husband "was murdering her by inches every week." She had had him before the Bench three times, and though he had been bound over to keep the trace he had broken his bond, but she had been "soft "with him. However, she could not live with him any longer, and she asked for a judicial separation.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for one month with hard labour ; and the Bench granted a judicial separation, and ordered the husband to contribute 83. per week towards the maintenance of his wife and family. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WARRINGTON. Charles Maguire, a decrepit-looking old man, described as a chair- maker, of Church-street, was charged at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with having attempted to commit suicide by drowning in the river Mersey, on Saturday.— P.C. Hollingworth said that he and P.C. Taylor were going along Mersev-street on Saturday evening, when they noticed a crowd and defendant in the midst of it apparently drunk. He was "dripping " wet, and two men said they had just got him out of the river. He was brought to the Police Station, and provided with another suit of clothes—Pri- soner, who is nearly blind, said the reason he had acted as he did was that his wife "plagued him jest a little bit." She had not behaved kindly to him for the last year or two. —Tlse njfe \vete crlled. and she said she had been married to detenuatit 16 years. tor the last three years he had heel' under the doctor's care, and sometimes he did not know what he was doing or saying. He had bad sight, and she I did not think he went into the river intentionally. She tried to make him as comfortable at home as she could.—Defen- dant was discharged on his wife and danghter promising to look well after him. ASSAULTING A Sua-coNTRAcToR.—John Waldron, forge labourer, residing at 42, Dallam-lane, was, on Monday, charged at Warrington Police Court with having, on S itur- day, assaulted Richard Smith, and done wilful damage to his hat to the amount of 63.—Complainant said he was a sub-contractor at the Bewsey forge, and on the Thursday before Walking Day defendant, who was under his super- vision, went home, leaving a portion of his work undone. He went to where defendant ',Aged cad told him that if the work were not done he should dismiss him. The work was not done, and on Saturday morning defendant came to the works and began to wheel a barrow, although he told him that he should not do any more work. Complainant went to him to take away the barrow, but defendant struck him a violent blow on the head and knocked him to the ground, his head coming in contact with the metal, but he was saved from any serious injury by his hat, which was very much dainaged.—Defendant said that complainant had no right to discharge him without giving him proper notice. The work whicS he was doing was the work he ought to do, and although he was under complainant, orders he had re— ceived from him had been countermanded by the master contractor many times. While he was between the barrow shafts complainant knocked him down, and he was provoked to do what he did.—A fine of 103. and costs was imposed for the assault, and defendant was ordered to pay for the damage done to the hat, or go to prison for three weeks. A REFRACTORY TRAMP SENT To GAOL. Charles Hawthorne, painter,, of no settled residence, was charged at Warrington Borough Court. on Tuesday, before Major Cartwright, with having, while a casual inmate of the vagrant wards of the Warrington Union, refused to perform the task of work set him by the master, on Monday.—Mr. ' Curry, porter, stated that on Monday morning the prisoner was placed in one of the cells to break stones' but he did nothing. He had his dinner and then refuaed to go back to his cell again. A man Came and told him the prisoner would not go back, and witness told him he must and plashed him with a rake he had in his hand. He, however, had to take the prisoner to the master, and he distinctly heard him tell the master he would not do the work. The prisoner entered the ward on Sunday night, and in the ordinary course would have left it that day.—Major Cart- wright: If he had done his task that morning would he have been released ?—Mr. Curry: No. He would have finished this morning. He must stay in two nights and a day.—Councillor Monks asked why the men were detained. —Major Cartwright said it was the law under the New Vagrancy Act, and the tramps did not like it.—Councillor Monks asked the prisoner why he did not break the, stones.. —The prisoner said he had never broken stones in his life. He tried his best but could not break them. He sent for the porter and asked him to give him another occupation. He was a painter.—Mr. Curry said the prisoner entered. himself as a labourer. If they had known he was a punter they would have put him to work on the house at his trade. —The prisoner was committed for 14 days' hard labour.

ALLEGED OUTRAGE ON AN IMBECILE.—Two young men named William Shaw, wire rope maker, 24, Brick-streetoud James Forsyth, moulder, 27, Hamilton street, were charged On Monday, at Warrington Police Court, with having, on Saturday, the 23rd inst., criminally assaulted Mary Ellen Parkin, a girl of weak intellect.—From the statement oft the Chief-Constable it appeared that prosecutria had formerly worked at Florence Mill as a factory hand, but about 12 months ago she received such a shock to the system.through an accident there that she had been of weak intellect ever since. Her father is a fitter at the Cheshire Lines new wag- gon works, and resides at 50, Orford-lane. On Saturday night prosecntrix came to market, and when passing Market- gate was accosted by the two prisoners, one of whom asked her for a finwer she had in her breast. She did not give them the flower, and refused to have a walk with them. One of them then said "Why, you look drunk." It seems that they then went clown Bold-street, along Wilson Patten-street, over the railway crossing at Slutcher's-lane and tanrards the Three Arches. When tbay had passed the Time Arches a short distance Shaw put his arms round prosecutria and kissed her, and then it is- alleged the prisoners committed the offence complained of. On arriving home prosecutrix told her sister what had taken place, but the parents were • not apprised of it until the following day.---P.C. Neill de- posed to apprehending the prisoners. When be brought • Shaw to the police station be said, "What do you want me for, I was in Manchester yesterday." Prosecutria was at •the police station, and she identified him, as being one of the two men who assaulted her,. Prisoner ultimately admitted that he had been with the prosecutrix in Arpley, and said that Forsyth was, with him. When witness apprehended Forsyth the latter denied knowing anything about the other prisoner, but he subsequently said, "I suppose it's about that girl lasl night; I wish I had never seen him"—mean- ing Shaw.—The plaoe where the offence was said to have been committed being outside the borough, the prisoners were remanded to the county police.—On Wednesday the prisoners were brought before Mr. Peter Stubs. at a special sessions, held at the Police Court, and Mr. Moore appeared for the defence. After the evidence had been given they were formally committed to the sessions to tri4l,

Tontratto. vivo SEWER CONTRACTORS.—The WIDNES LOCAL A. BOARD is prepared to receive TENDERS for the CON- STRUCTION of a MAIN SEWER, comprising about 750 yards of 6ft. tin, by 4ft. Oin., and 450 yards of 4ft. 61n. by 31t. Oin. brick sewer, extending from the Little Briton to Simm's Cross, Widnes. The plans may be seen at the Local Board Offices, Alforde-street, Widnes, after the 30th day (1 June, 1883. Copies of the specification, schedule of prices, and form of tender may be obtained upon payment of three guineas, in each case, to the ' undersigned, which will be returned upon receipt of a bona-fide tender, accompanied by the specification, schedule of prices, and the receipt given for the three guineas deposited. Sealed tenders. endorsed "Tender for construction of sewer, contract No 2," must be addressed to the Chairman of the Sewerage Committee, and be delivered at the Local Board Offices, Widnes, not later than 12 o'clock noon, on Wednesday, the first day of August, 1883. Tenders will not be accepted unless made out on the form above-named, with all the items in the schedule of prices, fully priced and moneyed out. The person whose tender is accepted will have to provide two responsible sureties, and be required to enter into a contract which will be prepared by a solicitor appointed by the Board. The Widnes Local Board does not bind itself to accept the lowest or any tender, or to defray any expenses incurreel in furnishing such tenders.—By order of the Board. JAB. T. ALLEN, Clerk.
